children.top_down_role: Single-operator, sum, composite-sum, and parallel-sum zero models.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(C:G\rightrightarrows G\) are monotone operators.
\(L:H\to G\) is bounded and linear in the composite model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) solves the selected model exactly when \(x\in\operatorname{zer}M:=\{u:0\in Mu\}\) for its displayed operator \(M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(C:G\rightrightarrows G\) be monotone operators, and let \(L:H\to G\) be bounded linear. The single-operator, additive, composite-sum, and parallel-sum models are, respectively, \[0\in Ax,\qquad 0\in Ax+Bx,\qquad 0\in Ax+L^{*}C(Lx),\qquad 0\in (A\mathbin{\square}B)x,\] where \(A\mathbin{\square}B=(A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\). Each model asks for an element of the zero set of the displayed set-valued operator; maximal monotonicity is an additional regularity hypothesis used to obtain everywhere-defined resolvents, not part of the zero-problem definition itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monotone zero problems seek a point where a single operator, operator sum, linearly composed sum, or parallel sum contains zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Zero Problems

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero and Zero Set of an Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational notation used to formulate single-operator monotone zero problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an operator \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\), a point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a zero of \(T\) if \(0\in Tx\). The zero set is
\[
\operatorname{Zer}T=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid 0\in Tx\}=T^{-1}(0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is a zero of an operator when its image contains zero. The zero set consists of all such points and equals the inverse image of zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Zer}T=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid 0\in Tx\}=T^{-1}(0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero set of a maximal monotone operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies zeros with resolvent fixed points and establishes closedness and convexity in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be maximal monotone and let \(J_{\mathbb A}=(I+\mathbb A)^{-1}\). Then \(\operatorname{Zer}\mathbb A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\mathbb A}\), and this set is closed and convex. In the stated argument, maximality supplies \(\operatorname{dom}J_{\mathbb A}=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a maximal monotone operator on Euclidean space, the zeros are exactly the fixed points of its resolvent, and this set is closed and convex. Maximality is used in this argument to ensure that the resolvent is defined on the whole space.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\text{ is maximal monotone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Zer}\mathbb A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\mathbb A}\text{ is a closed convex subset of }\mathbb R^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone inclusion problem and convex minimization representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a single-operator monotone zero problem and gives convex minimization as its subdifferential specialization; maximal monotonicity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a monotone set-valued operator \(\mathbb A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), the monotone inclusion problem is to find \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(0\in\mathbb A x\). If \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex, then \(x\) minimizes \(f\) if and only if \(0\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone inclusion problem seeks a point x whose image under a monotone set-valued operator contains zero. As a specialization, a point minimizes a proper convex function exactly when zero belongs to its convex subdifferential there.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex for the minimization specialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{find}\ x\in\mathbb R^n\text{ such that }0\in\mathbb A x;\qquad x\in\operatorname*{argmin} f\iff 0\in\partial f(x).\)

children.title: Fixed-Point Encodings
children.top_down_role: Solution and auxiliary-variable fixed-point representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent and auxiliary-variable encodings of monotone inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(\gamma>0\), define its resolvent by \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\). Then \[0\in Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\gamma A}x.\] More generally, an auxiliary-variable encoding of a problem with solution set \(S\subseteq H\) consists of a map \(T:Z\to Z\) and a recovery map \(P:Z\to H\) satisfying \[P(\operatorname{Fix}T)=S.\] Thus fixed points may be solutions themselves or auxiliary points from which solutions are recovered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero inclusion is a resolvent fixed-point problem; more general splittings may use auxiliary fixed points whose images are precisely the solutions.
assumptions_latex: The auxiliary encoding uses a specified recovery map \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}\), and a valid auxiliary encoding satisfies \(P(\operatorname{Fix}T)=S\).

notation.meaning: resolvent of the scaled operator gamma A
set of fixed points of T

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g_i:G_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, let \(h:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable, and let \(L_i:H\to G_i\) be bounded linear. Suppose there exists \(u_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that every \(g_i\) is continuous at \(L_i u_0\). Then \[x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in H}\left(f(u)+h(u)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_i(L_i u)\right)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial f(x)+\nabla h(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}L_i^{*}\partial g_i(L_i x).\] This inclusion exposes proximal, explicit-gradient, and linear-composition components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated continuity qualification, a convex composite minimizer is encoded exactly by a zero inclusion combining subgradients, a smooth gradient, and adjoint-composed subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Minimization Encodings

children.title: Variational-Inequality Encodings
children.top_down_role: Constrained monotone-field models represented by operator sums.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F:H\to H\) is single-valued; monotonicity is required only for the monotone-model classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) solves the variational inequality if and only if \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal-cone operator of C, empty outside C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space variational inequalities encoded by normal-cone sums.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.1 Examples of Variational Inequality Problems p. 264
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:H\to H\). The variational inequality is to find \(x\in C\) such that \[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\] Define the convex-analytic normal cone by \[N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}\] when \(x\in C\), and by \(N_C(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise. The variational inequality is exactly \[0\in F(x)+N_C(x).\] If \(F\) is monotone, this is a monotone operator-sum zero problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inequality over a closed convex set is equivalent to a zero of the field plus the set's normal-cone operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Encodings

children.title: Product-Space Liftings
children.top_down_role: Block variables, consensus subspaces, and lifted inclusions exposing separability.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal product-space reformulation of finite monotone sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), equip \(H^m\) with its product inner product, and define \(\boldsymbol A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=A_1x_1\times\cdots\times A_mx_m\). Let \(D=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in H\}\). Then \[0\in\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \boldsymbol x=(x,\ldots,x)\in D\ \text{ and }\ 0\in\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol x+N_D\boldsymbol x.\] The lifted operator is block separable, while the normal cone enforces consensus among the block variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite operator sum can be lifted to separable block operators plus a normal cone enforcing equality of all block variables.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m\geq2\).
\(H^m\) carries the unweighted product inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{zer}\sum_iA_i\) exactly when its diagonal lift belongs to \(\operatorname{zer}(\boldsymbol A+N_D)\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of the component operators
diagonal consensus subspace of the product space
normal-cone operator of the consensus subspace

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic-Regularity Criterion for Strong Convergence of a Linear Nonexpansive Orbit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between convergence to the fixed-point-space projection and vanishing successive differences for powers of a bounded linear nonexpansive operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)\) be nonexpansive, let \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), set \(V=\operatorname{Fix}T\), and define \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then \(x_n\to P_Vx_0\) if and only if \(x_n-x_{n+1}\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the orbit of a bounded linear nonexpansive operator, strong convergence to the projection of the initial point onto the fixed-point space is equivalent to asymptotic regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\to P_Vx_0\iff x_n-x_{n+1}\to0\).

children.title: Nonexpansive Maps
children.top_down_role: Global distance geometry for fixed-point mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexpansive Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global metric definition on a subset of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\). A mapping \(T:D\to H\) is nonexpansive on \(D\) if \[\|Tx-Ty\|\leq\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in D.\] Equivalently, \(T\) is globally Lipschitz on \(D\) with Lipschitz constant at most \(1\). The condition compares every pair of domain points and does not require \(T\) to possess a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is nonexpansive when it never increases the distance between any two points in its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is nonexpansive exactly when \(\|Tx-Ty\|\leq\|x-y\|\) for every \(x,y\in D\).

notation.meaning: domain on which the metric inequality is imposed

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexpansive and contractive operators and closure properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric definitions and closure under compatible composition and pointwise convex combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator \(T\) is nonexpansive if \(\|Tx-Ty\|\leq \|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}T\), equivalently, if it is \(1\)-Lipschitz. It is contractive if it is \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L<1\). If \(T\) and \(S\) are nonexpansive and their composition is well-defined, then \(T\circ S\) is nonexpansive; if either factor is contractive, then \(T\circ S\) is contractive. If \(T\) and \(S\) are nonexpansive maps with a common domain and vector-space codomain, then \(\theta T+(1-\theta)S\) is nonexpansive for every \(\theta\in[0,1]\). If \(T\) is contractive and \(\theta\in(0,1]\), this convex combination is contractive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive operator does not increase distances, while a contraction has a Lipschitz constant below one. Compatible compositions of nonexpansive operators remain nonexpansive and become contractive when either factor is contractive. Pointwise convex combinations remain nonexpansive and are contractive when a contractive component receives positive weight.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ and }S\text{ act between normed spaces with the indicated expressions well-defined}
T\text{ and }S\text{ have a common domain and codomain when }\theta T+(1-\theta)S\text{ is asserted}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T,S\text{ nonexpansive}\Rightarrow T\circ S\text{ and }\theta T+(1-\theta)S\text{ are nonexpansive};\quad T\text{ or }S\text{ contractive}\Rightarrow T\circ S\text{ is contractive};\quad T\text{ contractive},\ \theta\in(0,1]\Rightarrow\theta T+(1-\theta)S\text{ is contractive}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexpansive Maps and Their Fixed-Point Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of nonexpansiveness together with failure cases and the compact-convex fixed-point guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A self-map f:C\to C is nonexpansive if \|f(x)-f(y)\|\leq\|x-y\| for all x,y\in C. Nonexpansiveness alone does not guarantee a fixed point on a nonempty compact set or on a nonempty closed convex set: a nontrivial rotation of the unit circle and a translation of \mathbb R provide respective counterexamples. If C is nonempty, compact, and convex, then every nonexpansive self-map f:C\to C has a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive self-map never increases distances. It can lack fixed points on compact nonconvex sets or closed convex noncompact sets, whereas every such map on a nonempty compact convex set has a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the existence conclusion, }C\text{ is nonempty, compact, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Fix}(f)\neq\varnothing\quad\text{if }C\text{ is nonempty, compact, and convex}

children.title: Quasi-Nonexpansive Maps
children.top_down_role: Solution-set-relative distance geometry for fixed-point mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Nonexpansive Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance decrease measured only relative to fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(T:D\to D\) have at least one fixed point. The mapping \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive if \[\|Tx-p\|\leq\|x-p\|\qquad\text{for every }x\in D\text{ and every }p\in\operatorname{Fix}T.\] Thus every closed ball centered at a fixed point and containing \(x\) also contains \(Tx\); no distance comparison is required between two arbitrary nonfixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-nonexpansive map does not increase distance to any of its fixed points, but need not control arbitrary pairwise distances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive exactly when \(\|Tx-p\|\leq\|x-p\|\) for all \(x\in D\) and \(p\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: set of points p satisfying Tp=p

children.title: Global versus Solution-Relative Geometry
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between global control and fixed-point-relative control.

knowledge_statements.title: Global versus Solution-Relative Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of pairwise nonexpansiveness with fixed-point-relative contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T:D\to D\) is nonexpansive and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), then \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive, since the global inequality may be applied with \(y=p\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). The converse fails. For example, define \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(T(0)=0\) and \(T(x)=\tfrac{x}{2}\sin(1/x)\) for \(x\neq0\). Then \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\) and \(|T(x)|\leq|x|/2\), so \(T\) is quasi-nonexpansive; its unbounded derivative near zero prevents global nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global nonexpansiveness implies solution-relative quasi-nonexpansiveness, but the reverse implication fails even for a continuous real-valued map.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space.
\(T:D\to D\) has a nonempty fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ nonexpansive}\Rightarrow T\text{ quasi-nonexpansive}\), whereas the displayed scalar map disproves the converse.

notation.meaning: an arbitrary fixed point of T

children.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness
children.top_down_role: Geometry shared by resolvents, projections, and proximity operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space geometry characteristic of resolvents and metric projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq H\), where \(H\) is a real Hilbert space. A mapping \(T:D\to H\) is firmly nonexpansive if \[\|Tx-Ty\|^{2}\leq\langle Tx-Ty,x-y\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in D.\] Equivalently, \(2T-I\) is nonexpansive on \(D\), or \[\|Tx-Ty\|^{2}+\|(I-T)x-(I-T)y\|^{2}\leq\|x-y\|^{2}.\] In particular, every firmly nonexpansive map is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Firm nonexpansiveness strengthens nonexpansiveness by jointly controlling the displacement of the map and its residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inner-product inequality, residual inequality, and nonexpansiveness of \(2T-I\) are equivalent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Firm Nonexpansiveness of Euclidean Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric projection onto a nonempty closed convex set in a Euclidean space; firm nonexpansiveness implies ordinary nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathbb E$ be a Euclidean space and let $C\subseteq\mathbb E$ be nonempty, closed, and convex. Then, for all $v,w\in\mathbb E$, $\langle P_C(v)-P_C(w),v-w\rangle\ge \|P_C(v)-P_C(w)\|^2$. Consequently, $\|P_C(v)-P_C(w)\|\le \|v-w\|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set in Euclidean space is firmly nonexpansive and therefore nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall v,w\in\mathbb E,\quad \langle P_C(v)-P_C(w),v-w\rangle\ge \|P_C(v)-P_C(w)\|^2\quad\text{and}\quad \|P_C(v)-P_C(w)\|\le \|v-w\|

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged-Operator Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure formulas for relaxation, convex combination, and composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map \(T:H\to H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged, with \(0<\alpha<1\), when \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\) for some nonexpansive \(R\). If \(T_i\) is \(\alpha_i\)-averaged, then \(\sum_iw_iT_i\) is \(\sum_iw_i\alpha_i\)-averaged for \(w_i>0\) and \(\sum_iw_i=1\). If \(T_1,T_2\) are respectively \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\)-averaged, then \(T_1T_2\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \[\alpha=\frac{\alpha_1+\alpha_2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2}{1-\alpha_1\alpha_2}.\] Finally, \((1-\lambda)I+\lambda T\) is \(\lambda\alpha\)-averaged whenever \(0<\lambda<1/\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaged maps remain averaged under admissible relaxation, convex combination, and finite composition, with computable averaging constants.
assumptions_latex: Convex weights and relaxation parameters satisfy the displayed bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed combination, composition, and relaxation operations preserve averagedness with the stated constants.

notation.meaning: nonexpansive component in an averaged representation

children.title: Cocoercive Operator Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometry supporting uncorrected explicit evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Operator Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cocoercivity and averagedness of explicit forward steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B:H\to H\) and \(\beta>0\). The operator \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive if \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\|Bx-By\|^{2}\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\] For every \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), the forward map \(T=I-\gamma B\) is \(\gamma/(2\beta)\)-averaged and hence nonexpansive. Equivalently, \(\beta B\) is firmly nonexpansive. Thus cocoercivity supplies the geometry permitting an uncorrected explicit evaluation of \(B\) with stepsize below \(2\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cocoercive operator yields an averaged explicit forward step for every positive stepsize below twice its cocoercivity constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I-\gamma B\) is \(\gamma/(2\beta)\)-averaged and therefore nonexpansive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong monotonicity, cocoercivity, and their duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and principal consequences for set-valued operators on finite-dimensional Euclidean space, including convex-subdifferential specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathbb A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), \(\mu>0\), and \(\beta>0\), \(\mathbb A\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone when \(\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge \mu\|x-y\|^2\) for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{Gra}\mathbb A\), and is \(\beta\)-cocoercive when \(\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge \beta\|u-v\|^2\) for all such graph pairs. Cocoercivity is dual to strong monotonicity: \(\mathbb A\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive iff \(\mathbb A^{-1}\) is \(\beta\)-strongly monotone; the analogous equivalence holds for maximality. Both properties imply monotonicity. Every \(\beta\)-cocoercive operator is single-valued and \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz, but Lipschitz monotonicity does not imply cocoercivity: the rotation \(A(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,-x_1)\) is maximal monotone and Lipschitz but not cocoercive. A \(\beta\)-cocoercive operator is maximal \(\beta\)-cocoercive iff \(\operatorname{dom}\mathbb A=\mathbb R^n\). For a closed proper convex function \(f\), \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex iff \(\partial f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, and \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth iff \(\partial f\) is \(1/L\)-cocoercive; consequently, \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex iff \(f^*\) is \(1/\mu\)-smooth. Moreover, for convex subdifferentials, \(\partial f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz iff it is \(1/L\)-cocoercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is strongly monotone when its graph pairing controls squared input distance, and cocoercive when it controls squared output distance. Inversion exchanges cocoercivity and strong monotonicity, including their maximal versions. Cocoercivity implies single-valuedness and reciprocal-modulus Lipschitz continuity, but the converse fails, as shown by a planar skew rotation. Maximal cocoercivity is equivalent to full domain. For closed proper convex functions, strong convexity corresponds to strong monotonicity of the subdifferential, smoothness corresponds to cocoercivity of the subdifferential, and strong convexity is dual to smoothness of the conjugate.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb A\text{ \(\beta\)-cocoercive}\Rightarrow \mathbb A\text{ is single-valued, monotone, and \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz},\quad \mathbb A\text{ \(\beta\)-cocoercive}\Longleftrightarrow\mathbb A^{-1}\text{ \(\beta\)-strongly monotone};\quad f\text{ \(\mu\)-strongly convex}\Longleftrightarrow\partial f\text{ \(\mu\)-strongly monotone}\Longleftrightarrow f^*\text{ \(1/\mu\)-smooth},\quad f\text{ \(L\)-smooth}\Longleftrightarrow\partial f\text{ \(1/L\)-cocoercive}.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\) be an integer, let \(T_1,\ldots,T_m:H\to H\) be averaged mappings on a real Hilbert space, and suppose their common fixed-point set is nonempty. Then \[\operatorname{Fix}(T_mT_{m-1}\cdots T_1)=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}T_i.\] Hence composing the maps introduces no spurious fixed points and loses no shared fixed points. The nonempty-intersection hypothesis is essential to the equality; without it, a composition may have fixed points even though the component maps have no common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite composition of averaged maps with a common fixed point has exactly the intersection of their individual fixed-point sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Composition Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averagedness constant for the composition of two averaged operators on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. For \(i\in\{1,2\}\), suppose \(T_i=(1-\alpha_i)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha_iR_i\), where \(0<\alpha_i<1\) and \(R_i:H\to H\) is nonexpansive. Then \(T_2T_1\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with
\[
\alpha=\frac{\alpha_1+\alpha_2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2}{1-\alpha_1\alpha_2}\in(0,1).
\]
Consequently, the composition is nonexpansive and retains the averaged-operator geometry used by fixed-point splitting iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composition of two averaged operators is averaged, with an explicit parameter determined by the two original averaging constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_2T_1\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged for \(\alpha=(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2)/(1-\alpha_1\alpha_2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Preservation under Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of fixed-point sets for a finite composition of averaged operators having a common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(m\geq 1\), and let \(T_i:H\to H\) be \(\alpha_i\)-averaged with \(0<\alpha_i<1\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). If
\[
F=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}T_i\neq\varnothing,
\]
then
\[
\operatorname{Fix}(T_mT_{m-1}\cdots T_1)=F.
\]
Thus no additional fixed points are introduced by the ordered composition under the common-fixed-point and averagedness hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite composition of averaged operators has exactly their common fixed points, provided the common fixed-point set is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_m\cdots T_1)=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}T_i\).

children.title: Resolvent–Zero Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between operator zeros and resolvent fixed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent–Zero Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between zeros of an operator and fixed points of its positive-parameter resolvent, interpreted as a relation when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be an operator, and let \(\gamma>0\). Define \(J_{\gamma A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}=\{x\in H:x\in J_{\gamma A}(x)\}\). Then, for every \(x\in H\),
\[
x\in J_{\gamma A}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in x+\gamma A(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in A(x).
\]
Hence
\[
\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}=\operatorname{zer}A.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interpreting the resolvent as a relation when it is not single-valued, its fixed points are exactly the zeros of the underlying operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}=\operatorname{zer}A\).

notation.meaning: resolvent relation of the scaled operator gamma A
set of points x satisfying zero in A(x)
set of points x satisfying x in J(x)

children.title: Resolvent Geometry
children.top_down_role: Monotonicity and nonexpansiveness properties of resolvent transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Firm nonexpansiveness and full-domain single-valuedness of resolvents of maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). Then \(J_{\gamma A}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}\) is a single-valued mapping from \(H\) to \(H\) and is firmly nonexpansive:
\[
\|J_{\gamma A}x-J_{\gamma A}y\|^2
\leq
\langle J_{\gamma A}x-J_{\gamma A}y,\,x-y\rangle
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in H.
\]
In particular, \(J_{\gamma A}\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximally monotone operator has an everywhere-defined, single-valued resolvent that is firmly nonexpansive and therefore nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}:H\to H\) is firmly nonexpansive and hence nonexpansive.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflected-Resolvent Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonexpansive geometry of the reflection induced by a maximally monotone operator's resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, let \(\gamma>0\), and define \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-\operatorname{Id}\). For all \(x,y\in H\),
\[
\|R_{\gamma A}x-R_{\gamma A}y\|^2
=
\|x-y\|^2-4\bigl(\langle J_{\gamma A}x-J_{\gamma A}y,x-y\rangle-\|J_{\gamma A}x-J_{\gamma A}y\|^2\bigr)
\leq \|x-y\|^2.
\]
Thus \(R_{\gamma A}\) is nonexpansive, and
\[
J_{\gamma A}=\tfrac12(\operatorname{Id}+R_{\gamma A}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reflected resolvent of a maximally monotone operator is nonexpansive, and averaging it with the identity recovers the resolvent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-\operatorname{Id}\) is nonexpansive and \(J_{\gamma A}=\tfrac12(\operatorname{Id}+R_{\gamma A})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled inverse-resolvent decomposition for maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space and let \(\gamma>0\). For every \(x\in H\), the scaled inverse-resolvent identity is
\[
J_{\gamma A}x+\gamma J_{\gamma^{-1}A^{-1}}(\gamma^{-1}x)=x.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
J_{\gamma A}=\operatorname{Id}-\gamma J_{\gamma^{-1}A^{-1}}\circ(\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id}).
\]
The two resolvent terms encode complementary graph relations for \(A\) and \(A^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resolvent and a suitably scaled resolvent of the inverse operator decompose every input into complementary components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}x+\gamma J_{\gamma^{-1}A^{-1}}(\gamma^{-1}x)=x\) for every \(x\in H\).

children.title: Resolvent Asymptotics

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Asymptotics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong parameter limits of a maximally monotone resolvent at zero and infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space. For every \(x\in\overline{\operatorname{dom}A}\),
\[
\lim_{\gamma\downarrow0}J_{\gamma A}x=x.
\]
If additionally \(\operatorname{zer}A\neq\varnothing\), then for every \(x\in H\),
\[
\lim_{\gamma\to\infty}J_{\gamma A}x=P_{\operatorname{zer}A}x,
\]
where both limits are in norm. Thus small parameters recover the identity on the closed domain, whereas large parameters select the nearest zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the parameter vanishes the resolvent approaches the identity; as it diverges, it approaches projection onto the zero set when zeros exist.
assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}x\to x\) as \(\gamma\downarrow0\), and \(J_{\gamma A}x\to P_{\operatorname{zer}A}x\) as \(\gamma\to\infty\) under the stated domains.

notation.meaning: metric projection onto a nonempty closed convex set C

children.title: Proximal Realizations

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Realizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Realization of a convex subdifferential resolvent as a proximal minimization operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\gamma>0\). For every \(x\in H\),
\[
J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)
=
\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x)
=
\underset{y\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|y-x\|^2\right\}.
\]
The minimizer is unique, so the resolvent of \(\gamma\partial f\) is exactly the single-valued proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a scaled convex subdifferential equals the unique minimizer defining the corresponding proximal operator.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma\partial f}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Realizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Realization of projection onto a closed convex set as a normal-cone resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(N_C\) be its convex-analytic normal-cone operator. For every \(\gamma>0\) and \(x\in H\),
\[
J_{\gamma N_C}(x)=P_C(x)
=
\underset{y\in C}{\operatorname{argmin}}\,\frac12\|y-x\|^2.
\]
Because \(N_C\) is a cone at each point of \(C\), positive scaling does not alter the resolvent realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a positively scaled normal cone is the metric projection onto the underlying nonempty closed convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma N_C}=P_C\).

notation.meaning: resolvent of the scaled normal cone

children.title: Normal-Cone Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent normal-cone, projection, and variational-inequality descriptions of a constrained point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\in C\), let \(u\in H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). Then
\[
u\in N_C(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle u,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C(x+\gamma u).
\]
Moreover, if \(B:H\to H\) is single-valued, then
\[
0\in B(x)+N_C(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C(x-\gamma B(x)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal-cone membership is equivalent to the associated variational inequality and projection fixed-point relation. Consequently, a constrained inclusion involving a single-valued operator is equivalent to a projected fixed-point condition.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
For the constrained-inclusion equivalence, \(B:H\to H\) is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in N_C(x)\iff(\forall y\in C)\,\langle u,y-x\rangle\leq0\iff x=P_C(x+\gamma u)\), and \(0\in B(x)+N_C(x)\iff x=P_C(x-\gamma B(x))\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to C at x

children.title: Forward-Evaluation Access

knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Evaluation Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact explicit-oracle model for single-point evaluation of a single-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B:D\to H\) be a single-valued operator, where \(D\subseteq H\). An exact forward-evaluation oracle for \(B\) accepts any query \(x\in D\) and returns \(B(x)\). A forward step with stepsize \(\gamma>0\) is therefore computable as
\[
F_\gamma(x)=x-\gamma B(x).
\]
When \(B=\nabla f\) for a differentiable function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\), the same interface is a gradient oracle returning \(\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward oracle returns the operator value at a queried point, enabling an explicit step; gradient access is the differentiable special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\gamma(x)=x-\gamma B(x)\) requires one exact evaluation of \(B(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact implicit-access interface returning a resolvent value for a queried point and parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space. An exact resolvent oracle for \(A\) accepts a query \((x,\gamma)\in H\times(0,\infty)\) and returns the unique point
\[
y=J_{\gamma A}(x)=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}(x).
\]
Its response is characterized by the verifiable graph relation
\[
x-y\in\gamma A(y).
\]
Thus the oracle provides implicit access to \(A\) without requiring selection and forward evaluation of an element of \(A(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resolvent oracle returns the unique implicit point satisfying the scaled operator inclusion for a queried input and positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=J_{\gamma A}(x)\) is the unique oracle response satisfying \(x-y\in\gamma A(y)\).

children.title: Approximate Implicit Access
children.top_down_role: Accuracy models and admissible error interfaces for implicit evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Implicit Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-controlled inexact access to a resolvent of a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, let \(\gamma>0\), and let \(x\in H\). An absolute-error approximate implicit oracle with tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge 0\) returns \((p,a)\in H\times H\) such that \(a\in A(p)\) and \[\lVert p+\gamma a-x\rVert\le\varepsilon.\] Thus the returned point satisfies the resolvent inclusion up to a verifiable residual; when \(\varepsilon=0\), maximal monotonicity gives \(p=J_{\gamma A}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate implicit access returns a graph point whose resolvent-equation residual is at most the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\in A(p)\) and \(\lVert p+\gamma a-x\rVert\le\varepsilon\).

children.title: Linear-Operator Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Matrix-free application of coupling operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Operator Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward access to a bounded linear map without assuming access to its coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces and let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded and linear. A linear-operator evaluation oracle for \(L\) accepts any query \(x\in X\) and returns \(Lx\in Y\). The interface specifies only the action \(x\mapsto Lx\); it neither requires an explicit matrix representation nor, by itself, provides the adjoint action \(y\mapsto L^*y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-operator oracle returns the product of a queried vector with a bounded linear map, independently of any matrix representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_L(x)=Lx\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Hilbert adjoint of the linear map

children.title: Adjoint Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Matrix-free application of adjoint coupling operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle access to the Hilbert adjoint associated with a bounded linear coupling map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces and let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded and linear. An adjoint-evaluation oracle accepts any \(y\in Y\) and returns \(L^*y\in X\), where \(L^*:Y\to X\) is uniquely characterized by \[\langle Lx,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,L^*y\rangle_X\qquad\text{for all }x\in X,\ y\in Y.\] Access to \(L^*\) is a distinct interface requirement from access to \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjoint oracle returns the adjoint action characterized by preservation of the defining inner-product identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{L^*}(y)=L^*y\) for every \(y\in Y\).

notation.meaning: unique Hilbert adjoint of the bounded linear map

children.title: Matrix-Free Coupling Access
children.top_down_role: Joint access architectures that avoid explicit matrix storage.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Coupling Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling access through operator products rather than stored matrix coefficients or factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces and let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded and linear. Matrix-free coupling access consists of callable evaluations \(x\mapsto Lx\) and, when required by the splitting scheme, \(y\mapsto L^*y\), while no coefficient array representing \(L\) is supplied or formed. Consequently, any admissible iteration may use the coupling only through returned products and scalar or vector operations on previously available quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-free access exposes products with a coupling map and its required adjoint without forming or storing a coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupling interface exposes \(Lx\) and any required \(L^*y\), but not an explicit matrix for \(L\).

notation.meaning: Hilbert adjoint of the coupling map

children.title: Partial-Evaluation Access Interface

children.title: Blockwise Access
children.top_down_role: Partial evaluation organized by structured variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial oracle access under a fixed orthogonal product decomposition of the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) be a finite Hilbert direct sum, let \(P_i:H\to H_i\) be the canonical block projection, and let \(T:H\to H\). A blockwise evaluation oracle accepts \((x,i)\), with \(x\in H\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and returns \[T_i(x):=P_iT(x)\in H_i.\] The oracle need not compute or reveal \(P_jT(x)\) for blocks \(j\ne i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blockwise oracle returns one selected block of an operator value without requiring evaluation of the remaining blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\) is a finite Hilbert direct sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_T(x,i)=P_iT(x)\) for every \(x\in H\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).

notation.meaning: selected block component of the operator

children.title: Coordinatewise Access
children.top_down_role: Fine-grained evaluation organized by individual coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-coordinate specialization of blockwise operator access in a finite-dimensional product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R^n\), let \(e_i\) denote the \(i\)-th standard basis vector, and let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\). A coordinatewise evaluation oracle accepts \((x,i)\), with \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and returns the scalar \[T_i(x):=\langle e_i,T(x)\rangle.\] It provides the selected coordinate without requiring construction of the full vector \(T(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinatewise oracle returns one selected scalar coordinate of an operator value without constructing the full value.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R^n\) has its standard inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_T(x,i)=\langle e_i,T(x)\rangle\) for every admissible query \((x,i)\).

notation.meaning: i-th scalar coordinate of the operator value

children.title: Partial-Evaluation Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Representation features that permit valid partial operator access.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Evaluation Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure condition ensuring a selected block update can be produced from partial operator information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m H_i\), let \(P_i\) be the block projections, and let an iteration map be \(S:H\to H\). The iteration is compatible with partial evaluation on block \(i\) if there exist accessible data maps \(Q_{i,1},\ldots,Q_{i,r_i}\) and a reconstruction map \(\Phi_i\) such that, for every \(x\in H\), \[P_iS(x)=\Phi_i\bigl(P_ix,Q_{i,1}(x),\ldots,Q_{i,r_i}(x)\bigr),\] and computing these arguments does not require evaluating every block of any underlying operator. Compatibility with blockwise access holds when this condition is satisfied for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial-evaluation compatibility means each selected update block is reconstructible from accessible partial data without evaluating all operator blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m H_i\) is a finite Hilbert direct sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(P_iS(x)\) is computable from block-local and permitted partial oracle data alone.

children.top_down_role: Random samples, component operators, and variance-controlled estimators.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(F:H\to H\) is single-valued.
\(\mathcal F\) is the information available before the query, and \(x\) is an \(\mathcal F\)-measurable \(H\)-valued query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,\xi)\) is conditionally unbiased for \(F(x)\) and satisfies \(\mathbb E[\lVert G(x,\xi)-F(x)\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F]\le\sigma^2\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: information available before the oracle query

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased sampled access to a single-valued operator with conditional second-moment control.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(F:H\to H\), let \(\mathcal F\) represent the information available before a query, and let \(x\) be an \(\mathcal F\)-measurable \(H\)-valued query. A stochastic operator oracle draws a sample \(\xi\) after the query and returns \(G(x,\xi)\in H\). Unbiased variance-controlled access means that \(G(x,\xi)\) and \(F(x)\) are square-integrable and \[\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid\mathcal F]=F(x),\qquad \mathbb E[\lVert G(x,\xi)-F(x)\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F]\le\sigma^2\] almost surely for a finite constant \(\sigma^2\). In the finite-sum case, if \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(x)\) with \(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\), an oracle may draw \(I\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) conditionally independently of \(\mathcal F\) with \(\mathbb P(I=i)=p_i\) and return \(F_I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic operator oracle returns a square-integrable sampled operator estimate that is conditionally unbiased at the possibly adaptive query and has controlled conditional variance.

children.title: Picard Iterations
children.top_down_role: Direct iteration of contractive or suitably regular mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Picard Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct fixed-point iteration, with convergence stated for contractions on complete invariant domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonempty set \(C\) in a normed space, a mapping \(T:C\to C\), and an initial point \(x^0\in C\), the Picard iteration is \[x^{k+1}=T(x^k),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots.\] It stops when a prescribed test, such as \(\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\le\varepsilon\), is met and returns the latest iterate. If \(C\) is complete and \(T\) is a contraction with modulus \(q\in[0,1)\), then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^\star\), and every generated sequence converges to \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iteration repeatedly applies the map; for a contraction on a complete invariant set, all iterates converge to its unique fixed point.
assumptions_latex: For the convergence claim, \(C\) is complete and \(\lVert T(x)-T(y)\rVert\le q\lVert x-y\rVert\) with \(q<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\), and under contraction assumptions \(x^k\to x^\star\) where \(T(x^\star)=x^\star\).

notation.meaning: unique fixed point of the contraction

children.title: Krasnosel'skii–Mann Iterations
children.top_down_role: Relaxed iteration for nonexpansive and averaged mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relaxed Iteration of a Firmly Nonexpansive Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Firmly nonexpansive specialization of averaged-operator convergence allowing relaxation through two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be firmly nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and let \(x_0\in\mathcal H\). Suppose \(\lambda_n\in[0,2]\), \(\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\lambda_n(2-\lambda_n)=+\infty\), and \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(Tx_n-x_n)\). Then \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), \(Tx_n-x_n\to0\) strongly, and \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\) for some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a firmly nonexpansive operator with a fixed point, relaxation parameters in [0,2] satisfying the divergent weighted-sum condition yield Fejér monotonicity, strong residual decay, and weak convergence to a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is firmly nonexpansive and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), \(Tx_n-x_n\to0\) strongly, and \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of an Asymptotically Regular Nonexpansive Picard Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of the unrelaxed fixed-point iteration, with strong convergence under symmetry and oddness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), let \(T:D\to D\) be nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and let \(x_0\in D\). Define \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), and suppose \(x_n-Tx_n\to0\). Then \(x_n\rightharpoonup \bar x\) for some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). If additionally \(D=-D\) and \(T(-x)=-Tx\) for every \(x\in D\), then \(x_n\to\bar x\) strongly for some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotically regular Picard iteration of a nonexpansive self-map with a fixed point converges weakly to a fixed point. If the domain is symmetric and the map is odd, convergence is strong.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\mathcal H\) is closed and convex.
For strong convergence only: \(D=-D\) and \((\forall x\in D)\;T(-x)=-Tx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\); under the additional symmetry and oddness assumptions, \(x_n\to\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) strongly.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Krasnosel'skii–Mann Convergence for Nonexpansive Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fejér monotonicity, residual convergence, and weak convergence under the divergent-relaxation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), let \(T:D\to D\) be nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and let \(x_0\in D\). Suppose \(\lambda_n\in[0,1]\), \(\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\lambda_n(1-\lambda_n)=+\infty\), and \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(Tx_n-x_n)\). Then \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), \(Tx_n-x_n\to0\) strongly, and \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\) for some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonexpansive operator with a fixed point, the Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration is Fejér monotone, its residual converges strongly to zero, and its iterates converge weakly to a fixed point under the stated divergent-relaxation condition.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\mathcal H\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_n)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), \(Tx_n-x_n\to0\) strongly, and \(x_n\rightharpoonup\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

children.title: Constant Relaxation Regime
children.top_down_role: Fixed relaxation policies.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Relaxation Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration with one fixed relaxation parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space, let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), choose \(x^0\in C\), and fix \(\lambda\in(0,1)\). The constant-relaxation Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration is \[x^{k+1}=(1-\lambda)x^k+\lambda T(x^k),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots.\] A residual-based implementation may stop when \(\lVert T(x^k)-x^k\rVert\le\varepsilon\) and return \(x^k\). In finite-dimensional spaces the sequence converges to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-relaxation Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration uses the same convex-combination weight at every step and converges to a fixed point in finite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=(1-\lambda)x^k+\lambda T(x^k)\) and \(x^k\to x^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of the mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Varying Relaxation Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration with iteration-dependent convex relaxation weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space, let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and choose \(x^0\in C\). Given weights \(\lambda_k\in(0,1)\), the varying-relaxation Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration is \[x^{k+1}=(1-\lambda_k)x^k+\lambda_kT(x^k),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots.\] If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda_k(1-\lambda_k)=+\infty\), then \(\lVert T(x^k)-x^k\rVert\to0\); in finite-dimensional spaces, \((x^k)\) converges to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With sufficiently persistent varying relaxation, Krasnosel'skii–Mann residuals vanish and finite-dimensional iterates converge to a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert T(x^k)-x^k\rVert\to0\) and \(x^k\to x^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of the mapping

children.title: Underrelaxation Regime
children.top_down_role: Conservative relaxation choices and their qualitative effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Underrelaxation Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter regime below the unrelaxed Krasnosel'skii–Mann step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\), and define the relaxed operator \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda T\). The Krasnosel'skii–Mann update \(x_{k+1}=T_{\lambda_k}x_k\) is underrelaxed at iteration \(k\) precisely when \(0<\lambda_k<1\). If \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), every such step also satisfies \(0<\lambda_k<1/\alpha\), so \(T_{\lambda_k}\) remains averaged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krasnosel'skii–Mann step is underrelaxed when its relaxation parameter lies strictly between zero and one; for an averaged operator, the relaxed map remains averaged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\lambda_k<1\) characterizes underrelaxation, and \(T_{\lambda_k}\) is averaged.

notation.meaning: identity operator on the Hilbert space

children.title: Overrelaxation Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Overrelaxation Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overrelaxation relative to the ordinary Picard step for an averaged operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged on a real Hilbert space, where \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and set \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda T\). A Krasnosel'skii–Mann step \(x_{k+1}=T_{\lambda_k}x_k\) is overrelaxed when \(\lambda_k>1\). The standard averagedness-preserving overrelaxation regime is \(1<\lambda_k<1/\alpha\); within it, \(T_{\lambda_k}\) is \(\lambda_k\alpha\)-averaged and has the same fixed points as \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An overrelaxed step uses a parameter above one. For an alpha-averaged operator, parameters below one over alpha preserve averagedness and the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1<\lambda_k<1/\alpha\) implies that \(T_{\lambda_k}\) is \(\lambda_k\alpha\)-averaged and \(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\lambda_k}=\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: averagedness parameter of the base operator

children.title: Relaxation Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transition between admissible acceleration and unstable relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Stability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp averagedness boundary for constant relaxation of an averaged mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\), where \(R:H\to H\) is nonexpansive and \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). Then \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda\alpha)I+\lambda\alpha R\) is averaged whenever \(0<\lambda<1/\alpha\). At the boundary \(\lambda=1/\alpha\), it reduces to \(R\), whose Picard iterates need not converge. Indeed, on \(H=\mathbb{R}\), choosing \(R=-I\) and any \(x_0\ne0\) gives \(x_{k+1}=-x_k\), a nonconvergent two-cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generic averagedness guarantee ends at one over alpha. At the endpoint the relaxed map may merely be nonexpansive, and its iterates can oscillate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\lambda<1/\alpha\) preserves averagedness, whereas convergence can fail at \(\lambda=1/\alpha\).

notation.meaning: nonexpansive component in an averaged representation

children.title: Anchored Fixed-Point Iteration Family
children.top_down_role: Anchored schemes supporting strong convergence and improved residual behavior.

children.title: Halpern Iterations
children.top_down_role: Canonical anchor-based fixed-point iteration family.

knowledge_statements.title: Halpern Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical fixed-anchor Halpern scheme for a nonexpansive mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a real Hilbert space \(H\), a nonexpansive map \(T:H\to H\) with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), an anchor \(u\in H\), an initial point \(x_0\in H\), and weights \(a_k\in(0,1)\), compute \[x_{k+1}=a_k u+(1-a_k)Tx_k.\] Continue until a prescribed iteration or residual test is met and output the latest iterate. Under the standard conditions \(a_k\to0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|a_{k+1}-a_k|<\infty\), the iterates converge strongly to \(P_{\operatorname{Fix}T}u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Halpern iteration averages a fixed anchor with the mapped current iterate. Standard diminishing, nonsummable, regular weights yield strong convergence to the nearest fixed point to the anchor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to P_{\operatorname{Fix}T}u\) strongly.

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the fixed-point set

children.title: General Anchored Iterations
children.top_down_role: Anchor-based variants extending the canonical family.

knowledge_statements.title: General Anchored Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-anchor extension of the Halpern fixed-point scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(T:H\to H\), an initial point \(x_0\in H\), anchor points \((u_k)_{k\ge0}\subset H\), and weights \(a_k\in[0,1]\), define \[x_{k+1}=a_k u_k+(1-a_k)Tx_k.\] A stopping rule may use an iteration budget or the residual \(\lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\); the output is the latest iterate. The fixed-anchor Halpern iteration is recovered by taking \(u_k=u\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general anchored iteration combines a possibly varying anchor with the image of the current iterate; constant anchors recover the classical Halpern scheme.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=a_k u_k+(1-a_k)Tx_k\), with the Halpern scheme obtained when \(u_k\) is constant.

children.title: Anchor-Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural choices for reference points and anchor weighting.

knowledge_statements.title: Anchor-Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation regimes that make variable anchors asymptotically equivalent to a fixed anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the anchored update \(x_{k+1}=a_k u_k+(1-a_k)Tx_k\), fix a reference anchor \(u\in H\). Three useful regimes are: exact anchoring, defined by \(u_k=u\) for all \(k\); asymptotic anchoring, defined by \(u_k\to u\); and summably weighted perturbations, defined by \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k\lVert u_k-u\rVert<\infty\). The last condition makes the cumulative discrepancy from the fixed-anchor update absolutely summable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anchors may be fixed, merely convergent, or perturbations whose anchor-weighted deviations are summable. The summable regime controls total deviation from a fixed-anchor iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k a_k\lVert u_k-u\rVert<\infty\) implies summability of the per-step discrepancy from exact anchoring at \(u\).

children.title: Inertial Fixed-Point Iterations
children.top_down_role: Memory-based fixed-point schemes and their stability boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Inertial Fixed-Point Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-step fixed-point family using extrapolation from the preceding displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(T:H\to H\), starting points \(x_{-1},x_0\in H\), inertial parameters \(\beta_k\ge0\), and relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k>0\), compute \[y_k=x_k+\beta_k(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k+\lambda_k(Ty_k-y_k).\] Stop under a prescribed budget or residual test and output the latest iterate. The choice \(\beta_k=0\) recovers relaxed fixed-point iteration. Convergence requires joint restrictions on inertia, relaxation, and operator regularity; nonnegativity of \(\beta_k\) alone provides no stability guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inertial fixed-point method extrapolates using the previous displacement and then applies a relaxed fixed-point step. Zero inertia recovers ordinary relaxation; unrestricted inertia can destabilize the iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta_k=0\) yields relaxed fixed-point iteration, while stability for \(\beta_k>0\) requires additional parameter restrictions.

children.title: Fixed-Point Geometric-Ergodic Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Geometric and averaging mechanisms used to establish fixed-point convergence.

children.title: Fejér Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Distance-to-solution-set geometry for exact iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fejér Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact distance monotonicity relative to a nonempty target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset H\). The sequence is Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\) if \[\lVert x_{k+1}-z\rVert\le \lVert x_k-z\rVert\qquad\text{for every }z\in C\text{ and every }k\ge0.\] Consequently, for each \(z\in C\), the scalar sequence \((\lVert x_k-z\rVert)_k\) is nonincreasing and convergent, and \((x_k)_k\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence is Fejér monotone when its distance to every point of a nonempty target set never increases. Such a sequence is bounded and each target-point distance converges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_{k+1}-z\rVert\le\lVert x_k-z\rVert\) for all \(z\in C\) and \(k\ge0\).

children.title: Quasi-Fejér Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Perturbed distance geometry for inexact and stochastic iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Fejér Perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fejér distance geometry allowing a summable sequence of additive errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset H\). The sequence is quasi-Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\) if there exists \((\varepsilon_k)_{k\ge0}\subset[0,\infty)\) with \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_k<\infty\) such that \[\lVert x_{k+1}-z\rVert^2\le \lVert x_k-z\rVert^2+\varepsilon_k\qquad\text{for every }z\in C\text{ and every }k\ge0.\] Then \((x_k)_k\) is bounded and \(\lVert x_k-z\rVert\) converges for every \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-Fejér monotonicity permits summable additive errors in the squared-distance inequality. It still ensures boundedness and convergence of every distance to the target set.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_{k+1}-z\rVert^2\le\lVert x_k-z\rVert^2+\varepsilon_k\) for every \(z\in C\), with boundedness and convergence of target-point distances.

children.title: Asymptotic Regularity
children.top_down_role: Vanishing fixed-point discrepancy as an intermediate property.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing residual form of asymptotic regularity for a fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, let \(T:X\to X\), and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset X\). The sequence is asymptotically regular with respect to \(T\) if \[\lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\longrightarrow0.\] For the Picard iteration \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\), this condition is equivalent to \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert\to0\). Vanishing residual alone does not assert that \((x_k)_k\) converges or that its limit exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymptotic regularity means that the fixed-point residual vanishes. For Picard iteration this equals vanishing successive differences, but it does not by itself imply convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\to0\); for \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\), equivalently \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert\to0\).

children.title: Residual-to-Fixed-Point Identification
children.top_down_role: Passage from residual decay to fixed-point membership.

children.title: Demiclosedness Mechanism
children.top_down_role: Closure principles connecting weak limits with residual behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Demiclosedness Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak cluster points are identified through demiclosedness of the residual operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive. The operator \(I-T\) is demiclosed at \(0\): whenever a sequence \((x_{k_j})_j\subset H\) satisfies \(x_{k_j}\rightharpoonup\bar x\) and \(x_{k_j}-Tx_{k_j}\to0\) strongly, one has \((I-T)\bar x=0\). Thus every weak cluster point obtained along a vanishing-residual subsequence belongs to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonexpansive map, weak convergence together with a strongly vanishing residual forces the weak limit to be a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of T

children.title: Cluster-Point Identification
children.top_down_role: Identification of accumulation points as members of the target set.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Point Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing residual plus sequential closedness identifies cluster points as fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space equipped with a topology \(\tau\), let \(T:X\to X\), and define \(R=I-T:X\to X\). Assume that the graph of \(R\) is sequentially closed from \(\tau\) to the norm topology: whenever \(y_n\to y\) in \(\tau\) and \(R(y_n)\to r\) in norm, one has \(R(y)=r\). If a subsequence satisfies \(x_{k_j}\to\bar x\) in \(\tau\) and \(\lVert R(x_{k_j})\rVert\to0\), then \(R(\bar x)=0\), and hence \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cluster point is a fixed point when a subsequence converges in the selected domain topology, its residuals vanish in norm, and the residual graph is sequentially closed for those convergence modes.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space equipped with a topology \(\tau\).
The graph of \(R\) is sequentially closed from \(\tau\) to the norm topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\bar x)=0\), equivalently \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: fixed-point residual map from X to X
selected topology for convergence of iterates

children.title: Residual-to-Membership Interface
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from vanishing residuals to fixed-point membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-to-Membership Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero residuals and demiclosedness identify weak cluster points as fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(T:H\to H\). Define the fixed-point residual by \(r_T=\operatorname{Id}-T\). Then, for every \(x\in H\), \[r_T(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\operatorname{Fix}T.\] If, additionally, \(r_T\) is demiclosed at \(0\), then every sequence \((x_n)\subset H\) satisfying \(x_n\rightharpoonup \bar x\) and \(r_T(x_n)\to0\) strongly obeys \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual zero is equivalent to fixed-point membership; demiclosedness transfers asymptotically vanishing residuals through weak limits.
assumptions_latex: \(T:H\to H\), with \(\operatorname{Id}-T\) demiclosed at \(0\) for the sequential conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_T(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and weak limits of residual-vanishing sequences belong to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).

children.title: Nonlinear Ergodic Principles
children.top_down_role: Averaging mechanisms for nonexpansive fixed-point dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Ergodic Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of Cesàro averages for a nonexpansive orbit with fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\). For \(x_0\in C\), define the orbit \(x_k=T^k x_0\) and its Cesàro averages by \[a_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}x_k.\] Then \((a_n)\) converges weakly in \(H\) to some point \(a_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Cesàro averages of every nonexpansive orbit converge weakly to a fixed point when the fixed-point set is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, with \(H\) a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_n\rightharpoonup a_\star\) for some \(a_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: Cesàro average of the first \(n\) orbit points.

children.title: Averaged-Operator Convergence Principle
children.top_down_role: Convergence family for relaxed iterations of averaged mappings.

children.title: Weak Hilbert-Space Convergence
children.top_down_role: Baseline infinite-dimensional convergence regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Hilbert-Space Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Picard convergence for an averaged operator on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), meaning \(T=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R\) for a nonexpansive map \(R:H\to H\). If \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), then for every \(x_0\in H\), the iteration \(x_{n+1}=T x_n\) satisfies \(x_n-Tx_n\to0\) strongly and converges weakly to a point \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iterates of an averaged operator with a fixed point are asymptotically regular and converge weakly to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n-Tx_n\to0\) and \(x_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).

notation.meaning: Nonexpansive map representing the averaged operator.

children.title: Finite-Dimensional Convergence
children.top_down_role: Strong convergence consequences in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convergence of averaged-operator iterates in finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb{R}^d\) with its Euclidean inner product, and let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). If \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), then for every \(x_0\in H\), the Picard sequence \(x_{n+1}=T x_n\) converges in norm to some \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). In particular, \(\|x_n-Tx_n\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the weak convergence guarantee for averaged-operator iteration becomes norm convergence to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) such that \(\|x_n-x_\star\|\to0\).

notation.meaning: Limit fixed point of the iteration.

children.title: Strong-Convergence Enhancements
children.top_down_role: Anchoring, compactness, regularity, and monotonicity enhancements.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Convergence Enhancements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern anchoring upgrades nonexpansive fixed-point iteration to strong convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and choose \(u,x_0\in C\). Suppose \((\beta_n)\subset(0,1)\) satisfies \(\beta_n\to0\), \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\beta_n=\infty\), and \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|\beta_{n+1}-\beta_n|<\infty\). Then the Halpern iteration \[x_{n+1}=\beta_nu+(1-\beta_n)Tx_n\] converges strongly to \(P_Fu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing but persistent anchor makes Halpern iterates converge strongly to the fixed point nearest the anchor.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\to P_Fu\) strongly.

notation.meaning: Metric projection of the anchor \(u\) onto \(F\).

children.title: Fixed-Point Well-Posedness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Behavior when fixed points or regularity mechanisms are absent.

children.title: Empty Fixed-Point Regimes
children.top_down_role: Iteration behavior when no fixed point exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Fixed-Point Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An averaged map may have no fixed point, invalidating fixed-point convergence conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a nonzero real Hilbert space, choose \(a\in H\setminus\{0\}\), and define \(T:H\to H\) by \(Tx=x+a\). For every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \(T=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R\), where \(Rx=x+a/\alpha\) is nonexpansive; hence \(T\) is averaged. Nevertheless, \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\). Moreover, for any \(\lambda>0\), the relaxed iteration \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda(Tx_n-x_n)\) gives \(x_n=x_0+n\lambda a\), so no orbit converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero translation is averaged but has no fixed point; its relaxed iterates escape linearly.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nonzero real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is averaged, \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\), and \(\|x_n\|\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: Nonexpansive translation used in the averaged representation.

children.title: Nonregular Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior when regularity mechanisms needed for standard convergence are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonregular Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Without an error bound, averaged iterations need not admit a uniform linear rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb{N})\), define \(T:H\to H\) coordinatewise by \((Tx)_j=(1-j^{-1})x_j\). The operator \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive and \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\). Although \(T^n x\to0\) strongly for every \(x\in H\), no constants \(\kappa<\infty\) and \(q<1\) can satisfy, respectively, \(\|x\|\le\kappa\|x-Tx\|\) and \(\|Tx\|\le q\|x\|\) for all \(x\in H\), since these inequalities fail on the coordinate vectors \(e_j\) as \(j\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A firmly nonexpansive diagonal map can converge pointwise while lacking both a global residual error bound and a uniform linear rate.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is the diagonal operator with multipliers \(1-j^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^n x\to0\) for each \(x\), but no global residual error bound or uniform contraction factor exists.

children.title: Asymptotic Drift
children.top_down_role: Persistent displacement patterns outside standard fixed-point convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The minimal displacement vector determines linear drift when fixed points may be absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive on a real Hilbert space and let \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\). Define the minimal displacement vector by \[v=P_{\overline{\operatorname{ran}(\operatorname{Id}-T)}}0.\] Then \(x_n-x_{n+1}\to v\) and \(x_n/n\to-v\) strongly. Consequently, \(v\ne0\) implies linear asymptotic drift and \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\); when \(v=0\), the normalized orbit has zero linear drift, although a fixed point need not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive orbit drifts at the rate determined by the map's minimal displacement vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n-x_{n+1}\to v\) and \(x_n/n\to-v\) strongly.

notation.meaning: Projection of zero onto the closed range of \(\operatorname{Id}-T\).
