children.title: Exact Proximal-Point Iteration
children.top_down_role: Baseline resolvent iteration.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Proximal-Point Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact resolvent iteration for finding a zero of a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a real Hilbert space \(H\), a maximal monotone operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), a parameter \(\gamma>0\), an initial point \(x_0\in H\), and a tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute exactly \[x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A}x_n=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma A)^{-1}x_n.\] Equivalently, \((x_n-x_{n+1})/\gamma\in A x_{n+1}\). Stop when \(\|x_n-x_{n+1}\|/\gamma\le\varepsilon\) and output \(x_{n+1}\); otherwise continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each proximal-point step applies the exact resolvent and stops when its induced inclusion residual meets the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update produces \(x_{n+1}\) with \((x_n-x_{n+1})/\gamma\in A x_{n+1}\).

notation.meaning: Stopping tolerance for the inclusion residual.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence and R-Linear Rate of Exact Proximal-Point Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global convergence for uniformly bounded positive resolvent parameters, with an R-linear rate under strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be maximal monotone with \(T^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact proximal-point iterations for a maximal monotone operator with a zero converge when the resolvent parameters are uniformly bounded above and away from zero. Strong monotonicity yields at least R-linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^k\to x^*\in T^{-1}(0);\qquad T\text{ strongly monotone}\implies\{x^k\}\text{ converges at least R-linearly}.

children.title: Relaxed Proximal-Point Iteration

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Proximal-Point Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation of each exact resolvent step by a scalar weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a maximal monotone operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) on a real Hilbert space, \(x_0\in H\), \(\gamma>0\), a relaxation sequence \((\lambda_n)\subset(0,2)\), and \(\varepsilon\ge0\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[y_n=J_{\gamma A}x_n,\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(y_n-x_n).\] Since \((x_n-y_n)/\gamma\in Ay_n\), stop when \(\|x_n-y_n\|/\gamma\le\varepsilon\) and output \(y_n\); otherwise continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method relaxes the displacement from the current point to its exact resolvent image.
assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(J_{\gamma A}x_n-x_n)\), with a verifiable residual at \(y_n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Parameter Proximal Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal-point iteration with an iteration-dependent positive resolvent parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a maximal monotone operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), an initial point \(x_0\in H\), positive parameters \((\gamma_n)\), and a tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma_n A}x_n=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma_nA)^{-1}x_n.\] The inclusion \((x_n-x_{n+1})/\gamma_n\in Ax_{n+1}\) holds exactly. Stop when \(\|x_n-x_{n+1}\|/\gamma_n\le\varepsilon\) and output \(x_{n+1}\); otherwise continue. Standard convergence guarantees impose \(\inf_n\gamma_n>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent scale changes by iteration while remaining positive and, for standard convergence, bounded away from zero.
assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma_nA}x_n\) and \((x_n-x_{n+1})/\gamma_n\in Ax_{n+1}\).

children.title: Absolute-Error Criteria
children.top_down_role: Externally controlled approximation tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Error Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summable externally prescribed errors for approximate resolvent evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, let \(\gamma_n>0\), and let \((\varepsilon_n)\subset[0,\infty)\) be prescribed independently of the computed step. An inexact proximal sequence satisfies the absolute-error criterion if, for every \(n\), \[\|x_{n+1}-J_{\gamma_nA}x_n\|\le\varepsilon_n.\] Equivalently, there exists \(e_n\in H\) with \(\|e_n\|\le\varepsilon_n\) such that \(x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma_nA}x_n+e_n\). The standard summable-error regime additionally requires \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_n<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each approximate resolvent value has a prescribed absolute error, and standard convergence uses a summable tolerance sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{n+1}-J_{\gamma_nA}x_n\|\le\varepsilon_n\) for every \(n\).

children.title: Relative-Error Criteria
children.top_down_role: Approximation scaled to local implicit progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Error Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid proximal-extragradient relative-error criterion for one approximate resolvent evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximal monotone, let \(x\in\mathcal H\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(\sigma\in[0,1)\). A triple \((y,v,\varepsilon)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\times[0,\infty)\) satisfies the relative-error criterion when \(v\in T^{[\varepsilon]}(y)\) and
\[\|\lambda v+y-x\|^2+2\lambda\varepsilon\leq \sigma^2\|y-x\|^2,\]
where \(T^{[\varepsilon]}(y)=\{v:\langle y-z,v-w\rangle\geq-\varepsilon\text{ for every }(z,w)\in\operatorname{gra}T\}\). The right-hand side scales admissible error by the local implicit displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate resolvent evaluation has relative error when its graph-enlargement and equation errors are bounded by a fixed fraction of the local proximal displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\lambda v+y-x\|^2+2\lambda\varepsilon\leq\sigma^2\|y-x\|^2\).

children.title: Enlargement-Based Proximal Point

knowledge_statements.title: Enlargement-Based Proximal Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate proximal-point iteration expressed through epsilon-enlarged graph membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), sequences \((\lambda_k)\subset(0,\infty)\) and \((\varepsilon_k)\subset[0,\infty)\), choose at iteration \(k\) a pair \((x_{k+1},v_{k+1})\) satisfying
\[v_{k+1}\in T^{[\varepsilon_k]}(x_{k+1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_kv_{k+1}+e_k,\]
where \(e_k\in\mathcal H\) obeys the prescribed absolute or relative error rule. Stop when a selected residual test holds; otherwise output the generated sequence. With \(e_k=0\) and \(\varepsilon_k=0\), this is the exact proximal-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each step uses an epsilon-enlarged graph point and an approximate resolvent equation; zero enlargement and equation error recover exact proximal point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{k+1}\in T^{[\varepsilon_k]}(x_{k+1})\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_kv_{k+1}+e_k\).

children.title: Weak Convergence Regime
children.top_down_role: Baseline Hilbert-space convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Convergence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact proximal-point convergence for maximal monotone operators on Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximal monotone with \(S=\operatorname{zer}T\neq\varnothing\). Suppose \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kT}x_k\), where \(\inf_k\lambda_k>0\). Then \((x_k)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(S\), every weak sequential cluster point belongs to \(S\), and there exists \(x_\star\in S\) such that \(x_k\rightharpoonup x_\star\). Moreover, \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\). Strong convergence is not asserted in a general infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact proximal-point iterates with steps bounded away from zero converge weakly to a zero of a maximal monotone operator; strong convergence need not follow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x_\star\in\operatorname{zer}T\) such that \(x_k\rightharpoonup x_\star\), and \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\).

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Hilbert space

children.title: Proximal Residual Complexity
children.top_down_role: Progress measured by implicit residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Residual Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate pointwise residual bound for exact proximal-point iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\operatorname{zer}T\neq\varnothing\), let \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kT}x_k\), and define \(v_{k+1}=(x_k-x_{k+1})/\lambda_k\in T(x_{k+1})\). If \(\lambda_k\geq\underline\lambda>0\), then for every integer \(N\geq1\),
\[\min_{0\leq k<N}\|v_{k+1}\|\leq\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x_0,S)}{\underline\lambda\sqrt N}.\]
Consequently, obtaining an iterate whose implicit residual norm is at most \(\epsilon>0\) requires at most \(\lceil\operatorname{dist}(x_0,S)^2/(\underline\lambda^2\epsilon^2)\rceil\) proximal evaluations in this pointwise best-iterate sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among the first N exact proximal steps, one implicit residual is at most the initial solution distance divided by the minimum stepsize times square root of N.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\leq k<N}\|v_{k+1}\|\leq\operatorname{dist}(x_0,S)/(\underline\lambda\sqrt N)\).

notation.meaning: uniform positive lower bound on stepsizes

children.title: Strong-Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Strengthened operator geometries supporting faster proximal behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong metric subregularity condition supporting local proximal-point rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) and let \(0\in T(x_\star)\). The operator is strongly metrically subregular at \((x_\star,0)\) with modulus \(\kappa>0\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_\star\) such that
\[\|x-x_\star\|\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,T(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\]
This error bound makes \(x_\star\) an isolated zero within \(U\). It is a local regularity regime and imposes no corresponding estimate outside \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric subregularity bounds distance to an isolated solution by the operator residual throughout a neighborhood of that solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-x_\star\|\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,T(x))\) for all \(x\) near \(x_\star\).

notation.meaning: infimum norm of an element of T(x)

children.title: Linear-Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric decay behavior available under strengthened regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local contraction of exact proximal point under strong metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) be maximal monotone, let \(0\in T(x_\star)\), and suppose \(T\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((x_\star,0)\) with modulus \(\kappa\). For a fixed \(\lambda>0\), consider \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda T}x_k\). If the relevant iterates remain in the subregularity neighborhood, then
\[\|x_{k+1}-x_\star\|\leq q\|x_k-x_\star\|,\qquad q=\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{\kappa^2+\lambda^2}}<1.\]
Hence \(\|x_k-x_\star\|\leq q^{k-k_0}\|x_{k_0}-x_\star\|\) from the first index \(k_0\) for which the local hypotheses apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the regularity neighborhood, exact proximal-point iterates contract geometrically toward the isolated solution with an explicit factor below one.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is maximal monotone and strongly metrically subregular at \((x_\star,0)\) with modulus \(\kappa\).
The iterates used in the estimate lie in the subregularity neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{k+1}-x_\star\|\leq\kappa(\kappa^2+\lambda^2)^{-1/2}\|x_k-x_\star\|\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports the explicit local contraction factor.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local theorem and its explicit contraction factor are mathematically plausible and fit the Linear-Rate Regimes container, but no source supports the precise hypotheses or factor.

children.title: Locality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on extending local fast behavior to global guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Locality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation between local linear convergence and any global linear-rate claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), define \(f(x)=x^2/2\) for \(|x|\leq1\) and \(f(x)=|x|-1/2\) for \(|x|>1\), and set \(T=\partial f\). At \((0,0)\), \(T\) is strongly metrically subregular. For fixed \(\lambda>0\), proximal-point iterates satisfy \(x_{k+1}=x_k/(1+\lambda)\) locally. However, whenever \(x_k>1+\lambda\), they satisfy \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda\), so \(x_{k+1}/x_k\) can be arbitrarily close to \(1\). Thus local strong regularity does not imply a uniform global linear contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function can yield local geometric proximal convergence but only constant-distance progress far away, so local regularity cannot justify a global linear rate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is the displayed convex piecewise function.
\(T=\partial f\) and the proximal stepsize \(\lambda>0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No constant \(q<1\) satisfies \(|J_{\lambda T}x|\leq q|x|\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the displayed function

review_flags: Concrete counterexample is mathematically checkable but lacks a supplied external source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example appropriately demonstrates the boundary between local regularity and global contraction, and failure_boundary is the correct content kind. An external source or registered evidence is nevertheless required for this nontrivial counterexample.

children.title: Maximal-Monotone plus Cocoercive Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Canonical two-operator class.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal-Monotone plus Cocoercive Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical forward–backward inclusion and its fixed-point formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximal monotone and let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, meaning
\[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\|Bx-By\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathcal H.\]
The associated two-operator problem is to find \(x_\star\in\mathcal H\) such that \(0\in Ax_\star+Bx_\star\). For every \(\gamma>0\), this inclusion is equivalent to
\[x_\star=J_{\gamma A}(x_\star-\gamma Bx_\star).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical forward–backward problem adds a maximal monotone operator to a single-valued cocoercive operator and seeks a zero of their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in Ax_\star+Bx_\star\) if and only if \(x_\star=J_{\gamma A}(x_\star-\gamma Bx_\star)\).

children.title: Smooth–Nonsmooth Composite Minimization
children.top_down_role: Proximal-gradient specialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth–Nonsmooth Composite Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex composite minimization represented as a forward–backward inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(g:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. A point \(x_\star\) minimizes \(f+g\) if and only if
\[0\in\partial g(x_\star)+\nabla f(x_\star).\]
Equivalently, for every \(\gamma>0\),
\[x_\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}\bigl(x_\star-\gamma\nabla f(x_\star)\bigr).\]
Thus composite minimization is the forward–backward inclusion with \(A=\partial g\) and \(B=\nabla f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a smooth convex function plus a nonsmooth convex function is equivalent to a subdifferential-gradient inclusion and a proximal-gradient fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
A minimizer exists when existence is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)\) if and only if \(x_\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x_\star-\gamma\nabla f(x_\star))\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of gamma times g

children.title: Projected-Gradient Specialization

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Gradient Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward–backward iteration with a normal-cone resolvent realized as projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable. Given \(x_0\in C\) and stepsizes \(\gamma_k>0\), compute
\[x_{k+1}=P_C\bigl(x_k-\gamma_k\nabla f(x_k)\bigr).\]
Because \(J_{\gamma N_C}=P_C\), this is forward–backward splitting for \(0\in N_C(x)+\nabla f(x)\). Stop when a prescribed fixed-point residual is small and return the last iterate; any fixed point satisfies the constrained first-order optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected gradient takes a gradient step and projects onto the feasible convex set; it is forward–backward splitting with the set's normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\gamma_k\nabla f(x_k))=J_{\gamma_kN_C}(x_k-\gamma_k\nabla f(x_k))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained variational inequality represented as a normal-cone forward–backward inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\). The variational inequality asks for \(x_\star\in C\) such that
\[\langle Bx_\star,y-x_\star\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\]
This condition is equivalent to \(0\in Bx_\star+N_C(x_\star)\), and hence, for every \(\gamma>0\), to
\[x_\star=P_C(x_\star-\gamma Bx_\star).\]
When \(B\) is cocoercive, the inclusion lies in the canonical forward–backward class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained variational inequality is exactly a zero of the field plus the feasible set's normal cone, equivalently a projected fixed-point equation.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space.
For forward–backward convergence, \(B\) is additionally cocoercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle Bx_\star,y-x_\star\rangle\geq0\) for all \(y\in C\) if and only if \(0\in Bx_\star+N_C(x_\star)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrelaxed deterministic forward–backward iteration for a cocoercive perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximal monotone and let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive. Choose \(x_0\in\mathcal H\) and a stepsize \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute
\[x_{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_k-\gamma Bx_k).\]
Stop when a prescribed fixed-point residual, such as \(\|x_k-x_{k+1}\|/\gamma\), is below tolerance; otherwise output the generated sequence. Every fixed point of the update solves \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic forward–backward applies an explicit step to the cocoercive operator followed by the maximal monotone operator's resolvent, without relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_k-\gamma Bx_k)\), and every fixed point belongs to \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

children.title: Relaxed Forward–Backward

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed fixed-point iteration for a maximally monotone plus cocoercive inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, and let \(B:H\to H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive. Choose \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\), an initial point \(x^0\in H\), and relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k>0\). Define \(T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma B)\) and iterate
\[
x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k\bigl(T_\gamma x^k-x^k\bigr).
\]
Stop when a prescribed residual criterion, such as \(\|T_\gamma x^k-x^k\|\leq\varepsilon\), holds; otherwise output the generated sequence. Every fixed point of \(T_\gamma\) solves \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a relaxed displacement toward the forward–backward image. Fixed points of the splitting map are precisely solutions of the monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k(T_\gamma x^k-x^k)\), with \(\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible relaxation for an averaged forward–backward operator with constant forward step.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, and let \(B:H\to H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, with \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing\). For \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\), define \(T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma B)\). Then \(T_\gamma\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with
\[
\alpha=\frac{2\beta}{4\beta-\gamma}.
\]
Consequently, relaxed iteration uses \(0<\lambda_k<1/\alpha=2-\gamma/(2\beta)\). A standard uniform regime is
\[
0<\inf_k\lambda_k\leq\sup_k\lambda_k<\frac{1}{\alpha}.
\]
More generally, if \(0<\lambda_k<1/\alpha\) for every \(k\) and
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda_k(1-\alpha\lambda_k)=+\infty,
\]
then the corresponding Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration is asymptotically regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward–backward map is averaged with the stated constant. Relaxations below the reciprocal averagedness constant are admissible, and either uniform interior bounds or the stated divergence condition supplies standard asymptotic-regularity control when a fixed point exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Backtracking Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric backtracking for convex composite proximal-gradient steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=f+g\) on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, where \(f\) is convex and differentiable and \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Given \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}g\), \(\bar\gamma>0\), and \(\rho\in(0,1)\), at iteration \(k\) test \(\gamma=\bar\gamma\rho^j\), starting with \(j=0\), and set \(z=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x^k-\gamma\nabla f(x^k))\). Accept the first \(j\) satisfying
\[
f(z)\leq f(x^k)+\langle\nabla f(x^k),z-x^k\rangle+\frac{\|z-x^k\|^2}{2\gamma},
\]
then set \(x^{k+1}=z\). Stop under a prescribed proximal-residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly shrink the step geometrically until the smooth term satisfies its local quadratic upper model, then accept the proximal-gradient point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex, differentiable, and has locally Lipschitz gradient on the relevant level set.
\(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted iterate is \(x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma_k g}(x^k-\gamma_k\nabla f(x^k))\) and satisfies the displayed majorization test.

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the nonsmooth term

children.title: Linesearch Forward–Backward

knowledge_statements.title: Linesearch Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward–backward iteration with an Armijo test on the composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=f+g\), with \(f\) continuously differentiable and \(g\) proper and lower semicontinuous. Given \(x^k\), choose a trial \(\gamma_k>0\), form \(p^k=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma_k g}(x^k-\gamma_k\nabla f(x^k))\), and define \(d^k=p^k-x^k\). Starting from \(t=1\), replace \(t\) by \(\rho t\), where \(\rho\in(0,1)\), until
\[
F(x^k+td^k)\leq F(x^k)-\frac{\sigma t}{\gamma_k}\|d^k\|^2
\]
holds for a chosen \(\sigma\in(0,1)\). Set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+td^k\), and stop when \(\|d^k\|\) meets the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a proximal-gradient direction, then line-search along that direction until the composite objective achieves sufficient decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\operatorname{dom}g\).
\(g\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and the tested points have finite objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted point \(x^{k+1}=x^k+t_kd^k\) satisfies the stated composite Armijo decrease inequality.

children.title: Acceptance Calibration
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria governing acceptance of locally selected parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceptance Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient-decrease calibration connecting local smoothness and accepted forward steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F=f+g\), a current point \(x\), a trial step \(\gamma>0\), and \(z=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\), fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\). The calibrated acceptance predicate is
\[
f(z)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),z-x\rangle+\frac{1-\delta}{2\gamma}\|z-x\|^2.
\]
By proximal optimality, acceptance implies
\[
F(z)\leq F(x)-\frac{\delta}{2\gamma}\|z-x\|^2.
\]
If \(\nabla f\) is locally \(L\)-Lipschitz on the tested segment, every \(\gamma\leq(1-\delta)/L\) passes the predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the acceptance margin so the local smoothness model yields an explicit objective decrease; sufficiently small steps necessarily pass.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and convex on the tested segment.
\(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies \(F(z)\leq F(x)-\delta\|z-x\|^2/(2\gamma)\).

notation.meaning: local Lipschitz constant for the gradient

children.title: Inexact Forward–Backward

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively perturbed forward evaluation and resolvent computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and \(B:H\to H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive. Choose \(x^0\in H\), \(\gamma_k\in(0,2\beta)\), and \(\lambda_k>0\). Given a forward error \(e^k\in H\), compute \(p^k\) satisfying
\[
p^k=J_{\gamma_k A}\bigl(x^k-\gamma_k(Bx^k+e^k)\bigr)+r^k
\]
for a resolvent error \(r^k\in H\), and update \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k(p^k-x^k)\). A standard perturbation regime requires \(\sum_k\lambda_k(\gamma_k\|e^k\|+\|r^k\|)<\infty\). Stop using the computed residual and output the final iterate or sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perform forward–backward updates with explicit forward and resolvent errors; weighted summability makes the accumulated perturbation finite.
assumptions_latex: The exact forward–backward maps use steps uniformly inside \((0,2\beta)\).
The weighted error magnitudes are summable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k(p^k-x^k)\) with total weighted perturbation \(\sum_k\lambda_k(\gamma_k\|e^k\|+\|r^k\|)<\infty\).

children.title: Block Forward–Backward

knowledge_statements.title: Block Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial fixed-point updates on a finite Hilbert product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\), and let \(T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma B):H\to H\) have block components \((T_\gamma)_i\). Choose \(x^0\in H\), relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k>0\), and nonempty active sets \(I_k\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Compute the required active components of \(T_\gamma x^k\) and update
\[
x_i^{k+1}=\begin{cases}x_i^k+\lambda_k\bigl((T_\gamma x^k)_i-x_i^k\bigr),&i\in I_k,\\x_i^k,&i\notin I_k.\end{cases}
\]
Stop when a prescribed full or block residual tolerance is met; otherwise output the block-iterate sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, replace only selected blocks by relaxed forward–backward components and leave all inactive blocks unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite product of real Hilbert spaces.
\(T_\gamma\) is a well-defined forward–backward map with nonempty fixed-point set.
The activation schedule makes every block recurrently active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only blocks in \(I_k\) receive the relaxed fixed-point displacement at iteration \(k\).

notation.meaning: set of active blocks at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-coordinate specialization of block forward–backward splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\) and let \(T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma B)\) have components \((T_\gamma)_i\). Given \(x^0\in H\), select one coordinate \(i_k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) at iteration \(k\), evaluate \((T_\gamma x^k)_{i_k}\), and set
\[
x_i^{k+1}=\begin{cases}x_i^k+\lambda_k\bigl((T_\gamma x^k)_i-x_i^k\bigr),&i=i_k,\\x_i^k,&i\neq i_k.\end{cases}
\]
The index may be cyclic or random, subject to recurrent activation. Stop when an available coordinate or full fixed-point residual meets the chosen tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select one coordinate, apply its relaxed forward–backward displacement, and retain every other coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(T_\gamma:H\to H\) is a well-defined forward–backward map with a fixed point.
Every coordinate is selected recurrently, deterministically or with positive conditional probability.
The relaxation parameters lie in an admissible averaged-iteration regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At iteration \(k\), exactly coordinate \(i_k\) is updated toward \((T_\gamma x^k)_{i_k}\).

children.title: Activation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Deterministic or randomized patterns governing partial updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Activation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic and stochastic coverage conditions for partial-update splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For block indices \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and active sets \(I_k\), a bounded-gap deterministic activation regime requires an integer \(q\geq1\) such that
\[
\bigcup_{j=k}^{k+q-1}I_j=\{1,\ldots,m\}\quad\text{for every }k.
\]
For random activation adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_k)\), a uniform positive-probability regime requires a constant \(p>0\) satisfying
\[
\mathbb P(i\in I_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\geq p
\]
almost surely for every block \(i\) and iteration \(k\). Either predicate prevents permanent starvation; convergence additionally requires the underlying block operator and relaxation hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use bounded-gap deterministic coverage or uniformly positive conditional activation probabilities so that no block is permanently ignored.
assumptions_latex: Each \(I_k\) is a nonempty subset of the block indices.
In the stochastic regime, \(I_k\) has well-defined conditional probabilities relative to \(\mathcal F_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every block is activated recurrently; under the random predicate, each block is activated infinitely often almost surely.

notation.meaning: information available before the k-th activation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic coverage predicate is precise, but the stochastic conclusion depends on the filtration timing and measurability convention for the activation events. No source is supplied for either regime or for the almost-sure infinite-activation conclusion.

children.title: Stochastic Forward–Backward
children.top_down_role: Random information and variance-controlled regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Forward–Backward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward–backward splitting with conditionally unbiased noisy forward information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and let \(B:H\to H\) be cocoercive. Starting from an integrable \(x^0\), at iteration \(k\) obtain a stochastic estimate \(G_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=Bx^k\), and update
\[
x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k\left(J_{\gamma_k A}(x^k-\gamma_kG_k)-x^k\right).
\]
A variance-controlled diminishing-noise regime requires admissible \(\gamma_k,\lambda_k>0\) and
\[
\sum_k\lambda_k^2\gamma_k^2\mathbb E[\|G_k-Bx^k\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]<\infty
\]
almost surely. Stop using an estimated residual or a fixed sampling budget, and output the final iterate or an average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the forward operator by an unbiased stochastic estimate and control accumulated conditional variance through the step and relaxation sequences.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone and \(B\) is cocoercive.
The steps, relaxations, and conditional variances satisfy the displayed summability regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stochastic update uses \(J_{\gamma_k A}(x^k-\gamma_kG_k)\) with finite accumulated scaled conditional variance.

notation.meaning: resolvent used in the backward step

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Proximal-Gradient Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: FISTA-type inertial specialization of forward–backward splitting for convex composites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=f+g\) on a Hilbert space, where \(f\) is convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Initialize \(x^0=y^0\in\operatorname{dom}g\) and \(t_0=1\). For \(k\geq0\), set
\[
x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{g/L}\bigl(y^k-L^{-1}\nabla f(y^k)\bigr),\qquad t_{k+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2}}2,
\]
\[
y^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+\frac{t_k-1}{t_{k+1}}(x^{k+1}-x^k).
\]
Stop under a chosen residual, objective, or iteration-budget criterion and output \(x^k\). Detailed acceleration guarantees require the corresponding FISTA theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the proximal-gradient map at an extrapolated point and update the extrapolation coefficient by the standard FISTA recurrence.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(L>0\).
\(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed recurrence defines the FISTA interface to forward–backward splitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Objective-Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard nonergodic objective bound for constant-step proximal-gradient iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(g:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Suppose \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)\neq\varnothing\). For \(0<\gamma\le L^{-1}\), define \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x_k-\gamma\nabla f(x_k))\). Then, for every \(x_\star\in S\) and \(k\ge1\), \[ (f+g)(x_k)-\min(f+g)\le \frac{\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2}{2\gamma k}. \] Thus the last-iterate objective gap is \(O(k^{-1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-step proximal gradient for a convex smooth-plus-nonsmooth objective has a last-iterate objective gap of order one over the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f+g)(x_k)-\min(f+g)\le \lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2/(2\gamma k)\) for every \(k\ge1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient strong-monotonicity conditions making the forward–backward map contractive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally and \(\mu_A\)-strongly monotone, and let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive and \(\mu_B\)-strongly monotone, where \(\mu_A,\mu_B\ge0\). For \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), the forward–backward map \(T=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\) satisfies \[ \lVert Tx-Ty\rVert\le q\lVert x-y\rVert,\qquad q=\frac{\sqrt{1-\gamma\mu_B(2-\gamma/\beta)}}{1+\gamma\mu_A}. \] Consequently, \(T\) is a strict contraction whenever \(\mu_A+\mu_B>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity in either operator turns the admissibly stepped forward–backward map into a strict contraction with an explicit modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\) is contractive with modulus at most \(q<1\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of gamma times A, equal to the inverse of identity plus gamma A.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B):\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) have a fixed point \(x_\star\), and suppose \(T\) is \(q\)-contractive for some \(0\le q<1\). Starting from any \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), define \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\). The fixed point is unique and \[\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert\le q^k\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert,\qquad \lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\le(1+q)q^k\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert.\] For \(q>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), achieving \(\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert\le\varepsilon\) requires at most \[\max\!\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{\log(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert/\varepsilon)}{-\log q}\right\rceil\right\}\] iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contractive forward–backward operator yields global geometric decay of fixed-point distance and residual. For a positive contraction modulus, the iteration bound is logarithmic in the target accuracy and is zero when the initial point already meets that accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) is maximally and \(\mu_A\)-strongly monotone, \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive and \(\mu_B\)-strongly monotone, and \(\mu_A,\mu_B\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally and \(\mu_A\)-strongly monotone, and let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive and \(\mu_B\)-strongly monotone, where \(\mu_A,\mu_B\ge0\). For the forward–backward map \(T=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\), the standard estimate is \[\lVert Tx-Ty\rVert\le q(\gamma)\lVert x-y\rVert,\qquad q(\gamma)=\frac{\sqrt{1-\gamma\mu_B(2-\gamma/\beta)}}{1+\gamma\mu_A}.\] If \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), then \(q(\gamma)<1\) whenever \(\mu_A+\mu_B>0\), whereas \(q(\gamma)=1\) when \(\mu_A=\mu_B=0\). At the endpoint \(\gamma=2\beta\), the estimate becomes \(q(2\beta)=1/(1+2\beta\mu_A)\); it therefore remains strict when \(\mu_A>0\) and degenerates to \(1\) when \(\mu_A=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the open cocoercive step interval, strong monotonicity of either operator makes the standard certificate strict. At the endpoint, strictness survives only when the backward operator is strongly monotone.

children.title: Metric-Subregularity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Subregularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric subregularity of the forward–backward fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\), let \(R=I-T\), and fix \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). The residual mapping \(R\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa>0\) such that \[ \operatorname{dist}(x,R^{-1}(0))\le\kappa\lVert R x\rVert\qquad\text{for every }x\in U. \] For a forward–backward map \(T=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\), this condition locally controls distance to the solution set by the computable fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity locally bounds distance to the forward–backward solution set by a constant times the fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{Fix}T)\le\kappa\lVert x-Tx\rVert\) locally around \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Fixed-point residual mapping identity minus T.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local error bound stated through the proximal-gradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\), where \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable and \(g:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For \(\gamma>0\), define \(G_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\bigr)\). A local proximal-gradient error bound at a solution \(\bar x\in S=\operatorname*{argmin}F\) holds if some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa>0\) satisfy \[ \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\lVert G_\gamma(x)\rVert\qquad(x\in U). \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local error-bound regime controls distance to composite minimizers by the norm of the proximal-gradient mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable, while \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\lVert G_\gamma(x)\rVert\) throughout a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).

assumptions_latex: A neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\) and \(\kappa>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\lVert x-Tx\rVert\) for every \(x\in U\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(0<\alpha<1\), and let \(S=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Suppose a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\) and a constant \(\kappa>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\lVert x-Tx\rVert\) for every \(x\in U\). Assume \(\kappa^2\ge(1-\alpha)/\alpha\). If \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\) remains in \(U\), then \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)^2\le\left(1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\kappa^2}\right)\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2.\] Consequently, with \(q=\sqrt{1-(1-\alpha)/(\alpha\kappa^2)}\), the distances satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le q\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\), where \(0\le q<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an averaged map, a local residual error bound converts fixed-point decrease into local linear convergence of distance to the fixed-point set, provided the stated error-bound modulus makes the displayed rate factor nonnegative.

children.title: Perturbation-Robust Forward-Backward Convergence

children.title: Deterministic Perturbation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior under deterministic computational errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Perturbation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence under absolutely summable deterministic iteration errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be averaged on a real Hilbert space with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Consider the perturbed iteration \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k+e_k\), where \(e_k\in\mathcal H\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert e_k\rVert<\infty\). Then \((x_k)\) is quasi-Fejér with respect to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), its residuals satisfy \(\lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\to0\), and \((x_k)\) converges weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\). In finite-dimensional spaces, the convergence is in norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged forward–backward iteration tolerates absolutely summable deterministic errors and still converges to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\rightharpoonup x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(\lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\to0\).

notation.meaning: Deterministic additive perturbation at iteration k.

children.title: Stochastic Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior under random evaluations or sampling.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure convergence under unbiased square-summable stochastic perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be averaged with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and let \((\mathcal F_k)\) be a filtration. Consider \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k+\xi_{k+1}\), where \(x_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable, \(\mathbb E[\xi_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E[\lVert\xi_{k+1}\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]<\infty\) almost surely. Then \((x_k)\) converges almost surely to a random point \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and \(\lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\to0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, unbiased stochastic perturbations with summable conditional variance preserve almost-sure convergence of an averaged iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is averaged with a nonempty fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(\lVert x_k-Tx_k\rVert\to0\) almost surely.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be averaged on a real Hilbert space with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and consider \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k+e_k\). Absolute summability \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert e_k\rVert<\infty\) is sufficient for weak convergence to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\); in finite-dimensional spaces, this is norm convergence. This condition cannot be replaced uniformly over the averaged class by the weaker requirement \(e_k\to0\). Indeed, on \(\mathbb R\), take the forward–backward map \(T=I\), corresponding to \(A=0\) and \(B=0\), and let \(e_k=1/(k+1)\). Then \[x_k=x_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{1}{j+1}\] diverges although \(e_k\to0\). Thus vanishing errors alone do not ensure convergence without additional contraction or cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolutely summable errors preserve weak convergence for averaged iterations, with norm convergence in finite dimensions. Merely vanishing errors can accumulate and cause even a valid forward–backward iteration to diverge.

children.title: Forward–Backward Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Incompatible forward geometry, parameter, and error-control regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Backward Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp step-size failure for the scalar cocoercive forward operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H=\mathbb R\), \(A=0\), and \(B(x)=x/\beta\) with \(\beta>0\). Then \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, the unique zero of \(A+B\) is \(0\), and forward–backward iteration becomes \[ x_{k+1}=\left(1-\frac{\gamma}{\beta}\right)x_k. \] It converges to \(0\) for every initial point exactly when \(0<\gamma<2\beta\). At \(\gamma=2\beta\), every nonzero orbit alternates without converging; for \(\gamma>2\beta\), its magnitude diverges. Hence the standard upper step boundary is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar linear example shows cycling at the endpoint step and divergence beyond it, making the standard forward-step interval sharp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence holds exactly for \(0<\gamma<2\beta\); \(\gamma=2\beta\) cycles and \(\gamma>2\beta\) diverges.

notation.meaning: Cocoercivity constant of the scalar forward operator.

children.title: Douglas–Rachford Splitting
children.top_down_role: Averaged reflected-resolvent composition.

knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrelaxed Douglas–Rachford iteration for a sum of two maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given maximally monotone operators \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\), a parameter \(\gamma>0\), and \(z_0\in\mathcal H\), define \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\), \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-I\), and analogously for \(B\). Iterate \[ z_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{DR}}z_k,\qquad T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12\bigl(I+R_{\gamma A}R_{\gamma B}\bigr),\qquad x_k=J_{\gamma B}z_k. \] Stop when \(\lVert z_k-T_{\mathrm{DR}}z_k\rVert\le\varepsilon\), and output the shadow point \(x_k\). If \(z_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), then \(J_{\gamma B}z_\star\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford averages the identity with a composition of reflected resolvents; fixed points yield solutions through a resolvent shadow.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
\(\gamma>0\), \(z_0\in\mathcal H\), and the stopping tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed point \(z_\star\) produces \(x_\star=J_{\gamma B}z_\star\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

notation.meaning: Reflected resolvent of gamma times A.

children.title: Relaxed Douglas–Rachford Splitting
children.top_down_role: Relaxed and overrelaxed reflection variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Douglas–Rachford Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-relaxation Douglas–Rachford iteration for two maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space, let \(\gamma>0\), and set \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\), \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-I\), with analogous definitions for \(B\). Define \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\). Given \(x_0\in\mathcal H\) and relaxation parameters \(\lambda_n\in(0,2)\), iterate \[x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n\bigl(T_{\mathrm{DR}}x_n-x_n\bigr).\] Stop when \(\lVert T_{\mathrm{DR}}x_n-x_n\rVert\) satisfies a prescribed tolerance, and return the shadow \(J_{\gamma A}x_n\). Values \(\lambda_n>1\) give overrelaxation; \(\lambda_n=1\) gives ordinary Douglas–Rachford iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a relaxed fixed-point step to the averaged composition of two reflected resolvents; relaxation above one is overrelaxation, and the resolvent shadow is the recovered point.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on the real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(T_{\mathrm{DR}}x_n-x_n)\), with output shadow \(J_{\gamma A}x_n\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled operator gamma A.

children.title: Peaceman–Rachford Splitting
children.top_down_role: Unaveraged reflected-resolvent composition.

knowledge_statements.title: Peaceman–Rachford Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unaveraged reflected-resolvent composition for a two-operator monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone and let \(\gamma>0\). Define \(R_{\gamma A}=2(I+\gamma A)^{-1}-I\) and \(R_{\gamma B}=2(I+\gamma B)^{-1}-I\). From any \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), Peaceman–Rachford splitting performs \[x_{n+1}=R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}x_n.\] Equivalently, compute \(p_n=J_{\gamma A}x_n\), \(q_n=J_{\gamma B}(2p_n-x_n)\), and update \(x_{n+1}=x_n+2(q_n-p_n)\). Stop under a prescribed fixed-point residual tolerance and return an appropriate resolvent shadow. Unlike Douglas–Rachford splitting, the reflected-resolvent composition is not averaged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly apply the unaveraged composition of the reflected resolvents. Its two-resolvent implementation updates the iterate by twice the difference between consecutive shadows.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}=R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}x_n=x_n+2(q_n-p_n)\).

children.title: Spingarn Partial-Inverse Method
children.top_down_role: Subspace decomposition through partial inverses.

knowledge_statements.title: Spingarn Partial-Inverse Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-point formulation of a subspace-constrained monotone inclusion through a partial inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone and let \(V\subseteq\mathcal H\) be a closed vector subspace. Define Spingarn's partial inverse \(A_V\) by \[y\in A_Vx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}x\in A\bigl(P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}y\bigr).\] Given \(z_0\in\mathcal H\) and positive proximal parameters \(\gamma_n\), iterate \[z_{n+1}=J_{\gamma_n A_V}z_n.\] Stop when \(\lVert z_{n+1}-z_n\rVert\) meets a prescribed tolerance. If \(z\in\operatorname{zer}A_V\), then \(x=P_Vz\) satisfies \(x\in V\), and there exists \(u=P_{V^\perp}z\in V^\perp\) such that \(u\in Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply the proximal point method to Spingarn's partial inverse. A zero decomposes into a primal point in the subspace and an operator value in its orthogonal complement.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone on the real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\).
\(V\) is a closed vector subspace and \(\gamma_n>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{n+1}=J_{\gamma_nA_V}z_n\), and \(z\in\operatorname{zer}A_V\) yields \(P_Vz\in V\) with \(P_{V^\perp}z\in A(P_Vz)\cap V^\perp\).

notation.meaning: Partial inverse of A with respect to V.
Resolvent of the scaled partial inverse.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is mathematically plausible and the algorithm kind fits, but the exact partial-inverse definition and proximal-point formulation have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Convergence of Spingarn's Partial-Inverse Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of Spingarn's resolvent-projection iteration for a maximally monotone operator and a closed linear subspace of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone and let \(V\subseteq\mathcal H\) be a closed linear subspace. Suppose there exists \((x,u)\in V\times V^\perp\) with \(u\in Ax\). For \(x_0\in V\) and \(u_0\in V^\perp\), define, for every \(n\geq0\), \(y_n=J_A(x_n+u_n)\), \(v_n=x_n+u_n-y_n\), and \((x_{n+1},u_{n+1})=(P_Vy_n,P_{V^\perp}v_n)\). Then there exists \((x,u)\in V\times V^\perp\) satisfying \(u\in Ax\) such that \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) and \(u_n\rightharpoonup u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a maximally monotone operator and a closed linear subspace, if the associated constrained inclusion has a solution, then Spingarn's resolvent-projection iteration started in the subspace and its orthogonal complement converges weakly to a primal-dual solution.
assumptions_latex: \(V\subseteq\mathcal H\) is a closed linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(x,u)\in V\times V^\perp:\ u\in Ax,\quad x_n\rightharpoonup x,\quad u_n\rightharpoonup u.\)

children.title: Adaptive Reflection Methods
children.top_down_role: Reflection schemes with iteration-dependent parameter adaptation.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Reflection Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-driven relaxation of the Douglas–Rachford reflected-resolvent operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\) and define the residual \(r_n=Tx_n-x_n\). Choose constants \(0<\underline\lambda\leq\overline\lambda<2\), an initial \(\lambda_0\in[\underline\lambda,\overline\lambda]\), and a calibration rule \(\Phi_n\). At iteration \(n\), set \[\lambda_n=\operatorname{proj}_{[\underline\lambda,\overline\lambda]}\!\left(\Phi_n(x_n,r_n,\lambda_{n-1})\right),\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_nr_n.\] Stop when \(\lVert r_n\rVert\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(J_{\gamma A}x_n\). The projection safeguard makes every accepted step a relaxed Douglas–Rachford step even when the calibration rule changes with the observed residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adapt the reflection relaxation from residual information, project it onto a safe interval inside zero to two, and terminate using the fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(Tx_n-x_n)\) with \(\lambda_n\in[\underline\lambda,\overline\lambda]\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the parameter interval.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This defines a broad safeguarded adaptive relaxation template, but no authoritative source establishes it as the intended adaptive reflection method or specifies conditions on the calibration rule.

children.title: Linesearch Reflection Methods
children.top_down_role: Reflection schemes using local acceptance tests.

knowledge_statements.title: Linesearch Reflection Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backtracking selection of a relaxed reflected-resolvent step using residual decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\), \(r(x)=Tx-x\), and choose \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), \(\lambda_{\max}\in(0,2)\), \(\beta\in(0,1)\), and \(c>0\). At iteration \(n\), test \(\lambda=\lambda_{\max}\beta^j\) for \(j=0,1,\ldots\) until \[\bigl\lVert r(x_n+\lambda r(x_n))\bigr\rVert^2\leq \lVert r(x_n)\rVert^2-c\lambda\lVert r(x_n)\rVert^2.\] Set \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda r(x_n)\). Stop when \(\lVert r(x_n)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(J_{\gamma A}x_n\). If no trial is accepted, invoke a specified fallback step rather than accepting an uncertified parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtrack the reflection relaxation until a stated residual-decrease test holds, then take the accepted step; otherwise use a separately specified fallback.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted parameter satisfies the displayed residual-decrease test before \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda r(x_n)\) is formed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The particular residual-decrease test and existence of an accepted backtracking trial require a method-specific source and additional hypotheses. The fallback is also unspecified.

children.title: Calibration Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Structural protections for locally adjusted reflection parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Calibration Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter conditions preventing degenerate or excessively aggressive relaxed-reflection steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the variable relaxed iteration \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\lambda_n(Tx_n-x_n)\), a uniform calibration safeguard is the predicate \[\exists\,\delta\in(0,1]\ \text{such that}\ \delta\leq\lambda_n\leq 2-\delta\quad\text{for every }n.\] If a stepsize \(\gamma_n\) is also calibrated, impose \(0<\underline\gamma\leq\gamma_n\leq\overline\gamma<\infty\). A proposed pair \((\widehat\lambda_n,\widehat\gamma_n)\) is admissible only after projection or rejection places it in these intervals. These bounds certify parameter admissibility; by themselves they do not certify convergence when the reflected-resolvent operator also changes with \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep every relaxation uniformly away from zero and two, and every resolvent stepsize uniformly positive and finite. These bounds certify admissibility, not convergence of changing operators.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is the fixed Douglas–Rachford operator when only relaxation varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_n\in[\delta,2-\delta]\) and, when applicable, \(\gamma_n\in[\underline\gamma,\overline\gamma]\) for every \(n\).

notation.meaning: Uniform margin from the relaxation endpoints zero and two.

children.title: Douglas-Rachford Recovery Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationships among auxiliary iterates, shadow sequences, and solutions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Douglas–Rachford fixed-point recovery, convergence, and shadow feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary fixed points, resolvent recovery, and shadow-sequence behavior for two maximal monotone operators in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb A,\mathbb B:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be maximal monotone and let \(\alpha>0\). Then
\[
0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)x
\iff
\exists z\in\operatorname{Fix}\!\left(\tfrac12(I+R_{\alpha\mathbb A}R_{\alpha\mathbb B})\right)\ \text{with}\ x=J_{\alpha\mathbb B}z.
\]
Douglas–Rachford iteration can be written as
\[
x^{k+1/2}=J_{\alpha\mathbb B}z^k,\qquad
x^{k+1}=J_{\alpha\mathbb A}(2x^{k+1/2}-z^k),\qquad
z^{k+1}=z^k+x^{k+1}-x^{k+1/2}.
\]
If \(\operatorname{Zer}(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)\neq\varnothing\), the iteration converges for every \(\alpha>0\), and the resolvent shadow recovers a zero. If \(J_{\alpha\mathbb B}=P_C\) for a constraint set \(C\), then \(x^{k+1/2}\in C\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of A+B are recovered by applying the resolvent of B to fixed points of the averaged Douglas–Rachford reflection map. With a nonempty zero set, the iteration converges for every positive step size. If the B-resolvent is a projection onto a constraint set, every corresponding shadow iterate is exactly feasible.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb A,\mathbb B:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\text{ are maximal monotone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)x\iff \exists z\in\operatorname{Fix}\!\left(\tfrac12(I+R_{\alpha\mathbb A}R_{\alpha\mathbb B})\right):x=J_{\alpha\mathbb B}z;\quad z^k\text{ converges when the zero set is nonempty, and }x^{k+1/2}\in C\text{ if }J_{\alpha\mathbb B}=P_C.

children.title: Douglas–Rachford Fixed-Point Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary fixed-point sets and solution-set relationships.

knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Fixed-Point Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiber representation of Douglas–Rachford fixed points over primal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, set \(J_A=(I+A)^{-1}\), and let \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A)\). For \(Z=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\) and \(K_p=Ap\cap(-Bp)\), \[\operatorname{Fix}T=\bigcup_{p\in Z}(p+K_p).\] More precisely, \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) if and only if \(p=J_Ax\) and \(u=x-p\) satisfy \(u\in Ap\) and \(-u\in Bp\). Consequently, \(J_A(\operatorname{Fix}T)=Z\) whenever \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\); each fixed point consists of a primal solution plus a compatible primal-dual displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Douglas–Rachford fixed point decomposes into a primal zero and a compatible operator value; resolving a fixed point through the first resolvent recovers the primal solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\bigcup_{p\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)}\bigl(p+Ap\cap(-Bp)\bigr)\) and \(J_A(\operatorname{Fix}T)=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

notation.meaning: Compatible displacement set Ap intersected with -Bp.
Fixed-point set of the Douglas–Rachford operator.

children.title: Shadow Sequences
children.top_down_role: Resolvent images used for solution recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent images associated with a Douglas–Rachford governing sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_n)_{n\geq0}\) be generated by the Douglas–Rachford operator \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\). The first and second shadow sequences are defined by \[p_n=J_{\gamma A}x_n,\qquad q_n=J_{\gamma B}(2p_n-x_n).\] They satisfy \(x_{n+1}-x_n=q_n-p_n\) for the unrelaxed iteration \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\), and \(x_{n+1}-x_n=\lambda_n(q_n-p_n)\) for its relaxed form. The sequence \((x_n)\) is the governing sequence; \((p_n)\) and \((q_n)\) are its resolvent shadows used for recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Douglas–Rachford shadows are the two resolvent outputs computed during an iteration. Their difference is the governing fixed-point displacement, up to relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The reflection ordering is \(R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_n=J_{\gamma A}x_n\), \(q_n=J_{\gamma B}(2p_n-x_n)\), and \(x_{n+1}-x_n=\lambda_n(q_n-p_n)\).

children.title: Primal-Dual Recovery Pair
children.top_down_role: Recovery maps for primal, dual, and inclusion solutions.

children.title: Primal Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Maps from auxiliary iterates or shadows to primal solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a zero of the summed inclusion from a Douglas–Rachford fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone and \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A)\). If \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), define \(p=J_Ax\). Then \(x-p\in Ap\), while fixed-point consistency gives \(p-x\in Bp\). Hence \[0\in Ap+Bp,\qquad p\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B).\] Thus the primal recovery map for this operator ordering is \(x\mapsto J_Ax\). For a convergent governing sequence, primal recovery is performed on its first shadow rather than by identifying the governing limit itself with a primal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply the first resolvent to a Douglas–Rachford fixed point. The resulting shadow solves the primal inclusion, whereas the governing fixed point generally need not.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=J_Ax\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

children.title: Dual Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Maps from auxiliary iterates or shadows to dual solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a compatible dual displacement from a Douglas–Rachford fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A)\) and suppose \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). Set \(p=J_Ax\) and \(u=x-p\). Then \[u\in Ap,\qquad -u\in Bp.\] Therefore \(u\) is a dual solution in the primal-dual system associated with \(0\in A+B\). Equivalently, with \(B^{-\oplus}=(-I)\circ B^{-1}\circ(-I)\), it satisfies \[0\in A^{-1}u+B^{-\oplus}u.\] The sign of the recovered dual variable depends on the reflected-resolvent ordering and must be changed if the operators are interchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract the primal shadow from the Douglas–Rachford fixed point. This displacement is an A-value whose negative is a B-value, hence a compatible dual solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u=x-J_Ax\) satisfies \(u\in A(J_Ax)\), \(-u\in B(J_Ax)\), and \(0\in A^{-1}u+B^{-\oplus}u\).

notation.meaning: Attouch–Théra conjugate inverse (-I) composed with B^{-1} and (-I).

children.title: Recovery Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility among recovered primal, dual, and inclusion objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally verifiable consistency certificate for recovered primal and dual variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For candidate variables \((p,u)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\), define the recovery-consistency predicate \[u\in Ap\quad\text{and}\quad -u\in Bp.\] When both graph-membership tests hold, their sum gives \(0=u+(-u)\in Ap+Bp\), so \(p\) is a primal solution and \(u\) is its compatible dual displacement. For a Douglas–Rachford fixed point \(x\), the recovered pair \(p=J_Ax\), \(u=x-p\) satisfies this predicate. Conversely, any consistent pair generates a Douglas–Rachford fixed point \(x=p+u\) for \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recovered pair is consistent exactly when the dual displacement belongs to the first operator and its negative belongs to the second; then their sum certifies primal feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((p,u)\) is consistent if and only if \(p+u\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), \(u\in Ap\), and \(-u\in Bp\).

notation.meaning: Recovered primal point and dual displacement.

children.title: Inconsistent Shadow Regimes
children.top_down_role: Shadow behavior when exact solutions are absent.

children.title: Best-Approximation Shadows
children.top_down_role: Shadow limits associated with nearest-point structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Best-Approximation Shadows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shadow behavior for inconsistent feasibility between two closed affine subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U,V\) be nonempty closed affine subspaces of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_VR_U)\), and generate \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\). Define the shadows \(p_n=P_Ux_n\) and \(q_n=P_VR_Ux_n\). If the distance between \(U\) and \(V\) is attained, then the governing sequence may be unbounded when \(U\cap V=\varnothing\), while its shadows approach best-approximation geometry: \[\lVert p_n-q_n\rVert\longrightarrow d(U,V),\] and every limit pair \((p,q)\) of \((p_n,q_n)\) satisfies \(p\in U\), \(q\in V\), and \(\lVert p-q\rVert=d(U,V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For inconsistent affine feasibility, Douglas–Rachford iterates may diverge, yet shadow limit pairs realize the minimum distance between the two sets.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) are nonempty closed affine subspaces of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert P_Ux_n-P_VR_Ux_n\rVert\to d(U,V)\), and every shadow limit pair is a best-approximation pair.

notation.meaning: Infimum distance between U and V.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-subspace shadow claim is plausible, but the convergence of shadow distances and characterization of every limit pair require an exact theorem source and hypothesis check.

children.title: Inconsistent-Problem Shadows
children.top_down_role: Shadow behavior when the underlying feasibility or inclusion problem lacks a solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent-Problem Shadows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford shadows when the primal inclusion has no zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, let \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A)\), and generate \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\). Define the shadows \(a_n=J_Ax_n\) and \(b_n=J_BR_Ax_n\). Then \[x_n-Tx_n=a_n-b_n.\] Consequently, if \(x_n-Tx_n\to v\), where \(v=P_{\overline{\operatorname{ran}(I-T)}}0\), then \(a_n-b_n\to v\), even when \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)=\varnothing\). Any convergent shadow subsequences therefore recover a displaced, rather than exact, consistency relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an inconsistent inclusion, the two Douglas–Rachford shadows may approach a pair whose gap equals the minimal displacement vector.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A,B\) are maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_n-b_n\to P_{\overline{\operatorname{ran}(I-T)}}0\).
review_flags: Exact inconsistent-case shadow theorem and hypotheses require a dedicated Douglas–Rachford source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual identity is correct, but the cited record has no source for residual convergence to the minimal-displacement vector or for the intended inconsistent Douglas–Rachford shadow interpretation. A dedicated source is required before the mathematical scope and hypotheses can be confirmed.

children.title: Minimal-Displacement Regimes
children.top_down_role: Displacement geometry organizing asymptotic behavior without exact solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Displacement Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal displacement for a possibly fixed-point-free splitting operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive and suppose \(\overline{\operatorname{ran}(I-T)}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex. The minimal displacement vector of \(T\) is \[v_T=P_{\overline{\operatorname{ran}(I-T)}}0.\] The iteration \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\) is in the minimal-displacement regime when \(x_n-x_{n+1}\to v_T\). Here \(v_T=0\) is compatible with approximate fixed points, whereas \(v_T\ne0\) certifies that \(T\) has no fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal displacement vector is the smallest attainable limiting fixed-point residual; a nonzero vector rules out fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_T=P_{\overline{\operatorname{ran}(I-T)}}0\), and \(v_T\ne0\Rightarrow\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\).
review_flags: A source establishing convexity and residual convergence for the intended operator class is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of the minimal-displacement vector is standard, but no source is supplied for the operator-class assertions. The plain statement also calls the vector an attainable limiting residual, although the projection is defined using the closure of the displacement range and residual convergence is separately imposed as the regime condition.

children.title: Shadow-Sequence Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence of recovered solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow-Sequence Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of the recovered primal sequence for convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and suppose \(\operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)\ne\varnothing\). For \(A=\partial f\), \(B=\partial g\), and \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A)\), generate \(x_{n+1}=Tx_n\). Then the shadow sequence \(p_n=J_Ax_n=\operatorname{prox}_f(x_n)\) converges weakly to a point \(p_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)\). If \(H\) is finite-dimensional, this convergence is strong.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal shadow of Douglas–Rachford converges weakly to a minimizer, and converges strongly in finite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f,g\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_Ax_n\rightharpoonup p_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be firmly nonexpansive with nonempty fixed-point set \(F\). Suppose that near \(\bar x\in F\) there is \(\kappa\ge1\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\le\kappa\lVert x-Tx\rVert.\] Then every orbit remaining in that neighborhood satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(Tx,F)\le q\operatorname{dist}(x,F),\qquad q=\sqrt{1-\kappa^{-2}}<1.\] Thus metric subregularity or an equivalent local error bound yields local linear convergence of fixed-point distances; polyhedrality, transversality, or strong monotonicity can supply such an error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local residual error bound converts firm nonexpansiveness into linear contraction of distance to the fixed-point set.

children.title: Reflection Rate-Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundaries of rate guarantees and reflection stability.

children.title: Arbitrarily Slow Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convergent behavior lacking a useful uniform rate guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrarily Slow Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convergence without any uniform linear rate in infinite dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\ell^2\), define the self-adjoint firmly nonexpansive operator \(T\) by \(Te_k=(1-1/k)e_k\) for the standard basis \((e_k)\). Then \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\) and \(T^nx\to0\) for every \(x\in H\), but \[\lVert T^n\rVert=\sup_{k\ge1}(1-1/k)^n=1\] for every \(n\). Hence no constants \(C<\infty\) and \(q<1\) can give the uniform estimate \(\lVert T^nx\rVert\le Cq^n\lVert x\rVert\) for all \(x\) and \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal firmly nonexpansive map can converge pointwise while admitting no uniform geometric convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^nx\to0\) for every \(x\), while \(\lVert T^n\rVert=1\) for every \(n\).
review_flags: A dedicated source is needed to connect this fixed-point example explicitly to Douglas–Rachford rate pathology.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal example correctly shows pointwise strong convergence without a uniform geometric operator-norm rate. However, it is unsourced, does not explicitly realize the map as a Douglas–Rachford operator, and does not by itself state the stronger conventional arbitrarily-slow-orbit result. A source is needed to establish the intended terminal scope.

children.title: Nonconvergent Regimes
children.top_down_role: Reflection behavior that fails to approach the target fixed-point structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvergent Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unaveraged reflected-resolvent iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U,V\subset\mathbb R^2\) be distinct lines through the origin meeting at angle \(\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\), and set \(A=N_U\), \(B=N_V\). Then \(R_A\) and \(R_B\) are reflections across \(U\) and \(V\), so \(R_BR_A\) is rotation through angle \(2\theta\). For any \(x_0\ne0\), the unaveraged iteration \(x_{n+1}=R_BR_Ax_n\) preserves \(\lVert x_n\rVert\) and does not converge. Thus nonexpansiveness of a reflection composition alone does not ensure Picard convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two line reflections compose to a rotation, so the unaveraged reflection iteration can orbit forever without converging.
assumptions_latex: \(U,V\subset\mathbb R^2\) are distinct lines meeting at \(\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_n\rVert=\lVert x_0\rVert\) for all \(n\), and \((x_n)\) does not converge.

children.title: Reflection Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Geometric or parameter transitions separating stable reflection from pathological behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflection Stability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaging threshold for generic reflected-resolvent compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=R_BR_A\) be a nonexpansive reflected-resolvent composition and define \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda S\). For \(0<\lambda<1\), the map \(T_\lambda\) is averaged; if \(\operatorname{Fix}S\ne\varnothing\), its Picard iterates converge weakly to a fixed point. At \(\lambda=1\), only nonexpansiveness remains, and convergence can fail, as for a nontrivial planar rotation. For \(\lambda\notin[0,1]\), generic nonexpansiveness is no longer guaranteed. Thus \(\lambda=1\) is the general averaging-stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict averaging ensures baseline convergence; at the unaveraged reflection endpoint, rotations show that convergence may fail.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\lambda<1\) gives averaged fixed-point convergence, whereas \(\lambda=1\) admits nonconvergent examples.
