knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford–ADMM Dual Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus-form ADMM as Douglas–Rachford splitting of the dual inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x,z}\{f(x)+g(z):x=z\}\), where \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, convex functions and standard primal-dual qualification holds. Its dual optimality condition is \[0\in \partial(f^*\circ(-I))(y)+\partial g^*(y).\] Applying Douglas–Rachford splitting with stepsize \(\rho>0\) to these two dual subdifferentials, and identifying its resolvent variables through the Moreau identity, yields the scaled ADMM updates \[x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{f/\rho}(z^k-u^k),\quad z^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{g/\rho}(x^{k+1}+u^k),\quad u^{k+1}=u^k+x^{k+1}-z^{k+1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For consensus convex optimization, scaled ADMM is Douglas–Rachford splitting applied to the dual optimality inclusion under an affine variable identification.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
A standard qualification condition ensures valid Fenchel duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Douglas–Rachford dual iterates and scaled ADMM iterates correspond under Moreau-based affine variable identification.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford fixed points encode convex feasibility solutions through shadows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space and define \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_DR_C)\), where \(R_C=2P_C-I\) and \(R_D=2P_D-I\). If \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\), then \[P_C(\operatorname{Fix}T)=C\cap D.\] More explicitly, \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) if and only if \(p=P_Cz\) satisfies \(p=P_D(2p-z)\); in that case \(p\in C\cap D\). Conversely, every \(p\in C\cap D\) is itself a fixed point of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For consistent convex feasibility, projecting any Douglas–Rachford fixed point recovers a feasible point, and each feasible point is fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subset H\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(\operatorname{Fix}T)=C\cap D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Specializations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set feasibility as a specialization of monotone inclusion splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty closed convex sets \(C,D\subset H\), their indicator functions satisfy \(\partial\iota_C=N_C\) and \(\partial\iota_D=N_D\). Hence the feasibility problem \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\) is equivalent to \[\operatorname{zer}(N_C+N_D)=C\cap D.\] Under the resolvent identities \(J_{N_C}=P_C\) and \(J_{N_D}=P_D\), Douglas–Rachford splitting for \(0\in N_C(x)+N_D(x)\) becomes the projection-reflection iteration \[x_{n+1}=\tfrac12\bigl(I+(2P_D-I)(2P_C-I)\bigr)x_n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing monotone operators by convex normal cones turns Douglas–Rachford splitting into the standard projection-reflection method for set feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subset H\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}(N_C+N_D)=C\cap D\), and Douglas–Rachford uses the displayed projection-reflection operator.

children.title: Partial-Inverse Equivalences
children.top_down_role: Correspondences between reflection splitting and partial-inverse formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Inverse Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-set equivalence for Spingarn’s partial inverse relative to a closed subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(V\subset H\) be a closed vector subspace, and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). The partial inverse of \(A\) with respect to \(V\) is the operator \(A_V\) determined by
\[y\in A_Vx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}x\in A\bigl(P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}y\bigr).\]
Consequently,
\[0\in A_Vx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_{V^\perp}x\in A(P_Vx).\]
Thus zeros of \(A_V\) correspond exactly to pairs \((p,q)\in V\times V^\perp\) satisfying \(q\in Ap\), through \(x=p+q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero of the partial inverse encodes exactly a primal point in the subspace and an orthogonal dual vector belonging to the original operator at that point.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(V\subset H\) is a closed vector subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in A_Vx\iff P_{V^\perp}x\in A(P_Vx)\).

notation.meaning: Partial inverse of A relative to V.

children.title: Product-Space Equivalences
children.top_down_role: Correspondences produced by lifting decomposed problems into product spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal product-space reformulation of a finite sum of set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), define \(\mathcal H=H^m\), \(\mathcal A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=A_1x_1\times\cdots\times A_mx_m\), and let \(D=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in H\}\). Then
\[0\in\sum_{i=1}^m A_ix\]
holds if and only if there exist \(z=(x,\ldots,x)\in D\) and \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in\mathcal Az\cap D^\perp\). Equivalently, the sum inclusion is feasible precisely when
\[u_i\in A_ix\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m u_i=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum inclusion becomes a product-space feasibility problem between the diagonal subspace and operator values whose components sum to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m\geq 2\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\sum_iA_ix\iff \exists z=(x,\ldots,x)\in D,\ \exists u\in\mathcal Az\cap D^\perp\).

notation.meaning: Hilbert product space H^m with its standard product inner product.
Cartesian product of the component operators.
Diagonal subspace of the product space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a closed vector subspace of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). Define
\[\mathcal S=\{(p,q)\in V\times V^\perp:q\in Ap\}.\]
The mappings
\[x\longmapsto(P_Vx,P_{V^\perp}x),\qquad (p,q)\longmapsto p+q\]
are mutually inverse between \(\operatorname{zer}A_V\) and \(\mathcal S\). Hence every zero \(x\) has the unique orthogonal decomposition \(x=p+q\) with \(p\in V\), \(q\in V^\perp\), and \(q\in Ap\); conversely every such pair produces a zero of \(A_V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal projection gives a one-to-one correspondence between partial-inverse zeros and primal-dual pairs lying in complementary subspaces.

children.title: Tseng Forward–Backward–Forward Splitting
children.top_down_role: Two-forward-evaluation correction architecture.

knowledge_statements.title: Tseng Forward–Backward–Forward Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-stepsize form for a maximally monotone plus monotone Lipschitz inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in H\) and \(\gamma>0\), seek a zero of \(A+B\), where \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is resolvent-accessible and \(B:H\to H\) is explicitly evaluable. For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute
\[y_n=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Bx_n),\qquad x_{n+1}=y_n-\gamma(By_n-Bx_n).\]
The first forward evaluation forms the backward point, while the second supplies Tseng’s correction. Stop when a prescribed tolerance for \(\|x_n-y_n\|\) or another inclusion residual is met, and return \(y_n\) or \(x_n\); otherwise generate the infinite sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tseng splitting performs a forward evaluation, one resolvent step, and a second forward evaluation that corrects the new iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(x_0\in H\).
\(B:H\to H\) can be evaluated at both \(x_n\) and \(y_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_n=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Bx_n)\) and \(x_{n+1}=y_n-\gamma(By_n-Bx_n)\).

children.title: Extragradient Specialization
children.top_down_role: Projection-based corrected forward method.

knowledge_statements.title: Extragradient Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Korpelevich projection specialization for a monotone variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:H\to H\), choose \(x_0\in C\), and fix \(\gamma>0\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), compute
\[y_n=P_C(x_n-\gamma F(x_n)),\qquad x_{n+1}=P_C(x_n-\gamma F(y_n)).\]
Both projections use the same base point \(x_n\), while the second forward value is taken at the predictor \(y_n\). Stop when a chosen variational-inequality residual or gap is below tolerance and return \(y_n\) or \(x_{n+1}\); otherwise continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extragradient takes a projected predictor and then projects a corrected step using the operator evaluated at that predictor.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F:H\to H\) and the projection \(P_C\) are evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_n=P_C(x_n-\gamma F(x_n))\) and \(x_{n+1}=P_C(x_n-\gamma F(y_n))\).

children.title: Forward-Reflected–Backward Splitting
children.top_down_role: Correction using reflected forward information.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Reflected–Backward Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-new-forward-evaluation reflected correction for a two-operator inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
To solve \(0\in Ax+Bx\), choose \(x_{-1},x_0\in H\) and \(\gamma>0\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), perform
\[x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(x_n-2\gamma Bx_n+\gamma Bx_{n-1}\bigr).\]
After initialization, the stored value \(Bx_{n-1}\) makes each iteration require one new evaluation of \(B\) and one evaluation of the resolvent. Stop when a prescribed fixed-point or inclusion residual is below tolerance and return \(x_{n+1}\); otherwise continue the sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward-reflected–backward splitting extrapolates consecutive forward operator values before applying one backward resolvent step.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(x_{-1},x_0\in H\).
\(J_{\gamma A}\) and evaluations of \(B\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-2\gamma Bx_n+\gamma Bx_{n-1})\).

children.title: Reflected Forward–Backward Splitting
children.top_down_role: Reflection-based explicit correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflected Forward–Backward Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward evaluation at a reflected primal point followed by one resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
To solve \(0\in Ax+Bx\), choose \(x_{-1},x_0\in H\) and \(\gamma>0\). For \(n=0,1,\ldots\), form the reflected point and update
\[r_n=2x_n-x_{n-1},\qquad x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Br_n).\]
Each iteration evaluates \(B\) at the reflected primal point rather than reflecting the operator values. Stop when a prescribed fixed-point or inclusion residual is below tolerance and return \(x_{n+1}\); otherwise continue the sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reflected forward–backward splitting evaluates the forward operator at the extrapolated point twice the current iterate minus the previous iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(x_{-1},x_0\in H\).
\(J_{\gamma A}\) and evaluations of \(B\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_n=2x_n-x_{n-1}\) and \(x_{n+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Br_n)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence is mathematically well formed, but closely related reflected and forward-reflected schemes are named inconsistently across the literature. With no cited source, the exact association between this name and formula cannot be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Weak Convergence Regime
children.top_down_role: Baseline monotone Lipschitz regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Convergence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard constant-stepsize weak convergence of Tseng splitting in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, and let \(B:H\to H\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L>0\). Assume \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing\), choose \(0<\gamma<1/L\), and generate
\[y_n=J_{\gamma A}(x_n-\gamma Bx_n),\qquad x_{n+1}=y_n-\gamma(By_n-Bx_n).\]
Then there exists \(x_\star\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\) such that \(x_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\) and \(y_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\), and moreover \(\|x_n-y_n\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under maximal monotonicity, monotone Lipschitz continuity, solvability, and a stepsize below the reciprocal Lipschitz constant, Tseng iterates converge weakly to a solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone and \(B\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\), \(y_n\rightharpoonup x_\star\), and \(\|x_n-y_n\|\to0\) for some \(x_\star\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p>0\), let \(D\) be a nonempty bounded test set, and let \(G_D:H\to[0,+\infty]\) be a restricted gap satisfying \(G_D(x)=0\) at solutions. For reported points \(\widehat x_N\), an \(O(N^{-p})\) gap regime means that there is a constant \(C_D<+\infty\), independent of \(N\), such that
\[G_D(\widehat x_N)\leq C_DN^{-p}\qquad(N\geq1).\]
Equivalently, the number of iterations sufficient for \(G_D(\widehat x_N)\leq\varepsilon\) is \(O(\varepsilon^{-1/p})\). The designation must state whether \(\widehat x_N\) is a last iterate, a best iterate, or an average.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R:H\to[0,+\infty]\) be a computable residual satisfying \(R(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\) solves the target inclusion, and let \(p>0\). For iterates \((x_n)\), a last-iterate residual rate \(O(N^{-p})\) means that there is a constant \(C<+\infty\), independent of \(N\), such that
\[R(x_N)\leq CN^{-p}\qquad(N\geq1).\]
A best-iterate rate means that there is such a constant \(C\) with
\[\min_{0\leq n<N}R(x_n)\leq CN^{-p}\qquad(N\geq1).\]
In either case the corresponding iteration complexity for tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is \(O(\varepsilon^{-1/p})\). Rates for \(R\) and \(R^2\) must be distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual-rate classifications distinguish last-iterate from best-iterate decay, state the associated iteration complexity, and distinguish rates for a residual from rates for its square.

children.title: Ergodic Status
children.top_down_role: Distinction between averaged-iterate and pointwise complexity guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of convergence guarantees by the sequence to which they apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given iterates \((x_n)\), auxiliary points \((y_n)\), and weights \(w_n>0\), define the weighted average
\[\bar y_N=\frac{\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}w_ny_n}{\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}w_n}.\]
A gap or residual guarantee is ergodic when it is asserted for \(\bar y_N\) or another explicitly averaged sequence. It is nonergodic when it applies to an individual iterate such as \(x_N\), \(y_N\), or a best iterate selected from the first \(N\) steps. An ergodic rate alone makes no corresponding last-iterate assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ergodic guarantees concern weighted averages; nonergodic guarantees concern individual or best iterates. An averaged rate does not automatically imply a last-iterate rate.
assumptions_latex: The reported gap or residual identifies its evaluation sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A rate for \(\bar y_N\) is ergodic and, without an additional argument, does not imply the same rate for \(x_N\) or \(y_N\).

notation.meaning: Weighted ergodic average of auxiliary iterates.

children.title: Strong-Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Strengthened operator geometry supporting faster corrected-forward behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator conditions that can strengthen baseline weak convergence and support error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T=A+B\) and let \(x_\star\in T^{-1}(0)\). A local metric-subregularity regime holds when there exist \(\kappa>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_\star\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,T^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,Tx)\qquad(x\in U).\]
A global strong-monotonicity regime holds when there exists \(\mu>0\) such that
\[\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq\mu\|x-y\|^2\]
for all \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}T\). Strong monotonicity implies at most one zero, whereas metric subregularity may permit multiple zeros and is intrinsically local unless \(U=H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong-regularity regimes include local residual error bounds and global strong monotonicity; these conditions have different uniqueness and locality consequences.
assumptions_latex: Distances and graph inequalities are taken in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric subregularity supplies a local error bound; strong monotonicity supplies a global quadratic graph inequality and uniqueness of any zero.

children.title: Linear-Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric convergence behavior under strengthened regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence from averagedness and metric subregularity of the corrected-forward residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(0<\alpha<1\), and set \(S=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Suppose that for some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\in S\) and \(\kappa>0\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\|x-Tx\|\) for every \(x\in U\). If the iteration \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\) remains in \(U\), then
\[\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},S)^2\leq\left(1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\kappa^2}\right)\operatorname{dist}(x^k,S)^2.\]
Thus, whenever the displayed factor is nonnegative, the distance to the solution set converges locally Q-linearly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged corrected-forward map converges locally linearly when its fixed-point residual locally controls distance to the solution set.
assumptions_latex: The generated iterates remain in the regularity neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},S)\leq q\operatorname{dist}(x^k,S)\), where \(q=\sqrt{1-(1-\alpha)/(\alpha\kappa^2)}<1\).

children.title: Locality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on the neighborhood or conditions supporting fast local behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Locality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of conclusions derived solely from local strong regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A residual estimate on a neighborhood \(U\), such as \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{Fix}T)\leq\kappa\|x-Tx\|\), yields no convergence conclusion for an orbit before it enters and remains in \(U\). Indeed, define \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(T(x)=x/2\) when \(|x|\leq1\), \(T(x)=x+1\) when \(x>1\), and \(T(x)=x-1\) when \(x<-1\). Then \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\), and \(|x|=2|x-Tx|\) on \((-1,1)\), yet every orbit starting with \(|x^0|>1\) diverges in magnitude. Hence local regularity requires a basin or invariant-neighborhood hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local residual regularity cannot control iterates outside its neighborhood; an invariant neighborhood or separate globalization argument is required.
assumptions_latex: The regularity estimate is assumed only on a neighborhood of a fixed point.
No global averagedness, invariance, or entrance condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local strong regularity alone does not imply convergence from arbitrary initial points.

children.title: Insufficient-Correction Failures

knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient-Correction Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp correction threshold on a planar skew-monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\) be rotation through \(\pi/2\), let \(B=LR\) with \(L>0\), and consider \(0\in Bx\). For \(t=\gamma L>0\), the corrected-forward iteration with correction weight \(\theta\geq0\),
\[y^k=x^k-\gamma Bx^k,\qquad x^{k+1}=y^k-\theta\gamma(By^k-Bx^k),\]
has iteration matrix \((1-\theta t^2)I-tR\) and norm multiplier \(\rho(t,\theta)=\sqrt{(1-\theta t^2)^2+t^2}\). If \(\theta\leq1/2\), then \(\rho(t,\theta)\geq1\) for every \(t>0\). Thus no positive stepsize produces strict contraction when the correction is at or below one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a skew monotone linear operator, correction weight at most one half prevents contraction for every positive stepsize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x^{k+1}\|\geq\|x^k\|\) for every \(k\) and every \(\gamma>0\).

notation.meaning: Quarter-turn skew-symmetric isometry on the plane.

children.title: Stepsize Failures
children.top_down_role: Instability caused by parameters outside viable calibration ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Stepsize Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp normalized-stepsize failure for full corrected-forward splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=LR\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), where \(L>0\) and \(R\) is rotation through \(\pi/2\), and apply the fully corrected iteration
\[y^k=x^k-\gamma Bx^k,\qquad x^{k+1}=y^k-\gamma(By^k-Bx^k).\]
Writing \(t=\gamma L\), one obtains \(x^{k+1}=((1-t^2)I-tR)x^k\) and
\[\|x^{k+1}\|^2=(1-t^2+t^4)\|x^k\|^2.\]
Consequently, the iteration is strictly contractive exactly when \(0<t<1\), is norm-preserving when \(t=1\), and diverges geometrically for every nonzero initial point when \(t>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a planar skew operator, the full correction converges only below the normalized stepsize boundary; crossing it causes geometric divergence.
assumptions_latex: The correction weight equals one and \(x^0\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\gamma L>1\), \(\|x^k\|=(1-(\gamma L)^2+(\gamma L)^4)^{k/2}\|x^0\|\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=LR\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), where \(L>0\), \(R^*=-R\), and \(R^2=-I\). For the weighted corrected-forward iteration, let \(t=\gamma L>0\) and \(\theta>0\). The one-step norm multiplier satisfies
\[\rho(t,\theta)^2=(1-\theta t^2)^2+t^2.\]
Strict stability, meaning \(\rho(t,\theta)<1\), holds if and only if
\[\theta>\frac12\qquad\text{and}\qquad 0<t<\frac{\sqrt{2\theta-1}}{\theta}.\]
Equality \(t=\sqrt{2\theta-1}/\theta\) is the neutral-stability boundary. Thus correction and stepsize cannot be selected independently: decreasing the correction toward \(1/2\) collapses the admissible positive-stepsize interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar skew model is stable exactly above correction one half and below a correction-dependent normalized stepsize threshold.

children.title: Two-Maximal plus One-Cocoercive Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Canonical three-operator inclusion class.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Maximal plus One-Cocoercive Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical monotone inclusion underlying three-operator splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. A two-maximal plus one-cocoercive inclusion is the problem
\[\text{find }x\in H\text{ such that }0\in Ax+Bx+Cx,\]
where \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone and \(C:H\to H\) is single-valued and \(\beta\)-cocoercive for some \(\beta>0\), meaning
\[\langle Cx-Cy,x-y\rangle\geq\beta\|Cx-Cy\|^2\quad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\]
Its solution set is \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)=\{x\in H:0\in Ax+Bx+Cx\}\). The architecture permits separate resolvent evaluations of \(A\) and \(B\) and one explicit evaluation of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical three-operator problem sums two maximally monotone set-valued operators and one single-valued cocoercive operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target set is \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f,g:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, and let \(h:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(L>0\). Assume
\[0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g).\]
Then a point \(x^\star\in H\) minimizes
\[f(x)+g(x)+h(x)\]
if and only if
\[0\in\partial f(x^\star)+\partial g(x^\star)+\nabla h(x^\star).\]
Thus the model has two implicit components \(A=\partial f\) and \(B=\partial g\), while \(C=\nabla h\) is \(1/L\)-cocoercive.

knowledge_statements.title: Split-Feasibility Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-component convex formulation of constrained split feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H,G\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(C_1,C_2\subset H\) and \(Q\subset G\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(L:H\to G\) be bounded linear. The three-component split-feasibility model
\[\min_{x\in H}\ \iota_{C_1}(x)+\iota_{C_2}(x)+\frac12 d_Q(Lx)^2\]
has smooth term \(h(x)=d_Q(Lx)^2/2\) with
\[\nabla h(x)=L^*(Lx-P_Q(Lx)),\]
whose gradient is \(\|L\|^2\)-Lipschitz. If \(C_1\cap C_2\cap L^{-1}(Q)\neq\varnothing\), its minimizers are exactly the points \(x\in C_1\cap C_2\) satisfying \(Lx\in Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split feasibility with two domain constraints becomes two indicator terms plus a smooth squared-distance penalty in the image space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}(\iota_{C_1}+\iota_{C_2}+d_Q^2\circ L/2)=C_1\cap C_2\cap L^{-1}(Q)\).

notation.meaning: Convex indicator of a set C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation, gradient formula, Lipschitz bound, and feasible-case minimizer characterization are correct. No source is supplied, so the nontrivial split-feasibility encoding and smoothness claim do not satisfy the evidence contract.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(V\subset H\) be a closed vector subspace, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex, and let \(h:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(L>0\). Assume that there exists \(v\in V\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) at which \(f\) is continuous. Then
\[\min_{x\in V} f(x)+h(x)\]
is equivalently
\[\min_{x\in H} f(x)+\iota_V(x)+h(x),\]
and \(x^\star\in H\) solves these problems if and only if
\[0\in\partial f(x^\star)+N_V(x^\star)+\nabla h(x^\star).\]
Moreover, the resolvent of \(N_V\) is the orthogonal projector \(P_V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated continuity qualification, a convex problem constrained to a closed subspace is a three-operator model using the subspace normal cone and orthogonal projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Component Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space encoding of three closed-convex feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,C_2,C_3\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space \(H\). In the product space \(H^3\), define \(C=C_1\times C_2\times C_3\) and the diagonal subspace \(\Delta=\{(x,x,x):x\in H\}\). Then
\[C_1\cap C_2\cap C_3\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\cap\Delta\neq\varnothing.\]
Moreover, \(x\in C_1\cap C_2\cap C_3\) if and only if \((x,x,x)\) minimizes
\[\iota_C(z)+\frac12 d_\Delta(z)^2\]
over \(z\in H^3\) with minimum value zero. The two projectors are explicit: \(P_C\) acts componentwise and \(P_\Delta(z_1,z_2,z_3)=(\bar z,\bar z,\bar z)\), where \(\bar z=(z_1+z_2+z_3)/3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three-set feasibility is equivalently intersection of a product set with the diagonal, with componentwise and averaging projections.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2,C_3\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^3C_i\iff(x,x,x)\in(C_1\times C_2\times C_3)\cap\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Product set C1 times C2 times C3.
Diagonal subspace of the product space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(r_1,r_2:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, let \(\ell:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(L>0\), and let \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0\). Assume

children.title: Base Three-Operator Method

knowledge_statements.title: Base Three-Operator Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrelaxed Davis–Yin splitting for two maximal and one cocoercive operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, let \(C:H\to H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, choose \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), and initialize \(z^0\in H\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute
\[x_B^k=J_{\gamma B}(z^k),\qquad x_A^k=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(2x_B^k-z^k-\gamma Cx_B^k\bigr),\qquad z^{k+1}=z^k+x_A^k-x_B^k.\]
Stop when a prescribed residual test, such as \(\|x_A^k-x_B^k\|\leq\varepsilon\), is met, and return \(x_B^k\). Every fixed point \(z^\star\) of the update map yields a solution \(x^\star=J_{\gamma B}(z^\star)\) of \(0\in Ax+Bx+Cx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Davis–Yin splitting evaluates each maximal operator through one resolvent and the cocoercive operator through one forward evaluation per iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\gamma<2\beta\) and the solution set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^\star=Tz^\star\Rightarrow J_{\gamma B}(z^\star)\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of gamma A, equal to the inverse of I plus gamma A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Davis–Yin three-operator fixed-point method and convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base three-operator splitting for two implicit maximal-monotone terms and one explicit cocoercive term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb A,\mathbb B,\mathbb C:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be maximal monotone, with \(\mathbb C\) single-valued, and let \(\alpha>0\). Define
\[
T=R_{\alpha\mathbb A}\bigl(R_{\alpha\mathbb B}-\alpha\mathbb C J_{\alpha\mathbb B}\bigr)-\alpha\mathbb C J_{\alpha\mathbb B}.
\]
Then
\[
0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B+\mathbb C)x
\iff
\exists z\in\operatorname{Fix}\!\left(\tfrac12(I+T)\right)\ \text{with}\ x=J_{\alpha\mathbb B}z,
\]
where
\[
\tfrac12(I+T)=I-J_{\alpha\mathbb B}+J_{\alpha\mathbb A}\bigl(R_{\alpha\mathbb B}-\alpha\mathbb C J_{\alpha\mathbb B}\bigr).
\]
If \(\mathbb C\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive and \(0<\alpha<2\beta\), this fixed-point map is averaged, although \(T\) itself need not be nonexpansive. If additionally \(\operatorname{Zer}(\mathbb A+\mathbb B+\mathbb C)\neq\varnothing\), the iteration
\[
x^{k+1/2}=J_{\alpha\mathbb B}z^k,
\quad x^{k+1}=J_{\alpha\mathbb A}(2x^{k+1/2}-z^k-\alpha\mathbb Cx^{k+1/2}),
\quad z^{k+1}=z^k+x^{k+1}-x^{k+1/2}
\]
converges. It specializes to backward–forward splitting when \(\mathbb A=0\), forward–backward splitting when \(\mathbb B=0\), and Douglas–Rachford splitting when \(\mathbb C=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Davis–Yin splitting recasts a three-operator monotone inclusion as a fixed-point problem. When the explicit operator C is beta-cocoercive, the step size is between zero and 2 beta, and a zero exists, the iteration converges. Setting A, B, or C to zero gives backward–forward, forward–backward, or Douglas–Rachford splitting, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb A,\mathbb B,\mathbb C:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\text{ are maximal monotone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B+\mathbb C)x\iff \exists z\in\operatorname{Fix}\!\left(\tfrac12(I+T)\right):x=J_{\alpha\mathbb B}z;\quad\text{the stated iteration converges under cocoercivity, }0<\alpha<2\beta,\text{ and nonemptiness of the zero set, with the stated three reductions.}

knowledge_statements.title: Special-Case Lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies standard two-operator methods obtained by suppressing or specializing operators in the Davis–Yin map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(C:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be single-valued, and define \(x=J_{\gamma B}z\), \(y=J_{\gamma A}(2x-z-\gamma Cx)\), and \(Tz=z+y-x\). If \(C=0\), then \(T\) is the Douglas–Rachford fixed-point map for \(A+B\). If \(B=0\), then \(Tz=J_{\gamma A}(z-\gamma Cz)\), the forward–backward map for \(A+C\). If \(B=N_V\) for a closed vector subspace \(V\), then \(J_{\gamma B}=P_V\), and the same formula is the forward–Douglas–Rachford map associated with the subspace-constrained inclusion \(0\in Ax+Cx+N_Vx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford, forward–backward, and forward–Douglas–Rachford arise by setting the forward operator to zero, removing one backward operator, or choosing a subspace normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(\gamma>0\).
The displayed resolvents are everywhere defined.

children.title: Relaxed Three-Operator Variants
children.top_down_role: Three-operator methods modified through relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Three-Operator Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-relaxation Krasnosel'skii–Mann form of the Davis–Yin three-operator iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z^0\in\mathcal H\), choose \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\) and a constant \(\lambda\in(0,1/\alpha)\), where \(\alpha=2\beta/(4\beta-\gamma)\). For \(k\geq0\), compute \(x^k=J_{\gamma B}z^k\), \(y^k=J_{\gamma A}(2x^k-z^k-\gamma Cx^k)\), and \[z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda(y^k-x^k)=z^k+\lambda(Tz^k-z^k).\] Stop when \(\lVert y^k-x^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\), and return the shadow \(x^k\). The unrelaxed Davis–Yin method is recovered at \(\lambda=1\); admissible over-relaxation is possible whenever \(1<1/\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed method applies a Krasnosel'skii–Mann step to the three-operator map and returns the resolvent shadow when its fixed-point residual is small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is a relaxed fixed-point iteration for the \(\alpha\)-averaged Davis–Yin operator \(T\).

children.title: Inertial Three-Operator Variants
children.top_down_role: Three-operator methods modified through memory or momentum.

knowledge_statements.title: Inertial Three-Operator Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step extrapolated Davis–Yin iteration, stated independently of any particular convergence parameter theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z^{-1}=z^0\in\mathcal H\), stepsize \(\gamma>0\), and inertial parameters \(\theta_k\geq0\), form \(w^k=z^k+\theta_k(z^k-z^{k-1})\). Then compute \(x^k=J_{\gamma B}w^k\), \(y^k=J_{\gamma A}(2x^k-w^k-\gamma Cx^k)\), and set \[z^{k+1}=w^k+y^k-x^k=T w^k.\] Stop when both \(\lVert y^k-x^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) and \(\lVert z^k-z^{k-1}\rVert\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x^k\). Setting every \(\theta_k=0\) recovers the base three-operator iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inertial variant extrapolates the fixed-point variable from two consecutive iterates before applying one ordinary Davis–Yin step.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) have single-valued resolvents at the evaluated points.
Any convergence claim requires additional bounds on \((\theta_k)\) and \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=T(z^k+\theta_k(z^k-z^{k-1}))\), with the base method obtained when \(\theta_k=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed extrapolate-then-apply scheme is mathematically defined, but the leaf does not uniquely determine this inertial convention and no source supports its selection or stopping rule.

children.title: Combined Memory-Relaxation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compatibility and stability of simultaneous inertial and relaxed modifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Memory-Relaxation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic extrapolated and relaxed Davis–Yin fixed-point scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(z^{-1}=z^0\in\mathcal H\). Given \(\theta_k\geq0\) and \(\lambda_k>0\), define \(w^k=z^k+\theta_k(z^k-z^{k-1})\), \(x^k=J_{\gamma B}w^k\), and \(y^k=J_{\gamma A}(2x^k-w^k-\gamma Cx^k)\). Update \[z^{k+1}=w^k+\lambda_k(y^k-x^k)=w^k+\lambda_k(Tw^k-w^k).\] Stop when the fixed-point residual and inertial displacement satisfy \(\lVert y^k-x^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) and \(\lVert z^k-z^{k-1}\rVert\leq\varepsilon\); return \(x^k\). The choices \(\theta_k=0\) and \(\lambda_k=1\) recover the relaxed-only and inertial-only schemes, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime first extrapolates the fixed-point variable and then relaxes the three-operator correction, encompassing the two one-parameter variants as special cases.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) have resolvents at all evaluated points.
Convergence requires a compatible joint restriction on \((\theta_k)\), \((\lambda_k)\), and \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The combined update is \(z^{k+1}=w^k+\lambda_k(Tw^k-w^k)\) with \(w^k=z^k+\theta_k(z^k-z^{k-1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Several inequivalent inertial-relaxed three-operator schemes exist. An authoritative source is required to support this update ordering, its parameters, and its stopping rule.

children.title: Accelerated Strong-Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Acceleration available under stronger operator geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Strong-Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear acceleration obtained when additional geometry converts the splitting map into a local contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be a three-operator fixed-point map with nonempty fixed-point set \(F\). Suppose that, on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(F\), an accelerated or parameter-tuned update map \(S\) has the same fixed points and satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(Sz,F)\leq q\operatorname{dist}(z,F)\qquad(z\in U)\] for some \(q\in[0,1)\). If \(z^0\in U\) and all iterates remain in \(U\), then \(z^{k+1}=Sz^k\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(z^k,F)\leq q^k\operatorname{dist}(z^0,F)\). Strong monotonicity, Lipschitz regularity, or metric subregularity can supply the additional geometry needed to establish such a contraction, but the resulting factor is scheme-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stronger operator geometry can make a tuned three-operator update contractive, changing generic asymptotic convergence into geometric convergence with a scheme-dependent factor.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is locally contractive in distance to \(F\) with factor \(q<1\).
The accelerated orbit remains in the contraction neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(z^k,F)\leq q^k\operatorname{dist}(z^0,F)\) for every \(k\geq0\).

children.title: Weak Fixed-Point Convergence
children.top_down_role: Weak convergence behavior of splitting fixed-point iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Fixed-Point Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of relaxed averaged fixed-point iteration in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Generate \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(Tz^k-z^k)\), where \(0<\inf_k\lambda_k\leq\sup_k\lambda_k<1/\alpha\). Then \((z^k)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), \(\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert\to0\), and there exists \(z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) such that \(z^k\rightharpoonup z^\star\). Applied to an averaged Davis–Yin map, this establishes weak convergence of the fixed-point variable, not by itself strong convergence or weak continuity of every associated shadow map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A properly relaxed iteration of an averaged three-operator map converges weakly to a fixed point, while its fixed-point residual vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
The relaxation sequence stays in a compact subinterval of \((0,1/\alpha)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) such that \(z^k\rightharpoonup z^\star\) and \(\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert\to0\).

notation.meaning: Set of fixed points of T.
Weak convergence in the Hilbert space.

children.title: Shadow-Sequence Convergence

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow-Sequence Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of the primal resolvent shadow for the unrelaxed Davis–Yin method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(C:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and assume \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\neq\varnothing\). For \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\), generate \(z^{k+1}=Tz^k\) with the Davis–Yin map and define \(x^k=J_{\gamma B}z^k\). Then there exist \(z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(x^\star=J_{\gamma B}z^\star\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\) such that \(z^k\rightharpoonup z^\star\) and \(x^k\rightharpoonup x^\star\). Thus the convergent shadow is a solution of the original three-operator inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard Davis–Yin assumptions, the resolvent shadow converges weakly to a solution of the original three-operator inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k=J_{\gamma B}z^k\rightharpoonup x^\star\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\).

notation.meaning: Solution set of the monotone inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point-to-Shadow Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic transfer from a Davis–Yin fixed point to an inclusion solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\), let \(C:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). For \(z\in\mathcal H\), define \(x=J_{\gamma B}z\), \(y=J_{\gamma A}(2x-z-\gamma Cx)\), and \(Tz=z+y-x\). If \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), then \(x=y\) and \(0\in Ax+Bx+Cx\). Equivalently, \(J_{\gamma B}(\operatorname{Fix}T)\subseteq\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Davis–Yin fixed point has coincident resolvent shadows, and the primary shadow solves the original three-operator inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(\gamma>0\).
The displayed resolvents are defined at their arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma B}z\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B+C)\).

children.title: Ergodic Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Rates for averaged iterates or averaged certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An order-one-over-iterations bound for the averaged fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be nonexpansive, and let \(z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). Given \(z^0\in\mathcal H\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), define \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda(Tz^k-z^k)\). For every integer \(N\geq1\), define \(\bar r_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(z^k-Tz^k)\). Then \(\bar r_N=(z^0-z^N)/(\lambda N)\) and \(\lVert\bar r_N\rVert\leq2\lVert z^0-z^\star\rVert/(\lambda N)\). Consequently, \(\lVert\bar r_N\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) whenever \(N\geq2\lVert z^0-z^\star\rVert/(\lambda\varepsilon)\) for \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a constantly relaxed nonexpansive fixed-point iteration, the average of the first N residuals has norm at most two times the initial fixed-point distance divided by the relaxation parameter and N.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is nonexpansive on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\bar r_N\rVert\leq2\lVert z^0-z^\star\rVert/(\lambda N)\), yielding \(O(1/\varepsilon)\) fixed-point evaluations.

notation.meaning: Average of the first N fixed-point residuals.

children.title: Best-Iterate Nonergodic Rates

knowledge_statements.title: Best-Iterate Nonergodic Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate residual bound for relaxed averaged fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and let \(z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). Given \(z^0\in\mathcal H\) and a constant \(\lambda\in(0,1/\alpha)\), define \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda(Tz^k-z^k)\). Then, for every integer \(N\geq1\), \(\lambda(1/\alpha-\lambda)\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert^2\leq\lVert z^0-z^\star\rVert^2\) and \(\min_{0\leq k<N}\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert\leq\lVert z^0-z^\star\rVert/\sqrt{\lambda(1/\alpha-\lambda)N}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among the first N iterates of a constantly relaxed averaged fixed-point iteration, at least one fixed-point residual is bounded by the initial fixed-point distance divided by the square root of the relaxation-dependent coefficient times N.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged on a real Hilbert space and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\leq k<N}\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert=O(N^{-1/2})\), yielding an \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) evaluation bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Nonergodic Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Last-iterate asymptotic residual rate for constant-step averaged fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Given \(z^0\in\mathcal H\) and a constant \(\lambda\in(0,1/\alpha)\), define \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda(Tz^k-z^k)\). Then the unaveraged current residual satisfies \(\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert=o(k^{-1/2})\) as \(k\to\infty\). This asymptotic statement does not provide a uniform finite-time constant stronger than the corresponding order bound without additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a constantly relaxed averaged fixed-point iteration, the residual at the current iterate is little-o of one over the square root of k; stronger finite-time guarantees require additional regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged on a real Hilbert space and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
Residual accuracy is measured at the current unaveraged iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert=o(k^{-1/2})\).

notation.meaning: A sequence whose product with the square root of k tends to zero.

children.title: Strong-Regularity Geometry
children.top_down_role: Strengthened local or global geometry supporting faster convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Regularity Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-subregularity condition converting residual decrease into local linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) have fixed-point set \(F\neq\varnothing\), and define \(R=I-T\). The residual is metrically subregular for zero relative to \(F\) at \(z^\star\in F\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(z^\star\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(z,F)\leq\kappa\lVert Rz\rVert\qquad(z\in U).\] If an update \(z^+=Sz\) additionally satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(z^+,F)^2\leq\operatorname{dist}(z,F)^2-c\lVert Rz\rVert^2\) on \(U\), then \[\operatorname{dist}(z^+,F)^2\leq(1-c/\kappa^2)\operatorname{dist}(z,F)^2,\] provided \(0<c/\kappa^2\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound relating distance to the solution set with residual size turns sufficient residual descent into a linear distance contraction.
assumptions_latex: The residual \(R=I-T\) satisfies the displayed local error bound.
The update satisfies the displayed descent inequality and remains in \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local distance contraction factor is at most \(\sqrt{1-c/\kappa^2}<1\) when \(0<c/\kappa^2<1\).

children.title: Linear Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric-rate behavior under suitable regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence from averagedness and a residual error bound for the three-operator fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be the averaged fixed-point map induced by a three-operator splitting, let \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and suppose \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). If a neighborhood \(U\) of \(F\) and \(\kappa>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(z,F)\le \kappa\lVert z-Tz\rVert\) for every \(z\in U\), then every orbit \(z^{k+1}=Tz^k\) remaining in \(U\) satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(z^{k+1},F)\le q\operatorname{dist}(z^k,F),\qquad q=\sqrt{1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\kappa^2}}<1.\] Thus the fixed-point distance converges locally at least Q-linearly; when the fixed point is isolated, the iterates converge R-linearly to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged three-operator map converges locally linearly when its fixed-point residual controls distance to the solution set through a local error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
\(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and the orbit remains in the error-bound neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(z^{k+1},F)\le q\operatorname{dist}(z^k,F)\) for some \(q<1\).

children.title: Loss of Linear Behavior
children.top_down_role: Transitions arising when the strengthened geometry deteriorates.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Linear Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral accumulation at one destroys any uniform linear rate despite strong convergence of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\), choose \(0<\lambda_n<1\) with \(\lambda_n\uparrow1\) and define \((Tz)_n=\lambda_n z_n\). Then \(T\) is linear, self-adjoint, firmly nonexpansive, and \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\); moreover, \(T^kz\to0\) for every \(z\in H\). Nevertheless \(\lVert T\rVert=1\), so no constants \(q<1\) and \(C<\infty\) can satisfy \(\lVert T^kz\rVert\le Cq^k\lVert z\rVert\) simultaneously for all \(z\in H\) and \(k\ge0\). Hence a nonexpansive splitting map can converge strongly while losing every global uniform linear rate when its spectrum accumulates at one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If contraction factors approach one along infinitely many directions, fixed-point iteration may converge strongly but admit no uniform global linear rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^kz\to0\) for every \(z\), but no uniform estimate \(\lVert T^kz\rVert\le Cq^k\lVert z\rVert\) holds with \(q<1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal example is mathematically plausible, but no evidence is cited and its realization as a three-operator splitting map is not documented. An exact source is required for this failure-boundary claim.

children.title: Three-Operator Rate-Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundaries of acceleration, rate, and parameter stability.

children.title: Arbitrarily Slow Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergent behavior lacking a useful uniform rate.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrarily Slow Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A diagonal firmly nonexpansive map realizes convergence slower than any prescribed null sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\), let \(0<\lambda_n<1\) increase to \(1\), and define \((Tz)_n=\lambda_nz_n\). For every nonincreasing sequence \((\varepsilon_k)_{k\ge0}\) of positive numbers with \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), there exists \(z^0\in H\) such that the fixed-point orbit \(z^k=T^kz^0\) obeys \(\lVert z^k\rVert\ge\varepsilon_k\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). Although \(T^kz^0\to0\), no prescribed null sequence bounds the convergence rate uniformly over initial points. The mechanism is the absence of a spectral gap: coordinates with \(\lambda_n\) arbitrarily close to \(1\) retain mass for arbitrarily long intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a spectral gap, a firmly nonexpansive iteration can converge more slowly than any prescribed rate along a suitably chosen initial point.
assumptions_latex: \((\varepsilon_k)\) is positive, nonincreasing, and converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists z^0\in H\) such that \(\lVert T^kz^0\rVert\ge\varepsilon_k\) eventually, while \(T^kz^0\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong quantifier asserting eventual domination of every prescribed null sequence requires an exact arbitrarily-slow-convergence theorem or construction. No source is supplied.

children.title: Parameter-Induced Instability
children.top_down_role: Oscillation or divergence caused by unsuitable parameter choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Induced Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar three-operator instance exhibits the exact forward-step stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the three-operator iteration for \(0\in Ax+Bx+Cx\) with \(A=B=0\) and \(C=L\operatorname{Id}\) on \(H=\mathbb R\), where \(L>0\). Its update reduces to \(z^{k+1}=(1-\gamma L)z^k\). Therefore \(z^k\to0\) for every initialization exactly when \(0<\gamma L<2\). At \(\gamma L=2\), every nonzero orbit alternates between \(z^0\) and \(-z^0\), and for \(\gamma L>2\) its magnitude diverges geometrically. Thus crossing the admissible forward-step boundary converts convergence first to persistent oscillation and then to instability, even for a one-dimensional smooth convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a scalar quadratic instance, the three-operator step converges only below the threshold gamma times L equals two; equality oscillates and larger steps diverge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence holds iff \(0<\gamma L<2\); \(\gamma L=2\) oscillates and \(\gamma L>2\) diverges for \(z^0\ne0\).

notation.meaning: slope and Lipschitz constant of C

children.title: Acceleration Breakdown Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where accelerated behavior disappears or becomes unreliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Breakdown Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excessive inertial extrapolation destabilizes even a scalar contractive fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Tz=qz\) on \(\mathbb R\), where \(q\in(0,1)\), and apply inertial extrapolation \(y^k=z^k+\beta(z^k-z^{k-1})\), followed by \(z^{k+1}=Ty^k\). The resulting recurrence has characteristic polynomial \(p(r)=r^2-q(1+\beta)r+q\beta\). If \(\beta\ge1/q\), the product of its roots is \(q\beta\ge1\), so at least one root has modulus at least one. Consequently there are initial pairs \((z^{-1},z^0)\) for which the accelerated orbit fails to converge to the unique fixed point; strict inequality \(\beta>1/q\) yields an exponentially growing mode. Acceleration therefore requires a stability restriction beyond contractivity of the underlying map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inertial parameter at least the reciprocal contraction factor creates a nondecaying mode, so acceleration can destroy convergence of an otherwise contractive iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\beta\ge1/q\), some initialized orbits do not converge to zero; if \(\beta>1/q\), some diverge geometrically.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Saddle Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel lifting of a linearly composed convex objective into a primal–dual saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded linear, and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. Since \(g(Lx)=\sup_{y\in Y}\{\langle Lx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\}\), the primal problem admits the saddle representation \[\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Lx)\}=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}\mathcal L(x,y),\qquad \mathcal L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Lx,y\rangle-g^*(y).\] A pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a saddle point precisely when \(-L^*\bar y\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(L\bar x\in\partial g^*(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex objective with linear composition equals a convex–concave saddle problem whose saddle points satisfy coupled primal and dual subgradient conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are real Hilbert spaces and \(L:X\to Y\) is bounded linear.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_x(f(x)+g(Lx))=\inf_x\sup_y\mathcal L(x,y)\), with the displayed saddle-point conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Monotone Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space inclusion combining monotone subdifferentials with a skew linear coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded linear, and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(X)\) and \(g\in\Gamma_0(Y)\). Define operators on \(X\times Y\) by \(M(x,y)=\partial f(x)\times\partial g^*(y)\) and \(S(x,y)=(L^*y,-Lx)\). Then \(M\) is maximally monotone and \(S\) is bounded linear and skew-adjoint. Moreover, \[(x,y)\text{ is a saddle point of }f(\cdot)+\langle L\cdot,\cdot\rangle-g^*(\cdot)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in(M+S)(x,y),\] equivalently, \(0\in\partial f(x)+L^*y\) and \(0\in\partial g^*(y)-Lx\). Every such \(x\) minimizes \(f(x)+g(Lx)\), and every such \(y\) maximizes the associated Fenchel dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle-point conditions form a product-space zero problem consisting of a block maximal-monotone operator and a skew linear coupling.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are real Hilbert spaces and \(L:X\to Y\) is bounded linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y)\) is a saddle point exactly when \(0\in(M+S)(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on X

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioned Product-Space Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strongly positive block metric converts the coupled inclusion into a metric-resolvent fixed-point equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z=X\times Y\) be a real Hilbert product space, let \(M:Z\rightrightarrows Z\) be maximally monotone, let \(C:Z\to Z\) be single-valued, and let \(P:Z\to Z\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive. Then \[0\in Mz+Cz\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=J_{P^{-1}M}\bigl(z-P^{-1}Cz\bigr),\] where \(J_{P^{-1}M}=(\operatorname{Id}+P^{-1}M)^{-1}\). Equip \(Z\) with \(\langle u,v\rangle_P=\langle Pu,v\rangle\). If \(D=P^{-1}C\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive in this metric for some \(\beta>1/2\), meaning \[\langle Du-Dv,u-v\rangle_P\ge\beta\lVert Du-Dv\rVert_P^2\quad\text{for all }u,v\in Z,\] then \(\operatorname{Id}-D\) is averaged in the \(P\)-metric, and so is \(J_{P^{-1}M}(\operatorname{Id}-D)\). Block choices of \(P\) can encode primal and dual stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly positive block metric preserves the product-space zeros and represents them as fixed points of a metric resolvent followed by a forward step; an explicit metric cocoercivity threshold makes this map averaged.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is maximally monotone on the real Hilbert product space \(Z=X\times Y\).
\(P\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.
For averagedness, \(P^{-1}C\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive in the \(P\)-metric for some \(\beta>1/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}(M+C)=\operatorname{Fix}\bigl(J_{P^{-1}M}(\operatorname{Id}-P^{-1}C)\bigr)\), and the fixed-point map is averaged under the stated cocoercivity condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Dual Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Rockafellar duality for a convex objective composed with a bounded linear operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(L:X\to Y\) be bounded linear, and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(X)\) and \(g\in\Gamma_0(Y)\). The Fenchel dual of \[\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Lx)\}\] is \[\sup_{y\in Y}\{-f^*(-L^*y)-g^*(y)\}.\] If \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(L(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g)\) and the primal value is finite, then the primal and dual optimal values coincide and a dual maximizer exists under the standard attainment hypotheses. A primal–dual pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is optimal exactly when \(-L^*\bar y\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(L\bar x\in\partial g^*(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of minimizing f(x) plus g(Lx) maximizes the negative conjugates, with strong duality and subgradient optimality under qualification.
assumptions_latex: The primal value is finite and standard attainment hypotheses hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Lx)\}=\sup_y\{-f^*(-L^*y)-g^*(y)\}\), with the displayed optimality correspondence.

children.top_down_role: Operator-duality formulations associated with monotone inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Attouch–Théra Dual Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attouch–Théra duality for a sum of two maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone. The primal inclusion is \[0\in Ax+Bx.\] Define the reflected inverse \(B^{-\oplus}:=(-\operatorname{Id})\circ B^{-1}\circ(-\operatorname{Id})\). Its Attouch–Théra dual inclusion is \[0\in A^{-1}u+B^{-\oplus}u.\] Equivalently, \(u\) solves the dual precisely when there exists \(x\in H\) such that \(u\in Ax\) and \(-u\in Bx\). Thus the primal and dual inclusions encode the same Kuhn–Tucker pairs but exchange the primal variable with the balancing value contributed by the two operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Attouch–Théra dual inverts one operator and uses the reflected inverse of the other, encoding the same balanced primal–dual graph pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone operators on \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in A^{-1}u+B^{-\oplus}u\) iff \(\exists x\) with \(u\in Ax\) and \(-u\in Bx\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attouch–Théra dual inclusion and solvability equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Attouch–Théra dual of a two-operator maximal-monotone inclusion and states equivalence of primal and dual solvability. Since the formulation has no function values, objective-value strong duality is not defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathbb A,\mathbb B:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n be maximal monotone, and define \mathbb A^{-\oplus}:=(-I)\mathbb A^{-1}(-I), so that \mathbb A^{-\oplus}(u)=-\mathbb A^{-1}(-u). The Attouch\text{--}Th\'era dual of \operatorname{find}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\;0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)x is \operatorname{find}_{u\in\mathbb R^n}\;0\in(\mathbb A^{-\oplus}+\mathbb B^{-1})u. Moreover, \operatorname{Zer}(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)\neq\varnothing\iff\operatorname{Zer}(\mathbb A^{-\oplus}+\mathbb B^{-1})\neq\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximal monotone operators A and B, the Attouch–Théra dual of 0 in (A+B)x uses the reflected inverse of A together with the inverse of B. The primal inclusion has a solution if and only if the dual inclusion has a solution. Because there are no function values, there is no objective-value notion of strong duality.

children.title: Dual-Solution Correspondences

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kuhn–Tucker pairs give exact correspondences between primal and Attouch–Théra dual solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For maximally monotone \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\), define \(Z=\{x:0\in Ax+Bx\}\), \(K=\{u:0\in A^{-1}u+B^{-\oplus}u\}\), and \[\mathcal K=\{(x,u)\in H\times H:u\in Ax,\ -u\in Bx\}.\] Then \(Z\) and \(K\) are exactly the coordinate projections of \(\mathcal K\): \(Z=\{x:\exists u,(x,u)\in\mathcal K\}\) and \(K=\{u:\exists x,(x,u)\in\mathcal K\}\). More precisely, for each \(x\in Z\), its compatible dual solutions are \(Ax\cap(-Bx)\); for each \(u\in K\), its compatible primal solutions are \(A^{-1}u\cap B^{-1}(-u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual solution sets are the two projections of the Kuhn–Tucker set, with explicit fibers describing all compatible partners.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z=\operatorname{proj}_H^{(1)}\mathcal K\) and \(K=\operatorname{proj}_H^{(2)}\mathcal K\), with the displayed solution fibers.

children.title: Dual Fixed-Point Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Relationships between dual solutions, splitting iterates, and fixed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Fixed-Point Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford fixed points parameterize compatible primal and Attouch–Théra dual solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and define the Douglas–Rachford map \[T_{A,B}=\operatorname{Id}-J_A+J_B(2J_A-\operatorname{Id}).\] If \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{A,B}\), then \(x=J_Az\) and \(u=z-x\) satisfy \(u\in Ax\) and \(-u\in Bx\); hence \(x\) is primal and \(u\) is Attouch–Théra dual. Conversely, every compatible pair satisfying these two graph relations yields the fixed point \(z=x+u\). Consequently \[\operatorname{Fix}T_{A,B}=\{x+u:u\in Ax,\ -u\in Bx\},\] and the resolvent shadow \(J_A(\operatorname{Fix}T_{A,B})\) equals the primal solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each Douglas–Rachford fixed point splits uniquely into a primal shadow and a compatible dual displacement, and every compatible pair produces a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: The Douglas–Rachford resolvents are taken with unit scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{A,B}\) iff \(z=x+u\) for some \(u\in Ax\) and \(-u\in Bx\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal G\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(L:\mathcal H\to\mathcal G\) be bounded linear, and let \(B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone. The infimal postcomposition of \(B\) by \(L\) is

For a finite family \((L_i,B_i)\) with \(L_i:\mathcal H\to\mathcal G_i\) and \(B_i:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\), the corresponding witness relations can be expressed componentwise in the product space \(\prod_i\mathcal G_i\), enabling parallel block evaluations coupled through variables in \(\mathcal H\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal G\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathcal G\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, and let \(K:\mathcal H\to\mathcal G\) be bounded linear. Fenchel-Moreau duality gives the saddle representation
\[
\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\{f(x)+g(Kx)\}
=
\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\sup_{y\in\mathcal G}\{f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\}.
\]
Assume additionally a Fenchel-Rockafellar qualification ensuring strong duality and that the relevant primal and dual optima are attained. Then \((x^*,y^*)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal G\) is a primal-dual saddle point if and only if
\[
0\in\partial f(x^*)+K^*y^*,\qquad 0\in\partial g^*(y^*)-Kx^*.
\]
Thus explicit dualization converts the composite problem into a two-block monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel dualization represents a composed convex term using a dual variable. Under strong duality and attainment, primal-dual saddle points satisfy the coupled subdifferential inclusions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal Z\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(M:\mathcal Z\rightrightarrows\mathcal Z\) be maximally monotone, let \(C:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\) be single-valued, and let \(P:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive. The inclusion \(0\in Mz+Cz\) is equivalent to
\[
0\in P^{-1}Mz+P^{-1}Cz.

Writing \(J_T=(I+T)^{-1}\), the associated forward-backward step in the \(P\)-metric is
\[
z^{k+1}=J_{P^{-1}M}\bigl(z^k-P^{-1}Cz^k\bigr).
\]
If \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal G\) are real Hilbert spaces, \(\mathcal Z=\mathcal H\times\mathcal G\), and \(P\) has block structure relative to this product, its blocks encode primal-dual stepsizes and preconditioning, yielding a block primal-dual scheme from the metric resolvent step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly positive metric transforms a monotone inclusion into a preconditioned form. On an explicitly identified primal-dual product space, a block metric turns its resolvent step into coupled primal and dual updates.

children.top_down_role: Elimination of coupled blocks in a preconditioned inclusion.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal G\) are real Hilbert spaces.
\(Q_{xx}:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\), \(Q_{yy}:\mathcal G\to\mathcal G\), and \(K:\mathcal H\to\mathcal G\) are bounded linear.

notation.meaning: diagonal block operators on the primal and dual spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-complement elimination of a coupled block correction equation.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal G\) be real Hilbert spaces. Let \(Q_{xx}:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\), \(Q_{yy}:\mathcal G\to\mathcal G\), and \(K:\mathcal H\to\mathcal G\) be bounded linear operators, and let \(r_x\in\mathcal H\) and \(r_y\in\mathcal G\). Suppose the block correction equation is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}Q_{xx}&K^*\\K&Q_{yy}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\end{pmatrix}
=-\begin{pmatrix}r_x\\r_y\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(\Delta x\in\mathcal H\), \(\Delta y\in\mathcal G\), and \(Q_{yy}\) is boundedly invertible. Eliminating \(\Delta y\) gives
\[
(Q_{xx}-K^*Q_{yy}^{-1}K)\Delta x=-r_x+K^*Q_{yy}^{-1}r_y,
\qquad
\Delta y=-Q_{yy}^{-1}(r_y+K\Delta x).
\]
If the Schur complement \(Q_{xx}-K^*Q_{yy}^{-1}K\) is also boundedly invertible, the coupled system is equivalent to a primal Schur-complement solve followed by dual back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For explicitly typed primal and dual block operators, Gaussian elimination replaces the coupled correction equation by a Schur-complement primal solve followed by dual recovery.
