children.title: Ergodic Residual Rates
children.top_down_role: Rates for averaged iterates or residual quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Residual Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cesàro averaging of fixed-point residuals for averaged-operator iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\), \(T\), \(\alpha\), and \((x^k)\) satisfy the averaged-operator assumptions, and let \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). Define the averaged residual \(\bar r_N=(N+1)^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N}(x^k-Tx^k)\). Since \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\), the sum telescopes and \[\bar r_N=\frac{x^0-x^{N+1}}{N+1},\qquad \|\bar r_N\|\leq\frac{2\|x^0-z\|}{N+1}.\] Consequently, the norm of the averaged residual has an \(O(N^{-1})\) rate, although this does not by itself bound the residual at the averaged point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The average of fixed-point residual vectors telescopes and decays as one over N+1, without necessarily controlling the residual of the averaged iterate.

notation.meaning: Cesàro average of residual vectors through iteration N
an arbitrary fixed point of T

children.title: Last-Iterate Residual Rates
children.top_down_role: Nonergodic guarantees for current iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Residual Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonergodic residual bound for Picard iteration of an averaged operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged, where \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(0<\alpha<1\), and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Generate \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\) and set \(r_k=x^k-Tx^k\). Nonexpansiveness of \(T\) gives \(\|r_{k+1}\|\leq\|r_k\|\). Combined with averagedness, this yields, for every \(N\geq0\), \[\|r_N\|^2\leq\frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)(N+1)}\operatorname{dist}(x^0,\operatorname{Fix}T)^2.\] Hence the current, unaveraged iterate has residual \(O(N^{-1/2})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For ordinary iteration of an averaged operator, residual norms are nonincreasing and the current iterate has an order-one-over-square-root rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x^N-Tx^N\|\leq\sqrt{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}\,\operatorname{dist}(x^0,\operatorname{Fix}T)/\sqrt{N+1}\).

children.title: Residual-Rate Lower Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sharpness and arbitrarily slow behavior without stronger regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Rate Lower Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence of a uniform linear residual rate without quantitative regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider firmly nonexpansive linear maps \(T_q=qI\) on a nonzero Hilbert space, indexed by \(q\in(0,1)\), and the iteration \(x^{k+1}=T_qx^k\). Its residual is \[\|x^k-T_qx^k\|=(1-q)q^k\|x^0\|.\] Although every fixed instance converges geometrically, no constants \(C>0\) and \(\rho\in(0,1)\), uniform over all \(q\in(0,1)\), can satisfy \(\|x^k-T_qx^k\|\leq C\rho^k\|x^0\|\) for every \(k\). Thus averagedness and fixed-point existence alone do not furnish a uniform linear residual rate; a quantitative error bound or spectral separation is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averagedness alone gives no uniform linear rate: scalar contractions can have factors arbitrarily close to one, so quantitative regularity is essential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(C>0\) and \(\rho<1\) give a geometric residual bound uniformly over \(q\in(0,1)\).

notation.meaning: scalar firmly nonexpansive map q times the identity

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit scalar family directly establishes the stated uniform-rate boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar family correctly rules out constants uniform over all contraction factors, and failure_boundary is the right kind. A source is nevertheless required for this knowledge record.

children.title: Forward–Backward Residual
children.top_down_role: Composite stationarity certificate induced by the splitting map.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Backward Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient residual certificate for convex composite stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable, let \(g:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and take \(\gamma>0\). Define \[G_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\bigr).\] Then \(G_\gamma(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\), equivalently, \(x\) minimizes \(f+g\). Therefore \(\|G_\gamma(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\) is a directly computable forward–backward residual certificate induced by the splitting map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled displacement of a forward–backward step is computable, vanishes exactly at minimizers of the convex composite objective, and directly measures the forward–backward residual.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable on the Hilbert space.
\(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\gamma(x)=0\iff0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of gamma times g

children.title: Monotone-Inclusion Residuals
children.top_down_role: Natural, fixed-point, and enlargement-based residual notions.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Inclusion Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural, fixed-point, and enlargement residual representations for a monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone operators, and set \(M=A+B\). Assume that each value \(Mx\) is closed. For the inclusion \(0\in Mx\), define the natural residual \(r_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,Mx)\). If \(T:H\to H\) is a declared splitting map satisfying \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\operatorname{zer}M\), define \(r_{\mathrm{fp}}(x)=\gamma^{-1}\|x-Tx\|\) for \(\gamma>0\). An enlargement certificate is a triple \((x,u,\varepsilon)\) with \(\varepsilon\geq0\) and \(u\in M^{[\varepsilon]}x\), measured by \(\|u\|\) and \(\varepsilon\). Then \(r_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)=0\) and \(r_{\mathrm{fp}}(x)=0\) are each equivalent to \(x\in\operatorname{zer}M\), while \(u=0\) and \(\varepsilon=0\) give an exact enlargement certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural, fixed-point, and enlargement residuals are distinct representations of a monotone inclusion. Under the stated closed-value and fixed-point assumptions, their exact forms identify solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are monotone and every value of \(M=A+B\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{zer}M\iff r_{\mathrm{fp}}(x)=0\).

notation.meaning: epsilon-enlargement of the summed monotone operator M
set of points x satisfying zero in Mx

children.title: Primal–Dual Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Saddle and restricted-gap measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted saddle gap on prescribed primal and dual test sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex in its first argument and concave in its second. For nonempty test sets \(X_0\subseteq X\) and \(Y_0\subseteq Y\), define \[\mathcal G_{X_0,Y_0}(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y_0}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X_0}L(u,y).\] If \((x,y)\in X_0\times Y_0\), then \(\mathcal G_{X_0,Y_0}(x,y)\geq0\). The bound \(\mathcal G_{X_0,Y_0}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies the saddle inequalities over the test sets up to total error \(\varepsilon\); zero gap is equivalent to a saddle point relative to \(X_0\times Y_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted primal–dual gap compares the candidate against prescribed primal and dual test sets; a small finite gap certifies approximate saddle behavior on those sets.
assumptions_latex: \((x,y)\in X_0\times Y_0\), with both test sets nonempty.
The displayed supremum and infimum are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq\mathcal G_{X_0,Y_0}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies an \(\varepsilon\)-saddle pair relative to \(X_0\times Y_0\).

children.title: Feasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Observable measures of constraint violation.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-based certificate for membership in intersecting closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(x\in H\). Define \[r_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\operatorname{dist}(x,C_i).\] Each projection witness \(p_i=P_{C_i}x\) verifies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C_i)=\|x-p_i\|\). Hence \(r_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies that \(x\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) of every individual constraint set, and \(r_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\). A bound on distance to the intersection additionally requires a regularity or error-bound condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum distance to the constraint sets is a verifiable feasibility certificate; zero means exact feasibility, while distance to their intersection needs additional regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)=0\iff x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the ith constraint set

children.title: Consensus Certificates
children.top_down_role: Observable measures of disagreement among replicated variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact disagreement certificate for a finite family of Hilbert-space variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) belong to a Hilbert space \(H\), with \(m\geq2\), and define \(\bar x=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\). The consensus residual is \[r_{\mathrm{con}}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i-\bar x\|^2\right)^{1/2}.\] It is directly computable and satisfies \(r_{\mathrm{con}}=0\) if and only if \(x_1=\cdots=x_m\). Moreover, \(r_{\mathrm{con}}\leq\varepsilon\) implies \(\|x_i-x_j\|\leq2\varepsilon\) for every pair \(i,j\), providing a verifiable approximate-consensus certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Root-sum-square deviation from the mean vanishes exactly at consensus and bounds every pairwise disagreement by twice the residual.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in H\), where \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(m\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm{con}}=0\iff x_1=\cdots=x_m\), and \(r_{\mathrm{con}}\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow\|x_i-x_j\|\leq2\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: arithmetic mean of the local variables

children.title: Coupling Residual Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Coupling Residual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm certificate for an affine primal coupling constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) be normed spaces, let \(A:X\to Z\) and \(B:Y\to Z\) be bounded linear maps, and let \(c\in Z\). For a candidate \((x,y)\), define the coupling residual \[r_{\mathrm{cpl}}(x,y)=\|Ax+By-c\|_Z.\] This quantity is computable from the candidate and problem data. It satisfies \(r_{\mathrm{cpl}}(x,y)=0\) exactly when the affine coupling constraint holds, while \(r_{\mathrm{cpl}}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies violation at most \(\varepsilon\) in the declared norm. Conversion to distance from the feasible set requires an additional metric-regularity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The norm of an affine coupling violation is an exact, computable constraint certificate; converting it to distance from feasibility requires regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Z\) and \(B:Y\to Z\) are bounded linear maps.
The residual norm on \(Z\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm{cpl}}(x,y)=0\iff Ax+By=c\).

children.title: Objective Value Certificates
children.top_down_role: Observable measures of objective-value quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Value Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal upper bound paired with a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p^\star=\inf_{x\in C}F(x)\), where \(C\neq\varnothing\), and suppose a candidate \(\hat x\in C\) and a verified lower bound \(\ell\leq p^\star\) are available. Define \[g_{\mathrm{val}}(\hat x,\ell)=F(\hat x)-\ell.\] Then \(g_{\mathrm{val}}\geq0\) and \[0\leq F(\hat x)-p^\star\leq g_{\mathrm{val}}(\hat x,\ell).\] Consequently, feasibility of \(\hat x\), validity of \(\ell\), and \(g_{\mathrm{val}}\leq\varepsilon\) jointly certify that \(\hat x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal in objective value. In primal–dual models, \(\ell\) may be supplied by any dual-feasible point through weak duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible objective value minus any verified lower bound gives a computable upper bound on objective suboptimality.
assumptions_latex: \(\hat x\in C\) and \(F(\hat x)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{\mathrm{val}}(\hat x,\ell)\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow F(\hat x)-p^\star\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: verified lower bound on the optimal value

children.title: Stationarity Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual certificate for a monotone inclusion underlying an operator-splitting model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), and consider \(0\in T(x)\). A pair \((x,r)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity certificate when \(r\in T(x)\) and \(\lVert r\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). The certificate is verifiable whenever membership in \(T(x)\) can be checked from the splitting oracle outputs. For a composite model \(F=f+g\) with differentiable \(f\) and proper convex \(g\), one may take \(T=\nabla f+\partial g\), so the certificate condition is \(r\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\) with \(\lVert r\rVert\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is approximately stationary when an explicitly verifiable inclusion residual belongs to its optimality operator and has norm at most the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is the model's optimality operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\in T(x)\) and \(\lVert r\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) certify \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity of \(x\).

children.title: Absolute Residual Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on fixed residual tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Residual Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-independent termination test for a computed splitting residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^k)_{k\geq0}\) be iterates and let \(r^k\in H\) be a residual satisfying \(r^k=0\) exactly at the target fixed-point or inclusion condition. Given an absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}>0\), the absolute residual stopping rule terminates at the first index \(k\) for which \(\lVert r^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\). The returned output is \(x^k\), together with \(r^k\) and its norm as the termination certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop at the first iterate whose residual norm is no larger than a fixed absolute tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k_{\mathrm{stop}}=\inf\{k\geq0:\lVert r^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\}\).

children.title: Relative Residual Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on residuals normalized by problem or iterate scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Residual Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination test normalizing a residual by a positive problem-dependent scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r^k\in H\) be a residual and let \(s^k\geq0\) be a computable scale formed from current data, operator terms, or iterate magnitudes. Given \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}>0\), the relative residual rule terminates at the first \(k\) satisfying \(\lVert r^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}s^k\), equivalently \(\lVert r^k\rVert/s^k\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\) when \(s^k>0\). A strictly positive scale or a separate zero-scale convention is required for the ratio form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when the residual is small relative to a computable scale, with an explicit convention for a zero scale.
assumptions_latex: \(r^k\) is a computable residual whose zero characterizes the target condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k_{\mathrm{stop}}=\inf\{k\geq0:\lVert r^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}s^k\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic relative rule is coherent, including its zero-scale qualification, but no source is supplied for the normalization convention. Because admissible scales and zero-scale behavior are algorithm-dependent, authoritative support with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Hybrid Scale Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Combined tolerance design for small-scale or large-scale regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(r^k\in H\) and \(s^k\geq0\) are computable for every \(k\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k_{\mathrm{stop}}=\inf\{k\geq0:\lVert r^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}s^k\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined absolute-relative rule preventing degeneracy near zero scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r^k\in H\) be a computable residual, let \(s^k\geq0\) be a computable scale, and choose \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}>0\). The additive hybrid rule terminates at the first \(k\) such that \(\lVert r^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}s^k\). The positive absolute term ensures that a vanishing scale does not require the residual to be exactly zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when the residual satisfies an additive absolute-relative tolerance, so a vanishing scale does not require an exactly zero residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Scale Safeguards

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix primitive oracle classes \(\mathcal O=(O_1,\ldots,O_q)\), such as forward evaluations, resolvents, projections, and proximal maps. If iteration \(k\) invokes oracle \(O_i\) exactly \(n_{i,k}\) times and termination occurs after \(K\) iterations, define the operator-evaluation complexity vector by \(N(K)=(N_1(K),\ldots,N_q(K))\), where \(N_i(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}n_{i,k}\). children.title: Inner-Solve Complexity
children.top_down_role: Cost of approximate resolvents and nested solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Solve Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested-work accounting for approximate resolvent or proximal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose outer iteration \(k\) requires an approximate oracle output \(z^k\) satisfying an inner certificate \(e_k(z^k)\leq\delta_k\), and let \(m_k\) be the number of inner primitive steps used to obtain it. If the outer method terminates after \(K\) iterations, its inner-solve complexity is \(M(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}m_k\). If an inner solver guarantees \(m_k\leq\Psi_k(\delta_k)\), then \(M(K)\leq\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\Psi_k(\delta_k)\). The tolerance schedule must also satisfy the inexactness conditions required by the outer convergence result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total nested-solver work is the sum of inner iterations needed to meet each prescribed inexact-oracle tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Each inner problem has a verifiable error measure \(e_k\).
The outer method stops after \(K\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}m_k\leq\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\Psi_k(\delta_k)\).

children.title: Communication-Round Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Round Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous distributed cost measured by sequential communication phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a distributed algorithm on a fixed communication network. A communication round is one logical phase in which every participating agent may send the messages permitted by the protocol and receives all messages required before its next dependent local update. If outer iteration \(k\) uses \(q_k\) such phases and termination occurs after \(K\) iterations, the communication-round complexity is \(R(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}q_k\). Parallel messages within one phase contribute one round, whereas sequentially dependent exchanges contribute distinct rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication-round complexity counts sequential network phases through termination, treating parallel exchanges within one phase as a single round.
assumptions_latex: The communication protocol and network are fixed.
A round boundary is defined by message dependency, not message count.

notation.meaning: communication phases used in outer iteration k

children.title: Message Complexity
children.top_down_role: Transmission-count accounting across workers, agents, or network edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Message Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed cost measured by transmitted point-to-point messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a distributed execution over directed communication edges. Let \(m_{e,k}\) be the number of messages transmitted over edge \(e\) during outer iteration \(k\), counting each point-to-point transmission once. If termination occurs after \(K\) iterations, the message complexity is \(M(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sum_e m_{e,k}\). When payload sizes vary, a separate volume measure is \(B(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sum_e\sum_{j=1}^{m_{e,k}}b_{e,k,j}\), where \(b_{e,k,j}\) is the transmitted payload size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Message complexity counts point-to-point transmissions through termination; varying payload sizes require a separate total-volume measure.
assumptions_latex: The communication graph and addressing convention are fixed.
Broadcasts are expanded into point-to-point transmissions unless declared otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sum_e m_{e,k}\), with optional volume \(B(K)=\sum_{k,e,j}b_{e,k,j}\).

notation.meaning: messages sent over edge e during iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The count and payload-volume formulas are internally consistent, but no citation supports the point-to-point, broadcast-expansion, or payload conventions. Because these conventions materially determine the reported complexity, a specific authoritative source is required.

children.title: Synchronization-Barrier Complexity
children.top_down_role: Costs caused by coordinated progress points in parallel execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization-Barrier Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts globally blocking coordination events in a distributed splitting execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a distributed execution trace \(\tau=(e_1,\ldots,e_m)\). A synchronization barrier is an event at which a specified worker set \(W_j\) cannot begin its next local phase until every worker in \(W_j\) has completed its current phase. If \(b(e_i)\in\{0,1\}\) indicates such an event, the synchronization-barrier complexity of an execution terminating with certificate accuracy at most \(\varepsilon\) is \[B(\tau,\varepsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}b(e_i).\] The worst-case barrier complexity over an admissible instance class \(\mathcal I\) is \[B_{\mathcal I}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal I}B(\tau_P,\varepsilon),\] with nonterminating executions assigned value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Barrier complexity counts globally blocking synchronization events before the prescribed accuracy certificate is reached; its worst-case value is the supremum over admissible problem instances.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_P\) records all coordination events generated on instance \(P\).
Termination is defined by a fixed certificate with tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathcal I}(\varepsilon)\) measures blocking coordination independently of local arithmetic and message count.

notation.meaning: indicator that event e is a synchronization barrier

review_flags: No supplied locator directly defines synchronization-barrier accounting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the terminal container and is internally precise, but the proposed barrier-counting convention has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Delay-Sensitive Communication Cost
children.top_down_role: Communication accounting under latency, staleness, or heterogeneous worker speeds.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Sensitive Communication Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weights distributed messages by latency or staleness rather than counting messages uniformly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a terminating distributed execution produce messages \(M(\tau)=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). For message \(i\), let \(s_i\) and \(r_i\) be its send and receipt times, let \(d_i=r_i-s_i\geq0\) be its delay, and let \(a_i\geq0\) be a size, link, or importance weight. Given a nondecreasing penalty \(\psi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\), its delay-sensitive communication cost is \[C_{\psi}(\tau)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_i\psi(d_i).\] For tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) and instance class \(\mathcal I\), define \(C_{\psi,\mathcal I}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal I}C_\psi(\tau_P)\), assigning \(+\infty\) to executions that never attain the required certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delay-sensitive cost sums message weights multiplied by a nondecreasing penalty on delivery delay, then takes a worst case over instances when required.
assumptions_latex: Every counted message has finite send time, receipt time, and nonnegative weight.
The penalty \(\psi\) and termination certificate are fixed before instances are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\psi,\mathcal I}(\varepsilon)\) distinguishes executions having equal message counts but different communication delays.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this delay-weighted cost convention.

children.title: Metric Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Local residual-to-solution geometry for inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual-to-solution regularity for a set-valued inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be normed spaces, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) if there exist \(\kappa\geq0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,F^{-1}(\bar y)\bigr)\leq \kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\bar y,F(x)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The convention \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,\varnothing)=+\infty\) is used. For an inclusion \(0\in F(x)\), this bounds distance to the solution set by the inclusion residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity locally bounds distance to the inverse image of a target value by the residual distance from that value to the mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\) holds locally around \(\bar x\).
review_flags: Standard definition, but no supplied locator specifically addresses metric subregularity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard and mathematically precise definition of metric subregularity, but no source reference or locator is supplied.

children.title: Quadratic Growth
children.top_down_role: Objective growth near solution sets as a source of sharper local convergence behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic objective growth away from the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper on a normed space, let \(f_*=\inf_X f\), and suppose the minimizer set \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_X f\) is nonempty. The function \(f\) has local quadratic growth on a set \(U\subset X\) with modulus \(\mu>0\) if \[f(x)-f_*\geq \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] Quadratic growth at \(\bar x\in S\) means that such \(\mu\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) exist. This condition need not imply global strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a minimizer, quadratic growth requires objective suboptimality to dominate a positive multiple of squared distance to the full minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f_*\geq(\mu/2)\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) throughout the stated local region.

children.title: Functional Error Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Functional Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds solution distance by a prescribed function of objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(f_*=\inf_X f\), and suppose \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_X f\neq\varnothing\). Given a set \(U\subset X\) and a nondecreasing function \(\varphi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfying \(\varphi(0)=0\), a functional error bound holds on \(U\) if \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\varphi\bigl(f(x)-f_*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] A Hölder error bound has \(\varphi(t)=c t^\theta\) for constants \(c>0\) and \(\theta\in(0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional error bound controls distance to minimizers by a nondecreasing function of objective suboptimality; Hölder bounds use a power function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\varphi(f(x)-f_*)\) for all eligible \(x\) in the stated region.

notation.meaning: region on which the bound is asserted

review_flags: Standard formulation, but no supplied locator specifically supports functional error bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The functional and Hölder error-bound formulations are precise and fit the condition container, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Growth–Error-Bound Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Error-Bound Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex local equivalence between quadratic growth and a subdifferential residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with nonempty minimizer set \(S\). Fix \(\bar x\in S\). The following local properties are equivalent: there exist \(\mu>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[f(x)-f_*\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\quad(x\in U),\] and there exist \(\kappa>0\) and a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(0,\partial f(x)\bigr)\quad(x\in V).\] Thus quadratic growth is equivalent to metric subregularity of \(\partial f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex function, local quadratic growth at a minimizer is equivalent to a local error bound using the convex-subdifferential residual.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with \(S\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic growth at \(\bar x\) holds if and only if \(\partial f\) is metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(0\).
review_flags: Exact equivalence theorem requires an authoritative variational-analysis locator not supplied in the shard.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed convex equivalence is plausible and appropriately typed as a theorem, but its exact local hypotheses and equivalence require an authoritative variational-analysis source with a theorem or section locator.

children.title: Local Growth Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degenerate or nonuniform regimes where objective-level growth offers no sharper local control.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Growth Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A flat convex minimum can destroy quadratic growth and linear residual error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(f(x)=x^4\). Then \(S=\{0\}\), \(f_*=0\), and \(\partial f(x)=\{4x^3\}\). For every \(\mu>0\) and every neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\), some nonzero \(x\in U\) satisfies \[x^4<\frac{\mu}{2}x^2,\] so local quadratic growth fails. Likewise, no \(\kappa>0\) and neighborhood \(V\) satisfy \[|x|\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(0,\partial f(x)\bigr)=4\kappa|x|^3\quad(x\in V).\] Hence convexity and uniqueness of the minimizer alone do not ensure quadratic growth or metric subregularity of the subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function x to the fourth has a unique minimizer but is too flat for quadratic growth or a linear subdifferential error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither local quadratic growth nor metric subregularity of \(\partial f\) at \(0\) for \(0\) holds.
review_flags: Elementary counterexample is directly checkable, but the shard supplies no citable locator for it.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary counterexample is correct and fits a failure-boundary container, but the record supplies neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Polyhedral Regularity
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional regularity associated with polyhedral feasible or solution geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A polyhedral multifunction admits a local residual error bound at every graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) have a polyhedral graph, meaning that \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is a convex polyhedron. For every \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), there exist \(\kappa\geq0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,F^{-1}(\bar y)\bigr)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\bar y,F(x)\bigr)\qquad(x\in U).\] Thus every polyhedral multifunction is metrically subregular at each point of its graph. The constant and neighborhood may depend on \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction with a convex-polyhedral graph satisfies a local residual-to-solution distance bound at every point of that graph.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has a convex-polyhedral graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\).

notation.meaning: inverse image of the target value

review_flags: The classical polyhedral multifunction error-bound theorem needs a specific authoritative locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated polyhedral multifunction result requires a specific authoritative locator. Because it asserts a universal implication, theorem is a better mathematical role than property for this record.

children.title: Piecewise-Linear Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity arising from locally piecewise-linear mappings or residual structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous piecewise-affine residuals satisfy local linear error bounds around their zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuous and piecewise affine with respect to a finite polyhedral partition, and let \(S=R^{-1}(0)\). For every \(\bar x\in S\), there exist \(\kappa\geq0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\lVert R(x)\rVert\qquad(x\in U).\] Equivalently, the inverse multifunction \(R^{-1}\) is calm at \(0\) for \(\bar x\), and \(R\) is metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(0\). The result follows from the finite piecewise-polyhedral structure, not from differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous map built from finitely many affine pieces locally bounds distance to its zero set by the norm of its residual.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is continuous and affine on every cell of a finite polyhedral partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,R^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa\lVert R(x)\rVert\) locally around \(\bar x\).
review_flags: A specific locator for piecewise-polyhedral multifunction regularity is not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local error-bound claim is plausible, but the piecewise-polyhedral regularity theorem needs a precise source locator. Its universal implication is more accurately classified as a theorem than a property.

children.title: Polyhedral Error-Bound Consequences
children.top_down_role: Error-bound behavior supported by polyhedral structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Error-Bound Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A polyhedral residual error bound converts sufficient decrease into local linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be affine on every cell of a finite polyhedral partition, set \(R=I-T\), and let \(S=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Suppose an orbit \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) eventually lies in a neighborhood where \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\lVert R(x)\rVert\), and suppose for some \(\sigma>0\) it satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},S)^2\leq\operatorname{dist}(x^k,S)^2-\sigma\lVert R(x^k)\rVert^2.\] If \(0<\sigma\leq\kappa^2\), then eventually \[\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},S)\leq\sqrt{1-\sigma/\kappa^2}\operatorname{dist}(x^k,S).\] Thus the iterates converge locally Q-linearly in distance to the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a piecewise-affine fixed-point residual, a local error bound plus sufficient decrease yields an explicit local Q-linear contraction in distance to fixed points.
assumptions_latex: The orbit eventually satisfies the displayed error bound and sufficient-decrease inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eventually, \(\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},S)\leq\sqrt{1-\sigma/\kappa^2}\operatorname{dist}(x^k,S)\).
review_flags: The contraction is algebraically checkable, but the polyhedral error-bound premise needs an authoritative source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The contraction factor follows algebraically from the displayed error bound and decrease inequality, and the theorem fits the leaf. Nevertheless, the polyhedral error-bound premise and the packaged convergence result lack a supporting source locator.

children.title: Nonpolyhedral Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structured finite-dimensional models outside the reach of polyhedral regularity arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonpolyhedral residuals need not possess a local linear error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(R:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(R(x)=x^2\). Its zero set is \(S=\{0\}\), but no \(\kappa>0\) and neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\) satisfy \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=|x|\leq\kappa|R(x)|=\kappa x^2\qquad(x\in U).\] Indeed, the inequality for nonzero \(x\) would require \(1\leq\kappa|x|\), which fails as \(x\to0\). Hence continuity, smoothness, and an isolated zero do not replace polyhedral or other regularity assumptions. Only the weaker Hölder bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=|R(x)|^{1/2}\) holds here.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smooth residual R(x)=x squared has an isolated zero but no local linear residual error bound; it only satisfies a square-root Hölder bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is not metrically subregular at \(0\) for \(0\), despite being smooth with an isolated zero.
review_flags: Elementary failure example is directly checkable, but no supporting source locator is supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The smooth residual counterexample and Hölder identity are correct and fit the failure-boundary container, but no citation or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Partial Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Local smooth-manifold structure underlying nonsmooth objectives or operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex partial smoothness relative to an active manifold at a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\mathcal M\) be a \(C^2\) manifold containing \(\bar x\). The function \(f\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\mathcal M\) if: the restriction \(f|_{\mathcal M}\) is \(C^2\) near \(\bar x\); the sharpness identity \[T_{\mathcal M}(\bar x)=\operatorname{par}(\partial f(\bar x))^\perp\] holds; and the set-valued mapping \(\partial f\), restricted to \(\mathcal M\), is continuous at \(\bar x\). Here \(\operatorname{par}(C)=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is partly smooth when it is smooth along an active manifold, sharp transverse to it, and its subdifferential varies continuously along it.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(\mathcal M\) is a \(C^2\) manifold containing \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smoothness on \(\mathcal M\), the tangent-sharpness identity, and subdifferential continuity jointly define partial smoothness at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: tangent space to the manifold at the reference point
linear space parallel to the affine hull of C

children.title: Active-Structure Identification
children.top_down_role: Finite recognition of the locally relevant support, face, rank pattern, or manifold.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Structure Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification under partial smoothness and a relative-interior nondegeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional, let \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and suppose that \(g\) is partly smooth at \(x^\star\) relative to a \(C^2\) manifold \(\mathcal M\). If \(x^k\to x^\star\), \(v^k\in\partial g(x^k)\), \(v^k\to v^\star\), and \(v^\star\in\operatorname{ri}\partial g(x^\star)\), then the active manifold is identified finitely: there exists \(K<\infty\) such that \(x^k\in\mathcal M\) for every \(k\ge K\). Thus the nonsmooth active structure encoded by \(\mathcal M\) becomes constant after finitely many iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent primal-subgradient pairs identify a partly smooth active manifold in finite time when the limiting subgradient lies in the relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(g\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(g\) is partly smooth at \(x^\star\) relative to \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists K<\infty\;\forall k\ge K:\ x^k\in\mathcal M\).

children.title: Post-Identification Local Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local convergence behavior after the active structure has stabilized.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-Identification Local Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth local dynamics obtained after finite active-manifold identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an iteration \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) identifies a \(C^2\) active manifold \(\mathcal M\) at \(x^\star\), and the restriction \(T|_{\mathcal M}\) is differentiable at \(x^\star\). For all sufficiently large \(k\), the error \(e_k=x^k-x^\star\) satisfies \(e_{k+1}=J e_k+o(\|e_k\|)\), where \(J=D(T|_{\mathcal M})(x^\star)\) acts on the tangent space. If \(\rho(J)<1\), then \(x^k\to x^\star\) locally at a linear-type rate; if \(J=0\) and the remainder is \(O(\|e_k\|^2)\), the local rate is at least quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After identification, the method follows a smooth tangent-space iteration whose linearization determines linear or faster local convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{k+1}=J e_k+o(\|e_k\|)\); in particular, \(\rho(J)<1\) gives local linear-type convergence.

notation.meaning: derivative of the identified iteration on the active manifold

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: differentiable fixed-point linearization after identification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the post-identification container, but the statement is not reliably supported. Differentiability at the fixed point gives a first-order expansion along a convergent identified sequence, while spectral radius below one does not by itself establish the asserted local convergence without suitable neighborhood regularity, invariance, and initialization hypotheses. A method-specific source is required.

children.title: Identification Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degenerate regimes where active structures remain ambiguous or fail to stabilize.

knowledge_statements.title: Identification Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate boundary solutions may be approached without finite support identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2+|x|\) on \(\mathbb R\), whose unique minimizer is \(x^\star=0\). For proximal-gradient steps with \(0<\gamma<1\), \[x^{k+1}=\operatorname{soft}((1-\gamma)x^k+\gamma,\gamma).\] If \(x^0>0\), then \(x^{k+1}=(1-\gamma)x^k>0\) for every finite \(k\), although \(x^k\to0\). Here \(-\nabla\tfrac12(x-1)^2|_{x=0}=1\) lies on the boundary of \(\partial|0|=[-1,1]\), so relative-interior nondegeneracy fails and the zero active set is never identified finitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate boundary solution, proximal gradient can converge to zero while every finite iterate remains strictly positive, preventing finite active-set identification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k=(1-\gamma)^k x^0>0\) for every finite \(k\), while \(x^k\to x^\star=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: directly checkable one-dimensional proximal-gradient counterexample

children.title: Descent-Error Compatibility Framework
children.top_down_role: Abstract sequence framework used before invoking KL geometry.

children.title: Sufficient-Descent Control
children.top_down_role: Objective or Lyapunov decrease used to organize abstract sequence analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient-Descent Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform quadratic decrease relative to successive displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \((x^k)_{k\ge0}\subset\operatorname{dom}H\). The sequence satisfies sufficient-descent control if there exists \(a>0\) such that, for every \(k\ge0\), \[H(x^{k+1})+a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2\le H(x^k).\] Consequently, \((H(x^k))\) is nonincreasing and, whenever \(\inf H> -\infty\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration must decrease the Lyapunov value by at least a fixed positive multiple of the squared step length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(x^k)\) decreases and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2<\infty\).

children.title: Relative-Error Control
children.top_down_role: Residual or subgradient control relative to inter-iterate motion.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Error Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity residual controlled by the most recent displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. A sequence \((x^k)_{k\ge0}\subset\operatorname{dom}H\) satisfies relative-error control if there exist \(b>0\) and \(w^{k+1}\in\partial H(x^{k+1})\) such that, for every \(k\ge0\), \[\|w^{k+1}\|\le b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial H(x^{k+1}))\le b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\). Hence vanishing steps force asymptotic stationarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient at each new iterate is bounded by a uniform multiple of the latest step, so vanishing steps imply asymptotic stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\) implies \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial H(x^{k+1}))\to0\).

notation.meaning: selected limiting subgradient at the new iterate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical relative-error hypothesis in KL descent analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and formula match the relative-error leaf, and the stated implication from vanishing steps is correct. No inspectable source is supplied for the canonical KL-framework hypothesis.

children.title: Descent–Error Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Joint regimes where decrease information aligns with residual control before KL geometry is invoked.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent–Error Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A shared step measure couples Lyapunov decrease and stationarity error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Lyapunov sequence \((z^k)\) for \(H\) is descent–error compatible if there exist constants \(a,b,c>0\), step measures \(d_k\ge0\), and residuals \(w^{k+1}\in\partial H(z^{k+1})\) such that, for every \(k\), \[H(z^k)-H(z^{k+1})\ge a d_k^2,\qquad \|w^{k+1}\|\le b d_k,\qquad \|z^{k+1}-z^k\|\le c d_k.\] The same quantity \(d_k\) must therefore control decrease, stationarity error, and actual displacement with constants uniform in \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatibility requires one step measure to control objective decrease, stationarity residual, and actual displacement uniformly across iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_k\to0\) forces both \(\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|\to0\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial H(z^{k+1}))\to0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: abstract KL descent-error compatibility template

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the compatibility leaf and the formulas are internally consistent. Because abstract KL frameworks use several non-equivalent step, delay, and residual templates, an authoritative locator is required to establish that this particular shared-measure formulation is the intended one.

children.title: Framework Breakdown Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where descent or relative-error control is too weak for the abstract framework.

knowledge_statements.title: Framework Breakdown Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL regularity alone cannot replace descent or relative-error control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KL property of \(H\) alone does not imply convergence of an arbitrary sequence. For \(H(x)=x^2\), the nonconvergent sequence \(x^k=(-1)^k\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial H(x^{k+1}))\le\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\), but no positive sufficient-descent constant exists because \(H(x^k)\) is constant. Conversely, \(x^k=1/(k+1)\) satisfies a uniform quadratic sufficient-descent inequality, but \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial H(x^{k+1}))/|x^{k+1}-x^k|\to\infty\), so no uniform relative-error constant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for an analytic KL function, relative error without descent permits oscillation, while descent alone need not provide the residual estimate required by KL analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither sufficient descent nor relative-error control can generally be omitted from the descent–error KL framework.

notation.meaning: the singleton containing 2x in this example

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary counterexamples verified by direct calculation

Both elementary examples are mathematically consistent: the oscillating sequence satisfies the displayed relative-error estimate without descent, and the decreasing sequence has uniform quadratic descent while its residual-to-step ratio diverges. children.title: Finite-Length Property
children.top_down_role: Summable trajectory motion obtained through desingularized convergence analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Length Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summability of successive iterate displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \((x^k)_{k\ge0}\subset X\). The sequence has finite length if \[\operatorname{len}(x^k):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d(x^{k+1},x^k)<\infty.\] In a normed space this becomes \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty\). Finite length is stronger than square summability of the steps and implies that every tail displacement is bounded by the corresponding tail-length sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence has finite length when the sum of all successive displacements is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d(x^{k+1},x^k)<\infty\).

notation.meaning: total path length of the sequence

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard metric definition of finite-length sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind is the correct role, and the metric-space definition is precise and standard. The record supplies only a standard-field rationale and no inspectable textbook locator.

children.title: Finite-Length-to-Limit Mechanism
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from controlled trajectory length to exclusion of multiple cluster limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Length-to-Limit Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL desingularization upgrades square-summable steps to summable steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let a bounded sequence \((x^k)\) satisfy sufficient descent, relative-error control, and continuity of \(H\) along convergent subsequences. If \(H\) has the KL property on the compact cluster set of \((x^k)\), then uniformized KL desingularization yields a tail estimate \[\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\|x^{j+1}-x^j\|<\infty.\] Thus the sequence has finite length, converges to one point \(x^\star\), and the relative-error bound gives \(0\in\partial H(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformized KL control combines descent and residual bounds to make step lengths summable, producing convergence to a single critical point.
assumptions_latex: \((x^k)\) is bounded and satisfies sufficient descent and relative-error control.
\(H\) is continuous along convergent iterate subsequences.
\(H\) satisfies the KL property on the cluster set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty\), \(x^k\to x^\star\), and \(0\in\partial H(x^\star)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical abstract KL convergence mechanism

children.title: KL Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finite, linear-type, and sublinear classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: KL Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate classification for a power-type KL exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the descent–error KL framework converges to \(x^\star\), and near \(x^\star\) the KL inequality has power form \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial H(x))\ge c(H(x)-H(x^\star))^\theta\), with \(c>0\) and \(\theta\in[0,1)\). Writing \(r_k=H(x^k)-H(x^\star)\), the standard regimes are: \(\theta=0\), finite termination; \(0<\theta\le\tfrac12\), local linear-type decay of \(r_k\) and the iterate error; and \(\tfrac12<\theta<1\), \(r_k=O(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)})\) and \(\|x^k-x^\star\|=O(k^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KL exponent separates finite termination, linear-type convergence, and explicit sublinear objective and iterate rates.
assumptions_latex: The sufficient-descent and relative-error constants are uniform.
\(x^k\to x^\star\) and the displayed power-type KL inequality holds locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rate is finite for \(\theta=0\), linear-type for \(0<\theta\le\tfrac12\), and polynomial for \(\tfrac12<\theta<1\) with the displayed exponents.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard KL exponent rate trichotomy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind is suitable because the record gives explicit finite, linear-type, and polynomial rates matching the topic role. The rate trichotomy is standard under the displayed exponent convention, but the objective-gap and iterate-rate conclusions require an authoritative theorem locator and confirmation of all descent-error assumptions.

children.title: KL Applications to Splitting Families
children.top_down_role: Proximal-gradient, reflection, and alternating-direction applications.

knowledge_statements.title: KL Applications to Splitting Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common Lyapunov template transfers KL convergence to splitting algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a proximal-gradient, reflected proximal, or alternating-direction splitting method generate a state \(z^k\) and admit a proper lower-semicontinuous Lyapunov function \(H\). If its update equations yield uniform sufficient descent, a relative-error residual in \(\partial H(z^{k+1})\), boundedness, and continuity along cluster subsequences, then any KL property of \(H\) on the cluster set activates the finite-length mechanism. Consequently, \(z^k\) converges to a single critical state; convergence of the original primal and dual variables follows whenever they are continuous components of \(z^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal-gradient, reflection, and alternating-direction schemes inherit KL convergence once a suitable Lyapunov state satisfies the shared descent-error hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: The splitting scheme admits a bounded Lyapunov state \(z^k\).
\(H\) satisfies compatible descent, relative-error, and subsequence-continuity conditions.
\(H\) has the KL property on the cluster set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|<\infty\) and \(z^k\to z^\star\) with \(0\in\partial H(z^\star)\).

children.title: KL Analysis Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure of boundedness, descent, relative-error, or tame-geometry mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: KL Analysis Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies which hypotheses a standard KL finite-length argument cannot dispense with.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x^k)\subset\operatorname{dom}F\). A KL convergence argument based on sufficient descent and relative error does not apply if boundedness of \((x^k)\) fails, if no constants \(a,b>0\) satisfy \(F(x^{k+1})+a\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert^2\leq F(x^k)\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\), or if \(F\) lacks the KL property near the cluster set. In any such case, finite length and convergence to a critical point are not consequences of the KL mechanism alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual KL argument cannot ensure finite length or critical-point convergence when boundedness, sufficient descent, relative error, or the local KL property is absent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of any listed mechanism prevents the standard KL framework alone from implying \(\sum_k\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert<\infty\) and convergence to a critical point.

notation.meaning: distance from zero to the set S

In particular, critical-point convergence commonly also uses a subsequence/function-value continuity condition, so a specialized source is needed to establish exactly which hypotheses are indispensable and which conclusion follows.

children.title: Nonconvex Forward–Backward Interface
children.top_down_role: Stationarity-oriented composite specialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Forward–Backward Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic proximal-gradient specialization for composite nonconvex stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}g\) and stepsizes \(\gamma_k>0\), choose
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma_k g}\bigl(x^k-\gamma_k\nabla f(x^k)\bigr)
:=\mathop{\arg\min}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{g(z)+\frac{1}{2\gamma_k}\lVert z-x^k+\gamma_k\nabla f(x^k)\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Stop when a prescribed stationarity residual is below tolerance and output the current iterate. Any fixed point \(x\) of this update satisfies \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\), provided the selected proximal point obeys its limiting-subdifferential optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient step on the smooth term followed by a possibly set-valued proximal step targets limiting-stationary points of the nonconvex composite objective.
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and each displayed proximal subproblem attains a minimizer.
\(F=f+g\) is bounded below on the generated level set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fixed point satisfying proximal first-order optimality is stationary: \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\).

notation.meaning: possibly set-valued proximal mapping of g

children.title: Nonconvex Reflection-Splitting Interface
children.top_down_role: Weak-convexity and prox-regular reflection specializations.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Reflection-Splitting Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued Douglas–Rachford interface for weakly convex or prox-regular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For proper lower-semicontinuous functions \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), choose \(\gamma>0\), \(z^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\lambda_k\in(0,2)\). Select
\[
x^k\in\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(z^k),\qquad y^k\in\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(2x^k-z^k),\qquad z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(y^k-x^k).
\]
Equivalently, selected branches apply the relaxed reflection composition \(z^{k+1}=(1-\lambda_k/2)z^k+(\lambda_k/2)R_{\gamma g}R_{\gamma f}z^k\), where \(R_{\gamma h}=2\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}-I\). In the nonconvex setting these mappings may be set-valued; convergence requires additional regularity and parameter conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonconvex reflection splitting alternates selected proximal branches and a relaxed reflected update; weak convexity or prox-regularity is needed for local convergence analysis.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper and lower semicontinuous.
The displayed proximal subproblems attain selected minimizers.
The stepsize lies in a regime where the required proximal branches are locally single-valued or consistently selectable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration is a selected relaxed Douglas–Rachford reflection step; the formula alone supplies no global nonconvex convergence guarantee.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxed Douglas-Rachford formulas are algebraically consistent and the algorithm kind fits, but the scope specifically invokes weak convexity, prox-regularity, branch selection, and parameter regimes without a specialized citation. Those details materially determine whether this is a valid nonconvex reflection-splitting interface.

children.title: Nonconvex ADMM Interface
children.top_down_role: Structured nonconvex alternating-direction specialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex ADMM Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-block augmented-Lagrangian interface for structured nonconvex equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_{x,y}\{f(x)+g(y):Ax+By=c\}\), choose \(\rho>0\), \((y^0,u^0)\), and generate
\[
x^{k+1}\in\mathop{\arg\min}_x\left\{f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+By^k-c+u^k\rVert^2\right\},
\]
\[
y^{k+1}\in\mathop{\arg\min}_y\left\{g(y)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax^{k+1}+By-c+u^k\rVert^2\right\},\qquad
u^{k+1}=u^k+Ax^{k+1}+By^{k+1}-c.
\]
Stop when primal and prescribed dual residuals meet tolerance. In the nonconvex case the updates define an interface, while stationarity of cluster points requires separate boundedness, regularity, and penalty assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonconvex ADMM alternately minimizes the augmented Lagrangian and updates the scaled multiplier; stationarity requires assumptions beyond the iteration formula.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper and lower semicontinuous, with at least one possibly nonconvex.
Every displayed block subproblem attains a selected minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated sequence follows scaled two-block ADMM; no unconditional nonconvex convergence claim is attached to the update.

children.title: Spurious Limit Points
children.top_down_role: Accumulation points that do not represent the intended solution or criticality notion.

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Limit Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convergent fixed-point iteration whose limit is not stationary for the stated objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) given by \(F(x)=x^2\) and the iteration mapping \(T(x)=1\). From every \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}\), the recursion \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) satisfies \(x^k=1\) for all \(k\geq1\), hence converges to the fixed point \(\bar x=1\). Nevertheless, \(F'(\bar x)=2\neq0\), so \(\bar x\) is not stationary for minimizing \(F\). Therefore convergence of iterates, without a fixed-point-to-stationarity correspondence or vanishing stationarity residual, does not certify a solution-relevant limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant iteration converges to one, but one is not stationary for the quadratic objective, showing that convergence alone can be spurious.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limit \(\bar x=1\) is a fixed point of \(T\) but not a stationary point of \(F\).

children.title: Iterate Divergence
children.top_down_role: Unbounded or nonconvergent trajectories in nonconvex splitting regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A translation iteration demonstrating failure when boundedness or coercive control is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(T(x)=x+1\), and generate \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) from any \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(x^k=x^0+k\) for every \(k\geq0\), so \(\lvert x^k\rvert\to\infty\). The mapping has no fixed point, and the sequence has no cluster point. Hence an iteration formula without bounded level sets, coercivity, Fejér monotonicity, or another mechanism controlling distance cannot by itself provide subsequential or full convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated translation by one sends every real starting point to infinity, illustrating divergence when no boundedness mechanism controls the iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates satisfy \(\lvert x^k\rvert\to\infty\) and possess no cluster point.

children.title: Residual-Decrease Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of residual decrease as evidence for global convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Decrease Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded orbit whose fixed-point residual remains positive and never decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(T:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(T(x)=-x\), set the fixed-point residual \(r(x)=\lvert T(x)-x\rvert\). If \(x^0=a\neq0\) and \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\), then \(x^k=(-1)^ka\) and
\[
r(x^k)=2\lvert a\rvert>0
\]
for every \(k\geq0\). Thus neither strict residual decrease nor residual convergence to zero holds, despite boundedness of the orbit. Any convergence theorem requiring a decreasing or vanishing residual lies beyond its applicable boundary for this iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonzero reflection two-cycle, the fixed-point residual stays at a positive constant, so boundedness alone does not yield residual decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual is constant and positive: \(r(x^k)=2\lvert a\rvert\) for all \(k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifts a weighted sum inclusion to separable product operators coupled through the consensus subspace.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H=H^m\) carry the standard product inner product, define \(V=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in H\}\), and define
\[
\mathcal A_\omega(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=(\omega_1A_1x_1)\times\cdots\times(\omega_mA_mx_m).
\]
Then
\[
0\in\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_iA_i x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\mathcal A_\omega(x,\ldots,x)+N_V(x,\ldots,x).
\]
Moreover, for every \(\gamma>0\) and \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\in\mathcal H\),
\[
J_{\gamma\mathcal A_\omega}(v)=\bigl(J_{\gamma\omega_1A_1}(v_1),\ldots,J_{\gamma\omega_mA_m}(v_m)\bigr),
\]
so the component resolvents can be evaluated independently in parallel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the standard product inner product, a weighted sum inclusion is equivalent to a product-space inclusion formed from weighted component operators and the consensus-subspace normal cone. The product resolvent separates into independent component resolvents.

children.title: Parallel Proximal Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Concurrent evaluation of component proximal mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Proximal Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous proximal evaluation of separable component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f_i:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and choose \(\gamma_i>0\). Given inputs \(v_i^k\in H\), compute independently and simultaneously
\[
p_i^k=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma_i f_i}(v_i^k)
=\mathop{\arg\min}_{z\in H}\left\{f_i(z)+\frac{1}{2\gamma_i}\lVert z-v_i^k\rVert^2\right\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
After every component finishes, output \(p^k=(p_1^k,\ldots,p_m^k)\) to the aggregation step. Each subproblem depends only on its own component data and may therefore be evaluated concurrently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each component computes its own proximal point from local data at the same iteration, and the resulting tuple is passed to aggregation.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the componentwise product proximal evaluation \(p^k=(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma_i f_i}(v_i^k))_{i=1}^m\).

notation.meaning: proximal output of component i at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous resolvent calls for the components of a scaled product operator.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\), and define the scaled product operator \(\mathcal B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) by
\[
\mathcal B(v_1,\ldots,v_m)=(\gamma_1A_1v_1)\times\cdots\times(\gamma_mA_mv_m).
\]
Given \(v^k=(v_1^k,\ldots,v_m^k)\in\mathcal H\), compute concurrently
\[
p_i^k=J_{\gamma_iA_i}(v_i^k)=(I+\gamma_iA_i)^{-1}(v_i^k),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,
\]
and return \(p^k=(p_1^k,\ldots,p_m^k)\). Then
\[
p^k=J_{\mathcal B}(v^k),
\]
so no component call requires another component's input or output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of the product operator whose components are the individually scaled monotone operators is obtained by independent, simultaneous component resolvent calls.

children.title: Averaging-Based Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Combination of concurrently evaluated component outputs through averaging structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Averaging-Based Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted aggregation of simultaneously computed component outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let component outputs \(p_i^k\in H\) be available, and choose weights \(\omega_i^k\geq0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i^k=1\). Form
\[
\bar p^k=\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i^k p_i^k,
\qquad
x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k(\bar p^k-x^k),
\]
where \(\lambda_k>0\) is a prescribed relaxation parameter. Output \(x^{k+1}\), or stop when \(\lVert\bar p^k-x^k\rVert\) is below tolerance. The aggregation is a convex combination before relaxation; convergence requires conditions on the component mappings, weights, and relaxation regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel component outputs are combined by a convex weighted average, optionally followed by relaxation toward that average.
assumptions_latex: \(p_i^k\in H\) for a common real Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next iterate is the relaxed weighted aggregate \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k(\sum_i\omega_i^kp_i^k-x^k)\).

children.title: Aggregation Weight Regimes
children.top_down_role: Uniform, weighted, or heterogeneous aggregation choices for parallel outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Weight Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible fixed weights for averaging parallel block outputs in a weighted product Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(m\ge 2\). An aggregation-weight regime is admissible when \(\omega_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i=1\). On \(\mathcal H^m\), equip block vectors with \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}=\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i\langle x_i,y_i\rangle\), and aggregate them by \(G_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\boldsymbol{x}=\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i x_i\). Uniform aggregation has \(\omega_i=1/m\); nonuniform aggregation permits unequal positive weights. Positivity makes the product metric nondegenerate and ensures every block participates, while normalization gives \(G_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}(x,\ldots,x)=x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admissible aggregation uses positive weights summing to one. Uniform weights treat blocks equally; unequal positive weights define a nonuniform product metric while preserving consensus points.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega_i>0\), \(\sum_i\omega_i=1\), and \(G_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}(x,\ldots,x)=x\).

children.title: Parallel Partial-Inverse Splitting
children.top_down_role: Parallel splitting organized around partial inverses relative to subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Partial-Inverse Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed partial-inverse iteration for a product operator and a closed decomposition subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\), let \(\boldsymbol A=\prod_{i=1}^m A_i\) be maximally monotone, and let \(V\subset\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}\) be a closed vector subspace. Initialize \(z^0\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}\). For \(k\ge0\), compute \(p^k=J_{\boldsymbol A}z^k=(J_{A_i}z_i^k)_{i=1}^m\) in parallel, form \(q^k=P_Vp^k+P_{V^\perp}(z^k-p^k)\), and set \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(q^k-z^k)\), where \(0<\inf_k\lambda_k\le\sup_k\lambda_k<2\). Since \(q^k=J_{\boldsymbol A_V}z^k\), stopping may use \(\lVert q^k-z^k\rVert\le\varepsilon\); upon convergence, output the primal component \(P_Vz^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate all component resolvents simultaneously, combine their primal and residual components through complementary subspace projections, and apply a relaxed fixed-point update of the partial-inverse resolvent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda_k(J_{\boldsymbol A_V}z^k-z^k)\), with component resolvents evaluated in parallel.

notation.meaning: partial inverse of A with respect to V

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but the partial-inverse resolvent identity, relaxation range, and reported primal output depend on conventions that require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Parallel Operator Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Componentwise decomposition schemes supporting concurrent operator evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Operator Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space representation of a finite sum inclusion by separable operators and a consensus constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_i:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}=\mathcal H^m\), and define the consensus subspace \(V=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathcal H\}\). Define \(\boldsymbol A:\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}\rightrightarrows\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}\) by \(\boldsymbol A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=mA_1x_1\times\cdots\times mA_mx_m\). Then \(x\) solves \(0\in\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol x=(x,\ldots,x)\) solves \(0\in\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol x+N_V\boldsymbol x\). Moreover, \(J_{\boldsymbol A}\) is block separable, so its components \(J_{mA_i}\) can be evaluated concurrently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum inclusion becomes a two-operator product-space inclusion: one separable block operator and one consensus normal cone. The block resolvents are independently evaluable.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\sum_iA_ix\iff0\in\boldsymbol A(x,\ldots,x)+N_V(x,\ldots,x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the container and is internally coherent, but the chosen product-operator scaling and equivalence have no cited authoritative locator.

children.title: Subspace-Lifted Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Lifted subspace representations connecting partial-inverse structure to parallel decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Subspace-Lifted Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General lifting of a constrained decomposed inclusion to a product space and closed subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\), let \(V\subset\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}\) be a closed vector subspace encoding compatibility among blocks, and let \(A_i:\mathcal H_i\rightrightarrows\mathcal H_i\). With \(\boldsymbol A=\prod_{i=1}^mA_i\), the lifted decomposition problem is \(0\in\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol x+N_V\boldsymbol x\). Equivalently, it seeks \(\boldsymbol x\in V\) and \(\boldsymbol u\in V^\perp\) such that \(-u_i\in A_ix_i\) for every \(i\). Thus operator evaluations remain block separable, while all coupling is confined to the projections \(P_V\) and \(P_{V^\perp}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift block variables into a product space, encode their compatibility by a closed subspace, and isolate coupling in subspace projections while retaining separable operator evaluations.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\mathcal H_i\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol x+N_V\boldsymbol x\iff \boldsymbol x\in V\) and \(\exists\boldsymbol u\in V^\perp\) with \(-u_i\in A_ix_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subspace-lifted representation is precise and locally appropriate, but its equivalence and separation claim lack cited support.

children.title: Decomposition Compatibility Boundaries
