knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Compatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by combining nonuniform product weights with unscaled component operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\mathcal H^m\) with weights \(\omega_i>0\) satisfying \(\sum_i\omega_i=1\), and let \(V=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathcal H\}\). Then \(V^\perp=\{\boldsymbol u:\sum_i\omega_i u_i=0\}\). Consequently, using the unscaled product operator \(\prod_iA_i\) represents \(0\in\sum_i\omega_iA_ix\), not generally \(0\in\sum_iA_ix\). Concretely, for \(\mathcal H=\mathbb R\), \(A_1x=\{1\}\), \(A_2x=\{-2\}\), and \((\omega_1,\omega_2)=(2/3,1/3)\), the weighted lifted inclusion accepts every consensus point, whereas \(0\notin A_1x+A_2x\). Correct scaling, such as \(A_i/\omega_i\), is therefore necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonuniform product weights change the represented sum unless component operators are scaled compatibly. An explicit two-operator example produces false lifted solutions when scaling is omitted.
assumptions_latex: The lift uses the diagonal consensus subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\prod_iA_i\) with a weighted product metric encodes \(0\in\sum_i\omega_iA_ix\); unweighted-sum equivalence can fail.

notation.meaning: orthogonal complement in the weighted product metric

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary and counterexample are algebraically plausible and fit the leaf, but the weighted-metric scaling convention needs authoritative support or documented independent verification.

children.title: Heterogeneous-Cost Load-Balancing Interface
children.top_down_role: Parallel efficiency under unequal component costs.

children.title: Parallel Load Balance
children.top_down_role: Distribution of component work across concurrent processing resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Load Balance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Makespan-based balance condition for synchronous evaluation of decomposed operator blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\) operator blocks have deterministic evaluation costs \(c_i>0\), and assign them to \(p\) workers through a partition \((S_1,\ldots,S_p)\) of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Define worker loads \(L_j=\sum_{i\in S_j}c_i\), total work \(W=\sum_{i=1}^mc_i\), and synchronous makespan \(M=\max_{1\le j\le p}L_j\). The assignment is \(\rho\)-balanced when \(M\le\rho W/p\). Necessarily \(\rho\ge1\), and exact balance means \(L_j=W/p\) for every worker. This condition concerns computational allocation only and does not alter the mathematical aggregation weights of the splitting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block assignment is rho-balanced when its largest worker load is at most rho times the average load. Exact balance gives equal total cost on every worker.
assumptions_latex: Workers execute concurrently with a synchronous barrier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\le\rho W/p\), where necessarily \(\rho\ge1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The makespan balance condition fits the leaf, but the scheduling model and terminology have no source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Heterogeneous Operator Cost
children.top_down_role: Unequal evaluation costs across operator components or worker assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Operator Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic per-block cost model for one parallel operator-splitting iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decomposition with component update maps \(T_i\), assign each block a cost \(c_i>0\), measured in a fixed resource such as arithmetic operations, oracle calls, or expected execution time, for computing the data required by \(T_i\) once. The operator costs are heterogeneous when there exist \(i\ne j\) with \(c_i\ne c_j\). Their multiplicative heterogeneity is \(\kappa_c=\max_i c_i/\min_i c_i\), with \(\kappa_c=1\) exactly in the homogeneous regime. Costs must use the same resource convention and include any block-local proximal, resolvent, or communication work declared part of an update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operator costs are heterogeneous when component updates require unequal amounts of a consistently measured resource. Their maximum-to-minimum ratio quantifies multiplicative heterogeneity.
assumptions_latex: Every block cost \(c_i\) is finite and strictly positive.
All costs use one declared resource convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_c=\max_i c_i/\min_i c_i\ge1\), with equality exactly when all \(c_i\) coincide.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but the resource-accounting convention and heterogeneity measure are unsupported by a cited locator.

children.title: Cost-Aware Work Allocation
children.top_down_role: Allocation regimes adapted to differences in component evaluation expense.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Aware Work Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy list scheduling of operator blocks using estimated evaluation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input positive estimated block costs \((\widehat c_i)_{i=1}^m\) and a worker count \(p\ge1\). Initialize \(S_j=\varnothing\) and \(L_j=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\). Order the blocks so that \(\widehat c_{i_1}\ge\cdots\ge\widehat c_{i_m}\). For \(r=1,\ldots,m\), choose \(j_r\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le j\le p}L_j\), set \(S_{j_r}\leftarrow S_{j_r}\cup\{i_r\}\), and update \(L_{j_r}\leftarrow L_{j_r}+\widehat c_{i_r}\). Output the partition \((S_1,\ldots,S_p)\); at each splitting iteration, worker \(j\) evaluates precisely the blocks in \(S_j\). Reallocate when the cost estimates or available workers change materially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort blocks by decreasing estimated cost and repeatedly assign the next block to the currently least-loaded worker. The resulting partition is reused until costs or resources change.
assumptions_latex: Each block is assigned to exactly one worker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S_1,\ldots,S_p)\) is a cost-aware partition produced by decreasing-cost greedy list scheduling.

children.title: Straggler-Limited Parallel Efficiency
children.top_down_role: Efficiency loss caused by slow components or imbalanced worker completion times.

knowledge_statements.title: Straggler-Limited Parallel Efficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous iteration bound determined by the most heavily loaded or slowest worker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one synchronous iteration assigns blocks \(S_j\) to \(p\) workers, incurs no overlap between workers' local costs and the barrier, and has worker times \(L_j=\sum_{i\in S_j}c_i\). With total serial work \(W=\sum_i c_i\), the parallel iteration time is \(M=\max_jL_j\), its idealized speedup is \(S=W/M\), and its efficiency is \(E=S/p=W/(pM)\le1\). Since \(M\ge c_{\max}=\max_i c_i\), one also has \(E\le W/(pc_{\max})\). Thus a single expensive block imposes a straggler ceiling even when all remaining work is perfectly balanced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A synchronous iteration lasts as long as its slowest worker. Efficiency is total work divided by worker count times makespan and is capped by the most expensive block.
assumptions_latex: Block costs are deterministic and additive within each worker.
Workers run concurrently and synchronize once per iteration.
Communication and barrier overhead are excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=\max_jL_j\), \(S=W/M\), and \(E=W/(pM)\le\min\{1,W/(pc_{\max})\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits and the formulas follow from the declared idealized model, but that model and its overhead exclusions lack a cited locator.

children.title: Randomized Coordinate Splitting
children.top_down_role: Partial-update fixed-point methods organized by separability and sampling.

children.title: Randomized Coordinate Fixed-Point Iteration
children.top_down_role: Random block activation in a global fixed-point map.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Coordinate Fixed-Point Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent random block activation for a global fixed-point residual on a finite product Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\), let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\), and define \(S=\operatorname{Id}-T\). Choose probabilities \(p_i\in(0,1]\), initialize \(x^0\in\mathcal H\), and for each \(k\ge0\) sample a mask \(\varepsilon^k\in\{0,1\}^m\), independently of the past, with \(\mathbb P(\varepsilon_i^k=1)=p_i\). Given \(\lambda_k>0\), update each block by \(x_i^{k+1}=x_i^k-\lambda_k\varepsilon_i^kS_i(x^k)\). Stop when a declared residual estimate is at most \(\epsilon\), or after a prescribed number of iterations, and output the latest iterate. Simultaneous activation of several coordinates is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, randomly activate blocks and apply only their components of the global fixed-point residual. Every block has positive activation probability.
assumptions_latex: Each mask is independent of the iteration history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i^{k+1}=x_i^k-\lambda_k\varepsilon_i^k(\operatorname{Id}-T)_i(x^k)\).

children.title: Coordinate-Friendly Representation Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Representations permitting inexpensive partial updates.

children.title: Coordinate-Friendly Operators
children.top_down_role: Operator representations supporting inexpensive single-coordinate or block-coordinate evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Friendly Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational definition comparing one coordinate update with evaluation of the full operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H^m\to\mathcal H^m\) have coordinate maps \(T_i\), and let \(C_T(m)\) denote the cost of evaluating all coordinates of \(T(x)\). The operator \(T\) is coordinate-friendly when, uniformly over \(i\) and admissible \(x\), the information needed to replace only coordinate \(x_i\) by \(T_i(x)\) can be computed with cost \(C_i(m)=O(C_T(m)/m)\), using the same computational model. Thus one coordinate update is asymptotically no more expensive than its proportional share of a full evaluation. The definition concerns implementation cost and does not assert separability of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is coordinate-friendly when one coordinate update costs, up to constants, no more than one m-th of a full operator evaluation under the same cost model.
assumptions_latex: Full and partial costs use the same computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_i(m)=O(C_T(m)/m)\) uniformly over coordinates.

children.title: Extended Coordinate-Friendly Operators
children.top_down_role: Broader representations using maintained auxiliary state or structured partial computations.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended Coordinate-Friendly Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate friendliness obtained by maintaining auxiliary state updated together with each selected coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H^m\to\mathcal H^m\). It is extended coordinate-friendly if there exist an auxiliary state space \(\mathcal Z\), a consistent encoding \(z=E(x)\), and coordinate procedures \(U_i\) such that \(U_i(x,z)=(x^+,z^+)\) satisfies \(x_i^+=T_i(x)\), \(x_j^+=x_j\) for \(j\ne i\), and \(z^+=E(x^+)\). If \(C_T(m)\) is the cost of evaluating \(T(x)\), each combined coordinate-and-state update must cost \(O(C_T(m)/m)\), uniformly in \(i\). The auxiliary state may cache shared quantities, but consistency must be restored after every completed update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is extended coordinate-friendly when cached auxiliary state makes a coordinate update proportionally cheap and the cache can be updated consistently at the same cost.
assumptions_latex: Costs use one fixed computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_i\) computes \(x_i^+=T_i(x)\) and \(z^+=E(x^+)\) in cost \(O(C_T(m)/m)\).

children.title: Partial-Update Cost Advantage
children.top_down_role: Cost reductions available when partial evaluations avoid full operator recomputation.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Update Cost Advantage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-iteration arithmetic advantage for coordinate-friendly fixed-point operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\), let \(T:H\to H\), and write \(T_i=P_iT\). Let \(I\) be a coordinate sampled with \(\mathbb P(I=i)=p_i\), where \(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\). Suppose that a full evaluation of \(T\) costs \(C_{\mathrm{full}}>0\), while evaluating coordinate \(i\) and maintaining every reusable state quantity costs \(C_i\). Then \(\mathbb E[C_I]=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iC_i\). Hence partial updating has a strict expected per-step cost advantage whenever \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_iC_i<C_{\mathrm{full}}\). If \(C_i\le K C_{\mathrm{full}}/m\) for every \(i\), with a constant \(K\) independent of \(m\), then \(\mathbb E[C_I]\le K C_{\mathrm{full}}/m\), so the ratio \(C_{\mathrm{full}}/\mathbb E[C_I]\) is at least \(m/K\) whenever \(\mathbb E[C_I]>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected cost of a sampled coordinate update is the probability-weighted average of its complete evaluation and maintenance costs. If every coordinate costs at most a constant times one m-th of a full evaluation, the per-step speedup is at least proportional to m.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) includes every auxiliary-state update required by subsequent iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[C_I]=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iC_i\), and \(C_i\le K C_{\mathrm{full}}/m\) for all \(i\) implies \(\mathbb E[C_I]\le K C_{\mathrm{full}}/m\).

notation.meaning: orthogonal projection onto coordinate space H_i
complete cost of evaluating and maintaining coordinate i

children.title: Coordinate-Friendliness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Representations where partial updates lose their computational advantage.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Friendliness Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense coupling can eliminate the computational benefit of single-coordinate updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(m\ge 2\), let \(H=\mathbb R^m\) and let \(T(x)=Ax\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is dense and has no exploitable structure or maintained sufficient statistic. Computing one coordinate \(T_i(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m A_{ij}x_j\) requires \(\Theta(m)\) arithmetic operations, while computing all coordinates requires \(\Theta(m^2)\). Thus coordinate evaluation is not sublinear in the full-evaluation cost beyond the trivial factor \(m\), and updating all \(m\) coordinates over one sweep costs \(\Theta(m^2)\), matching a full evaluation. If changing one input coordinate also invalidates \(\Theta(m)\) stored outputs, incremental maintenance has the same boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an unstructured dense linear operator, one output coordinate costs linear time and a full coordinate sweep costs the same order as one full evaluation.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is dense and admits neither sparsity nor a faster structured transform.
No reusable statistic makes a row product asymptotically cheaper than direct evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_i=\Theta(m)\), \(C_{\mathrm{full}}=\Theta(m^2)\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i=\Theta(C_{\mathrm{full}})\).

notation.meaning: i-th coordinate of the operator output
arithmetic cost of one coordinate update

children.title: Coordinate Sampling Policy Family
children.top_down_role: Uniform, nonuniform, adaptive, and data-dependent sampling.

children.title: Uniform Sampling Policies
children.top_down_role: Coordinate or block selection with equal sampling probabilities.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Sampling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent uniform selection of one coordinate at each randomized splitting step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_k\) be the history before iteration \(k\), and let \(I_k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) denote the coordinate selected for update. A uniform sampling policy satisfies \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)=1/m\) almost surely for every \(i\) and \(k\). Conditional uniformity implies that \(I_k\) is independent of the past history, although different implementations may use additional randomness after selection. For a block update of fixed size \(q\), uniform sampling without replacement analogously assigns probability \(1/\binom{m}{q}\) to every subset of \(q\) coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform sampling chooses every coordinate with conditional probability 1/m; fixed-size uniform block sampling gives every block of that size equal probability.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_k\) contains all information available before coordinate selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)=1/m\) almost surely for all \(i\) and \(k\).

children.title: Importance-Weighted Sampling
children.top_down_role: Nonuniform selection based on coordinate-specific cost, smoothness, or influence.

knowledge_statements.title: Importance-Weighted Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniform coordinate selection matched to coordinate-specific difficulty or cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_k\) be the information available before iteration \(k\), and let positive \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable weights \(w_1^k,\ldots,w_m^k\) encode coordinate importance. Define \(p_i^k=w_i^k/\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^k\), and sample \(I_k\) according to \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)=p_i^k\). This is an importance-weighted sampling policy. If \(g_1^k,\ldots,g_m^k\in\mathbb R^d\) are \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable coordinate contributions, then the inverse-probability estimator \(g_{I_k}^k/(mp_{I_k}^k)\) is conditionally unbiased for their uniform aggregate: \(\mathbb E[g_{I_k}^k/(mp_{I_k}^k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance-weighted sampling chooses a coordinate conditionally in proportion to positive history-measurable weights. Inverse-probability scaling then gives an unbiased estimate of the uniform aggregate of coordinate contributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)=p_i^k\) and \(\mathbb E[g_{I_k}^k/(mp_{I_k}^k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i^k\).

notation.meaning: positive importance weight of coordinate i
conditional selection probability of coordinate i

children.title: Adaptive Sampling Policies
children.top_down_role: Selection probabilities that evolve with observed iteration behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Sampling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent coordinate probabilities chosen before the current random draw.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With pre-selection filtration \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0}\), an adaptive sampling policy is a sequence of \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable probability vectors \(p^k=(p_1^k,\ldots,p_m^k)\) satisfying \(p_i^k\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i^k=1\), followed by a draw obeying \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)=p_i^k\). A persistent-exploration policy additionally requires a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(p_i^k\ge\varepsilon\) almost surely for every coordinate and iteration. Adaptation may use past iterates, residuals, delays, or observed costs, but not information revealed only after the current draw.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive sampling chooses the next probability vector from the observed history, then draws accordingly; persistent exploration uniformly bounds every coordinate probability away from zero.
assumptions_latex: The coordinate draw occurs after \(p^k\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)=p_i^k\), with \(p_i^k\ge\varepsilon>0\) under persistent exploration.

children.title: Data-Dependent Sampling
children.top_down_role: Selection mechanisms tied to the structure or distribution of problem data.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Dependent Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate probabilities derived from the fixed problem instance or observed data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) denote the observed problem data and let \(s_i(D)\ge0\) be measurable coordinate scores with \(\sum_{j=1}^m s_j(D)>0\). A data-dependent sampling policy assigns \(p_i(D)=s_i(D)/\sum_{j=1}^m s_j(D)\) and samples \(I_k\) so that \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid D)=p_i(D)\). Conditional on \(D\), the policy may be stationary across iterations. To guarantee that every potentially necessary coordinate remains reachable, one requires \(p_i(D)>0\) for each such coordinate; a common safeguarded policy is \(p_i^{\varepsilon}(D)=(1-\varepsilon)p_i(D)+\varepsilon/m\) with \(0<\varepsilon\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data-dependent sampling converts coordinate scores computed from the problem data into probabilities; uniform mixing prevents any necessary coordinate from receiving zero probability.
assumptions_latex: The data \(D\) are observed before the coordinate draw.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I_k=i\mid D)=p_i(D)\), and \(p_i^{\varepsilon}(D)\ge\varepsilon/m\) under safeguarding.

children.title: Pathwise-Expectation Convergence Pair
children.top_down_role: Pathwise and expectation-based convergence organization.

children.title: Almost-Sure Convergence
children.top_down_role: Pathwise convergence organization for randomized coordinate splitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise convergence criterion for randomized coordinate-splitting iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X_k)_{k\ge0}\) be random iterates in a separable Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(S\subseteq H\) be the solution set. Strong almost-sure convergence to an \(S\)-valued random variable means that there exists \(X_\infty\) with \(\mathbb P(X_\infty\in S)=1\) such that \(\mathbb P(\lim_{k\to\infty}\lVert X_k-X_\infty\rVert=0)=1\). Weak almost-sure convergence replaces norm convergence by \(\langle X_k-X_\infty,h\rangle\to0\) for every \(h\in H\), on a single event of probability one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-sure convergence means that, outside one null event, the entire random iterate sequence converges strongly or weakly to a solution-valued random limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(X_k\to X_\infty\text{ and }X_\infty\in S)=1\), with the stated strong or weak topology.

children.title: Expected Convergence
children.top_down_role: Expectation-based convergence organization for objectives, distances, or residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence measured through an integrable error or merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_k\) be random iterates and let \(V:H\to[0,\infty]\) be a measurable error or merit function with \(V(x)=0\) for every solution \(x\in S\). Convergence in expectation with respect to \(V\) means that \(V(X_k)\) is integrable for every \(k\) and \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb E[V(X_k)]=0\). If \(V(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^q\) for \(q\ge1\), this is mean \(q\)-th-power convergence to the solution set. It does not by itself specify convergence of individual sample paths or convergence to a single random solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected convergence means an integrable nonnegative error has expectation tending to zero; by itself it neither gives pathwise convergence nor identifies a single limiting solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb E[V(X_k)]=0\).

children.title: Pathwise–Expectation Comparison
children.top_down_role: Differences in interpretation, strength, and transfer between probabilistic guarantee types.

knowledge_statements.title: Pathwise–Expectation Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implications between almost-sure and expected convergence require additional integrability or summability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_k\ge0\) be measurable errors. If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E[V_k]<\infty\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\), Markov's inequality and the first Borel–Cantelli lemma give \(\mathbb P(V_k>\varepsilon\text{ infinitely often})=0\), hence \(V_k\to0\) almost surely. Conversely, if \(V_k\to0\) almost surely and the family \(\{V_k:k\ge0\}\) is uniformly integrable, then \(\mathbb E[V_k]\to0\). A sufficient condition for uniform integrability is the existence of an integrable \(Y\) satisfying \(0\le V_k\le Y\) almost surely for all \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable expected errors imply almost-sure error convergence; almost-sure convergence implies convergence of expectations when the errors are uniformly integrable, for example under integrable domination.
assumptions_latex: For the converse direction, \(\{V_k\}\) is uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\mathbb E[V_k]<\infty\Rightarrow V_k\to0\) almost surely, while \(V_k\to0\) almost surely plus uniform integrability implies \(\mathbb E[V_k]\to0\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative random error at iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated implications are standard and mathematically sound, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the Borel–Cantelli and uniform-integrability claims.

children.title: Probabilistic Guarantee Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sampling or dependence regimes where standard pathwise or expectation guarantees weaken.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Guarantee Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neither expectation convergence nor almost-sure convergence implies the other without added hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Expectation convergence alone need not imply almost-sure convergence: for independent events \(A_k\) with \(\mathbb P(A_k)=1/k\), the errors \(V_k=\mathbf 1_{A_k}\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[V_k]=1/k\to0\), yet \(V_k=1\) infinitely often almost surely. Almost-sure convergence alone need not imply expectation convergence: if \(U\) is uniform on \((0,1)\) and \(W_k=k\mathbf 1_{\{U\le1/k\}}\), then \(W_k\to0\) almost surely while \(\mathbb E[W_k]=1\) for every \(k\). Thus summability, domination, uniform integrability, or comparable assumptions are essential when translating between guarantee types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit random-error sequences show that convergence of expectations need not be almost sure, and almost-sure convergence need not pass to expectations without integrability control.
assumptions_latex: The events \((A_k)\) are independent with \(\mathbb P(A_k)=1/k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[V_k]\to0\not\Rightarrow V_k\to0\) almost surely, and \(W_k\to0\) almost surely \(\not\Rightarrow\mathbb E[W_k]\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both counterexamples are mathematically valid, but the record supplies no source or locator for them or for the asserted guarantee boundaries.

children.title: Asynchronous Splitting
children.top_down_role: Partially synchronized fixed-point updates using delayed information.

children.title: Bounded-Delay Models
children.top_down_role: Asynchronous regimes with controlled staleness.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Delay Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic staleness bound for asynchronous coordinate reads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Index commits by \(k\ge0\), and let \(x^k\) be the shared state after the first \(k\) commits, so update \(k\) reads before producing \(x^{k+1}\). Assume atomic component reads and writes. A bounded-delay read is a vector \(\hat x^k\) whose components satisfy \(\hat x_j^k=x_j^{k-d_{k,j}}\), where \(d_{k,j}\) is an integer satisfying \(0\le d_{k,j}\le\min\{\tau,k\}\) for a fixed finite \(\tau\). Thus every component used by update \(k\) comes from one of the committed states \(x^{\max\{0,k-\tau\}},\ldots,x^k\). An inconsistent-read model permits different \(d_{k,j}\) across components; a consistent-read specialization requires a single \(d_k\) such that \(\hat x^k=x^{k-d_k}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With commits indexed consistently and component accesses atomic, a bounded-delay model requires every component read by update k to come from at most τ earlier commits. Inconsistent reads may use different delays for different components.
assumptions_latex: \(x^k\) is the shared state after the first \(k\) commits, and update \(k\) produces \(x^{k+1}\).
Component reads and writes are atomic.
There exists a deterministic finite delay bound \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\hat x_j^k=x_j^{k-d_{k,j}}\) with \(0\le d_{k,j}\le\min\{\tau,k\}\) for every \(k\) and \(j\).

notation.meaning: possibly stale vector read by update k
commit-age of component j used by update k

children.title: Stochastic-Delay Models
children.top_down_role: Probabilistically controlled delay regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-Delay Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic control of unbounded or random asynchronous staleness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_k=\max_j d_{k,j}\) be the maximum age of any component used by asynchronous update \(k\), measured in commit order. A stochastic-delay model specifies nonnegative random variables \(D_k\), adapted to the execution history, together with a deterministic tail envelope \((q_t)_{t\ge0}\) satisfying \(q_t\downarrow0\) and \(\mathbb P(D_k\ge t\mid\mathcal F_{k-t})\le q_t\) almost surely whenever \(k\ge t\). Moment-controlled variants require \(\sup_k\mathbb E[D_k^r]<\infty\) for a stated \(r>0\). Unlike bounded-delay models, such conditions may allow arbitrarily large delays with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic-delay model bounds delay tails or moments uniformly over iterations while allowing rare, arbitrarily stale reads; the conditioning history and moment order must be specified.
assumptions_latex: \(D_k\) is a nonnegative integer-valued delay measurable at commit \(k\).
\((\mathcal F_k)\) records the execution history in commit order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(D_k\ge t\mid\mathcal F_{k-t})\le q_t\) with \(q_t\to0\), or explicitly \(\sup_k\mathbb E[D_k^r]<\infty\) in a moment-controlled model.

children.title: Server–Worker Splitting
children.top_down_role: Central parameter ownership with asynchronous workers.

knowledge_statements.title: Server–Worker Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asynchronous fixed-point splitting with one authoritative parameter vector and delayed worker evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_i:H\to H\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), be component operators on a Hilbert space \(H\), and let the server own \(x^k\). Initialize \(x^0\in H\). At server event \(k\), a worker \(i_k\) reads a snapshot \(x^{k-d_k}\), computes \(u^k=T_{i_k}(x^{k-d_k})-x^{k-d_k}\), and returns \(u^k\). The server atomically performs \[x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k u^k,\] where \(\lambda_k>0\); other workers may compute concurrently. Stop when a prescribed residual or event budget is reached, and output the current server state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers evaluate component residuals on possibly stale snapshots, while a server serially applies their relaxed updates to the authoritative parameter vector.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and each \(T_i:H\to H\) is well defined.
Each returned update carries its worker index and snapshot delay \(d_k\ge 0\).
Server writes are atomic and totally ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k\bigl(T_{i_k}(x^{k-d_k})-x^{k-d_k}\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: staleness of the snapshot used at server event k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: AC-FPI updates and asynchronous server–worker pseudocode
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Displayed asynchronous proximal coordinate updates together with their parameter-server/worker realization; the extract does not explicitly reconcile the pseudocode's \(\rho\)-scaled proximal maps with the subsequently stated \(\alpha\)-scaled access assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(k\), for the selected component \(i(k)\), define
\[
\widehat u_{i(k)}^k=u_{i(k)}^{k-d_{i(k)}(k)},\qquad
\widehat u_{\mathrm{sum}}^k=\sum_{i=1}^m u_i^{k-d_i(k)}.
\]
The corresponding asynchronous coordinate fixed-point iteration is
\[
y^{k+1}=\operatorname{Prox}_{\rho g}\!\left(\widehat u_{\mathrm{sum}}^k/m\right),
\]
\[
x_{i(k)}^{k+1}=\operatorname{Prox}_{\rho f_{i(k)}}\!\left(2y^{k+1}-\widehat u_{i(k)}^k\right),
\qquad
u_{i(k)}^{k+1}=u_{i(k)}^k+2\eta\left(x_{i(k)}^{k+1}-y^{k+1}\right).
\]
For \(p=m\) workers, the stated parameter-server pseudocode accumulates queued increments into \(u_{\mathrm{sum}}\), computes \(y=\operatorname{Prox}_{\rho g}(u_{\mathrm{sum}}/m)\), and broadcasts \(y\). Worker \(i\) computes \(x_i=\operatorname{Prox}_{\rho f_i}(2y-u_i)\), sends \(2\eta(x_i-y)\) to the server, and adds that increment to \(u_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm asynchronously updates one component from delayed local and aggregate states. In the parameter-server pseudocode, the server accumulates worker corrections and broadcasts a shared proximal point, while each worker computes its component proximal point and sends and applies a relaxed correction.
assumptions_latex: \text{The displayed updates and pseudocode use the required proximal maps }\operatorname{Prox}_{\rho g}\text{ and }\operatorname{Prox}_{\rho f_i}.

\text{Separately, the framework description assumes server access to }\operatorname{Prox}_{g/(\alpha m)}\text{ and worker }i\text{ access to }u_i\text{ and }\operatorname{Prox}_{f_i/\alpha};\text{ no relation between }\alpha\text{ and }\rho\text{ is specified in this extract.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The source specifies the displayed AC-FPI iteration and the stated asynchronous server--worker execution procedure.}

children.title: Asynchronous Memory-Consistency Models

children.title: Exclusive-Memory Updates
children.top_down_role: Update regimes using isolated or exclusively owned memory regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Exclusive-Memory Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutual-exclusion condition for shared-state splitting updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let update event \(k\) access coordinate set \(S_k\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) during a half-open interval \(I_k=[a_k,b_k)\). The execution has exclusive-memory updates when \[S_k\cap S_\ell\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_k\cap I_\ell=\varnothing\] for every pair \(k\ne\ell\). Thus no two overlapping events read-modify-write a common coordinate, and every completed shared-state update is observationally equivalent to inserting that entire update at one position in a serial order consistent with completion times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Updates touching a common coordinate cannot overlap, so each shared-state modification has a serializable, indivisible effect.
assumptions_latex: Each update has a declared access set and finite execution interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_k\cap S_\ell\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow I_k\cap I_\ell=\varnothing\), hence conflicting updates are serializable.

children.title: Lock-Free Updates
children.top_down_role: Concurrent update regimes that avoid global locking.

knowledge_statements.title: Lock-Free Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonblocking shared-memory update model for asynchronous splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shared-memory splitting implementation is lock-free if workers never acquire mutual-exclusion locks and, whenever workers collectively take infinitely many execution steps, infinitely many update operations complete. A typical event reads a possibly inconsistent snapshot \(\hat x^k\), computes a sparse increment \(\Delta^k\), and applies coordinate writes \[x_j\leftarrow x_j+\Delta_j^k\qquad(j\in S_k)\] using atomic coordinate primitives. Lock-freedom guarantees system-wide progress, but it does not guarantee that any specified worker completes within a bounded number of its own steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers update shared coordinates without locks; continued system execution guarantees some updates finish, though individual workers may starve.
assumptions_latex: Each coordinate write uses an atomic read-modify-write primitive.
The execution model distinguishes worker steps from completed update operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Infinite aggregate execution implies infinitely many completed updates, without a per-worker completion guarantee.

children.title: Read Consistency Models
children.top_down_role: Consistency regimes governing the coordinate values observed by asynchronous workers.

knowledge_statements.title: Read Consistency Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal snapshot models governing values observed by an asynchronous worker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^t\in H_1\times\cdots\times H_n\) denote the shared state after committed write \(t\). A read used at event \(k\) is consistent if \(\hat x^k=x^{t_k}\) for one index \(t_k\le k\). It is coordinatewise inconsistent if there exist indices \(t_{k,j}\le k\) such that \[\hat x_j^k=x_j^{t_{k,j}}\quad(j=1,\ldots,n),\] with the indices not necessarily equal. Under bounded staleness \(\tau\), either model additionally requires \(k-\tau\le t_k\le k\) or \(k-\tau\le t_{k,j}\le k\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent read equals one historical state; an inconsistent read may combine coordinates from different historical states, optionally within a delay bound.
assumptions_latex: Committed writes are indexed by a total logical order.
Each coordinate value read was produced by some committed write.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Read consistency is characterized by one common timestamp; coordinatewise inconsistency permits coordinate-dependent timestamps.

children.title: Write-Collision Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Collision regimes limiting safe or effective concurrent memory updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Write-Collision Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating serializable overlapping writes from executions that may lose updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two events concurrently apply increments \(a,b\in H_j\) to the same coordinate whose initial value is \(z\). If the coordinate operation is atomic, the final value is \(z+a+b\), independently of write order. With non-atomic read-modify-write, both events may read \(z\) and subsequently store \(z+a\) and \(z+b\); the final value can then be either \(z+a\) or \(z+b\). Hence the boundary is crossed when conflicting writes overlap without an atomic accumulation or mutual-exclusion mechanism: the realized state need not equal any serial application of both declared increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overlapping writes are safe only when accumulation is atomic or exclusive; otherwise one increment can be lost and serial equivalence fails.
assumptions_latex: Two update events target the same shared coordinate.
Each event intends to add its declared increment exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without atomicity or exclusion, the post-collision value may differ from \(z+a+b\).

children.title: Staleness Instability
children.top_down_role: Loss of convergence caused by excessively outdated worker information.

knowledge_statements.title: Staleness Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar delayed-gradient example showing loss of convergence under stale evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\). Synchronous gradient descent with stepsize \(\gamma=1\) satisfies \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\gamma x^k=0\) after one step. If every gradient is delayed by one event, the same nominal stepsize gives \[x^{k+1}=x^k-x^{k-1}.\] With \(x^0=x^1=1\), the sequence is \(1,1,0,-1,-1,0,1,\ldots\), so it is periodic and does not converge to the unique minimizer \(0\). Thus a stepsize stable without delay can lie on an instability boundary after staleness is introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-step stale gradient turns a synchronously terminating quadratic iteration into a nonconvergent periodic sequence.
assumptions_latex: The delay is exactly one and \(\gamma=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The delayed iterates are periodic and fail to converge to \(0\).

notation.meaning: one-event stale point used at event k

children.title: Collision Instability
children.top_down_role: Failure caused by conflicting concurrent reads or writes.

knowledge_statements.title: Collision Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated lost-write execution preventing convergence despite a zero intended aggregate update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the shared scalar be initialized at \(x^0=1\). At round \(k\), two workers read the same value \(x^k\) and compute the cancelling increments \(a_k=-2x^k\) and \(b_k=2x^k\), whose atomic aggregate is \(a_k+b_k=0\). Under non-atomic read-modify-write, the workers may prepare the stores \(x^k+a_k=-x^k\) and \(x^k+b_k=3x^k\). If the first store overwrites the second in every round, then \[x^{k+1}=-x^k,\] so \(x^k=(-1)^k\). The collided execution therefore fails to converge to the collision-free state \(x^0=1\), even though every round has zero intended aggregate increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two cancelling same-snapshot increments would leave the state unchanged if accumulated atomically, but repeatedly losing one write can make the shared state oscillate.
assumptions_latex: Both workers read the same pre-round value \(x^k\).
Their non-atomic stores may overwrite one another, and the store equal to \(-x^k\) survives each round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k=(-1)^k\), so the collided execution is nonconvergent.

notation.meaning: cancelling increments computed from the shared pre-round value

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Race conditions and inconsistent shared-memory accesses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions, method-specific read requirements, and exclusive-access prevention for parallel coordinate updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A race condition is harmful behavior of a parallel method whose result depends on the order in which agents complete their tasks. An inconsistent read occurs when an agent reads a memory block during a concurrent write and obtains a mixture of old and new data, possibly a value that was never an actual stored state. An inconsistent write occurs when concurrent writes to the same block partially overwrite one another. AC-FPI requires a consistent read within each block, while allowing different blocks of \(x\) to have different delays. Exclusive access to a block during a write prevents inconsistent reads and writes on that block; concurrent read-only access requires no exclusivity. A method subject to the described races is not an instance of ARock.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A race condition makes a parallel method depend adversely on task-completion order. A read overlapping a write can return mixed old and new data, and overlapping writes can partially overwrite each other. AC-FPI requires coherence within each block but permits different delays across blocks. Exclusive access during writes prevents these failures; the raced implementation is not ARock.
assumptions_latex: \text{AC-FPI requires a common delay within each block but permits different delays across blocks.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exclusive access to a block during a write prevents inconsistent reads and writes on that block.}

children.title: Delay–Collision Interaction
children.top_down_role: Instability regimes where stale information amplifies memory-access conflicts.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay–Collision Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar recurrence exposing the joint dependence on delay and concurrent update multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^2/2\), let \(q\ge1\) be an integer and let \(\tau\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Suppose \(q\) workers evaluate the same delayed gradient \(x^{k-\tau}\), and all \(q\) increments are accumulated at event \(k\) with common stepsize \(\gamma>0\). The resulting linear dynamics are \[x^{k+1}=x^k-q\gamma x^{k-\tau}.\] An exponential mode \(x^k=r^k\) has characteristic equation \[r^{\tau+1}-r^\tau+q\gamma=0.\] The recurrence converges to zero for every initial history exactly when every root of this polynomial has modulus strictly below one; hence its asymptotic stability depends jointly on \(\tau\), \(q\), and \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delay changes the recurrence order, while accumulated concurrent updates scale the effective step; convergence for every initial history is determined by the roots of their joint characteristic polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(q\ge1\) is an integer and all workers use the same delay \(\tau\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
All \(q\) increments are accumulated without loss and use a common stepsize \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence to zero for every initial history holds exactly when \(\lvert r\rvert<1\) for every root of \(r^{\tau+1}-r^\tau+q\gamma=0\).

children.title: Excessive-Parallelism Boundary
children.top_down_role: Worker-count regimes where added concurrency undermines stability or useful progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Excessive-Parallelism Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent multiplicity threshold for a scalar accumulated-gradient model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=x^2/2\) and a synchronous round in which \(q\) workers all read \(x^k\) and their gradient increments are accumulated with per-worker stepsize \(\gamma>0\). Then \[x^{k+1}=(1-q\gamma)x^k.\] The iterates converge to \(0\) for every initial value exactly when \(0<q\gamma<2\). At \(q\gamma=2\), every nonzero trajectory alternates sign with constant magnitude; when \(q\gamma>2\), its magnitude grows geometrically. Thus \(q\gamma=2\) is the excessive-parallelism boundary for this simultaneous accumulated-update model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulating too many same-snapshot updates multiplies the effective step; the scalar quadratic becomes nonconvergent once their total step reaches two.
assumptions_latex: All q workers read the same current scalar.
Every computed increment is accumulated exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence holds exactly for \(0<q\gamma<2\), with boundary \(q\gamma=2\).

children.title: Consensus Product-Space Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Agreement constraints represented by duplicated variables and consensus subspaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consensus product-space representation of a finite convex sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replicated-variable equivalence, consensus normal-cone inclusion, projection formula, and extension to sums of maximal monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, convex functions and define \[C=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathbb R^{nm}:x_1=\cdots=x_m\}.\] Then \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x)\quad\text{is equivalent to}\quad\min_{\mathbf x\in C}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x_i).\] If \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}g_i\neq\varnothing\), its optimality system can be written as \[0\in(\partial g_1(x_1),\ldots,\partial g_m(x_m))+N_C(\mathbf x).\] Moreover, \[\Pi_C\mathbf x=(\bar x,\ldots,\bar x),\qquad \bar x=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m x_i.\] The same consensus construction represents inclusions \(0\in\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbb A_i x\) for maximal monotone operators \(\mathbb A_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum of closed proper convex functions can be lifted to local variable copies constrained to agree. Projection onto the consensus subspace replaces all copies by their average. Under the common-interior qualification, the lifted optimality condition is a sum of component subdifferentials and the consensus normal cone. The construction also applies to sums of maximal monotone operators.
assumptions_latex: g_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\ \text{is closed, proper, and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
\mathbb A_1,\ldots,\mathbb A_m\ \text{are maximal monotone for the operator-inclusion extension}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_x\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x)\equiv\min_{\mathbf x\in C}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x_i),\qquad \Pi_C\mathbf x=(\bar x,\ldots,\bar x).

children.title: Consensus-Constraint Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations that encode agreement through explicit consensus constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus-Constraint Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent replicated-variable formulation of a finite-sum convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(m\ge1\) be finite, and let \(f_i:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions satisfying \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\ne\varnothing\). Define the consensus set \(C=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in H^m:x_1=\cdots=x_m\}\). Then \[\inf_{x\in H}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)=\inf_{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in H^m}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)+\iota_C(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\right\}.\] Their minimizers correspond exactly through \(x\mapsto(x,\ldots,x)\); thus the lifting separates the component functions while enforcing agreement through one constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicating the decision variable separates the proper convex component objectives, and the consensus indicator restores exact equivalence in value and minimizers to the original problem.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m\ge1\) is finite.
Each \(f_i:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and consensus-lifted problems have equal values and diagonally corresponding minimizers.

notation.meaning: diagonal consensus subset of the product space
zero on C and positive infinity outside C
effective domain of the component function

children.title: Product-Space Liftings
children.top_down_role: Duplicated-variable formulations embedded in a product space.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space reformulation of a finite sum of set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\). On \(H^m\), define \(\boldsymbol A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=A_1x_1\times\cdots\times A_mx_m\) and \(C=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in H\}\). Then \[0\in\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in \boldsymbol A\boldsymbol x+N_C(\boldsymbol x)\ \text{ for }\ \boldsymbol x=(x,\ldots,x).\] Thus the sum inclusion on \(H\) is represented by a product operator plus the consensus normal cone on \(H^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum of operators on one space becomes a separable product operator coupled to the normal cone of the diagonal consensus subspace.
assumptions_latex: The product space has its standard Hilbert inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zeros of \(\sum_i A_i\) correspond exactly to diagonal zeros of \(\boldsymbol A+N_C\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of the component operators

children.title: Consensus-Subspace Representation
children.top_down_role: Subspace geometry linking duplicated variables to agreement requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus-Subspace Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection and normal-cone formulas for the diagonal subspace of a Hilbert product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in H\}\subset H^m\). For \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), set \(\bar x=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\). Then \[P_C\boldsymbol x=(\bar x,\ldots,\bar x),\qquad C^\perp=\left\{(u_1,\ldots,u_m):\sum_{i=1}^m u_i=0\right\}.\] Consequently, \(N_C(\boldsymbol x)=C^\perp\) when \(\boldsymbol x\in C\), and \(N_C(\boldsymbol x)=\varnothing\) otherwise. These formulas isolate consensus and disagreement components in product-space splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto consensus replaces all coordinates by their mean; disagreement vectors are exactly those whose coordinate sum is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(H^m\) uses the unweighted product inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C\boldsymbol x=(\bar x,\ldots,\bar x)\) and \(N_C(\boldsymbol x)=C^\perp\) on \(C\).

notation.meaning: orthogonal projector onto the consensus subspace

children.title: Lifting Overhead
children.top_down_role: Memory, dimension, or communication costs introduced by lifted consensus formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifting Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional storage and averaging overhead of an explicit consensus product-space lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the original decision variable lie in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and lift it to \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^m\). Explicit storage increases from \(d\) to \(md\) scalars. Computing the orthogonal projection onto the consensus subspace \(D=\{(u,\ldots,u):u\in\mathbb{R}^d\}\) requires forming \(\bar x=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\) and returning \((\bar x,\ldots,\bar x)\). In a unit-cost arithmetic model, this projection uses \(O(md)\) arithmetic operations and, without structure-aware implicit storage, \(O(md)\) memory. Thus lifting incurs an \(m\)-fold ambient-dimension increase while leaving each component proximal computation separable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consensus lift replaces one d-vector by m copies, requiring md storage and linear-in-md averaging work unless the consensus structure is represented implicitly.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic and scalar storage each have unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim((\mathbb{R}^d)^m)=md\), and explicit consensus projection has time and storage complexity \(O(md)\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal consensus subspace in the product space.
Arithmetic mean of the lifted component vectors.

children.title: Centralized Consensus Splitting
children.top_down_role: Coordinator-mediated agreement and aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Centralized Consensus Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinator-mediated product-space formulation of finite-sum convex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a real Hilbert space. The centralized problem \(\min_{u\in\mathcal H}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(u)\) is equivalently lifted as \(\min_{x\in\mathcal H^m}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)+\iota_D(x)\), where \(D=\{(u,\ldots,u):u\in\mathcal H\}\). A coordinator implements the coupling resolvent through \(P_Dx=(\bar x,\ldots,\bar x)\), with \(\bar x=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\), while the resolvent of the separable term acts componentwise. Solutions correspond by \(x_i=u\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centralized consensus lifts one shared decision into local copies; a coordinator averages the copies, while local convex terms retain componentwise proximal steps.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(m\geq 2\).
Each \(f_i\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
The displayed problems attain their minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^\star\) solves the original problem if and only if \((u^\star,\ldots,u^\star)\) solves the lifted problem.

notation.meaning: Indicator function of the consensus subspace.
Orthogonal projection onto the consensus subspace.

children.title: Graph-Consensus Splitting
children.top_down_role: Edge and incidence formulations for decentralized agreement.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Consensus Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-operator representation of agreement on a fixed undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph with \(|V|=m\), choose an orientation, and let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{|E|\times m}\) be its incidence matrix. For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal H^m\), define \(K=B\otimes I_{\mathcal H}\). Then \(Kx=0\) precisely when \(x_i=x_j\) on every edge, and connectedness gives \(\ker K=D=\{(u,\ldots,u):u\in\mathcal H\}\). Consequently, \(\min_{u\in\mathcal H}\sum_i f_i(u)\) is equivalent to \(\min_{x\in\mathcal H^m}\sum_i f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(Kx=0\), exposing only edge-local consensus couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected undirected graph, annihilation by the lifted incidence operator is exactly global consensus, yielding an edge-local constrained formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
Each \(f_i:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(B\otimes I_{\mathcal H})=D\), so the shared-variable and graph-constrained problems are equivalent.

notation.meaning: Incidence operator lifted to the decision space.

children.title: Mixing-Matrix Splitting
children.top_down_role: Consensus coupling through mixing operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixing-Matrix Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus represented by the fixed-point space of a symmetric mixing operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be symmetric and doubly stochastic, with \(W_{ij}=0\) for nonadjacent distinct nodes, and suppose eigenvalue \(1\) is simple. On \(\mathcal H^m\), set \(\mathcal W=W\otimes I_{\mathcal H}\). Then \(\operatorname{Fix}(\mathcal W)=D\), and \(I-\mathcal W\) is self-adjoint positive semidefinite. Hence consensus may be imposed equivalently by \((I-\mathcal W)x=0\), by \((I-\mathcal W)^{1/2}x=0\), or by the normal-cone term \(N_D(x)\). These forms expose communication through multiplication by \(W\) while preserving the same feasible consensus set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric doubly stochastic mixing matrix with a simple unit eigenvalue represents consensus through its fixed-point space or the kernel of its disagreement operator.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}(W\otimes I_{\mathcal H})=\ker(I-W\otimes I_{\mathcal H})=D\).

notation.meaning: Mixing matrix lifted to the product Hilbert space.
Normal-cone operator of the consensus subspace.

children.title: Edge-Based Primal–Dual Splitting
children.top_down_role: Dual variables attached to network agreement constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Based Primal–Dual Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle representation with one dual agreement variable per oriented edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected undirected graph, \(K=B\otimes I_{\mathcal H}\) its lifted incidence operator, and \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\). The graph-consensus problem \(\min_x F(x)\) subject to \(Kx=0\) has Lagrangian \(L(x,y)=F(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle\), where \(y=(y_e)_{e\in E}\) assigns a dual variable to each oriented edge. Its primal-dual optimality system is \(0\in\partial F(x)+K^*y\) and \(0=Kx\). Splitting these two coupled operators yields node-local proximal evaluations of \(f_i\) and edge-local applications of \(K\) and \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-based primal–dual splitting attaches multipliers to incidence constraints, producing node-local proximal operations and edge-local primal–dual communication.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a saddle point exactly when \(0\in\partial F(x^\star)+K^*y^\star\) and \(Kx^\star=0\).

notation.meaning: Oriented incidence matrix of the network.
Dual multiplier for the agreement constraint on edge e.

children.title: Static Connected Networks
children.top_down_role: Fixed communication graphs and stationary mixing.

knowledge_statements.title: Static Connected Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed undirected communication regime with stationary contraction of disagreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a fixed connected undirected graph on \(m\) nodes, and let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be a nonnegative, graph-compatible, symmetric doubly stochastic matrix. With \(J=m^{-1}\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top\), the static mixing regime is contractive when \(\rho=\lVert W-J\rVert_2<1\). For symmetric \(W\), this is equivalent to eigenvalue \(1\) being simple and every other eigenvalue having modulus strictly below one. Under this condition, \(W^k\to J\), so repeated communication converges to arithmetic-average consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed connected network is a contractive static consensus regime when its symmetric doubly stochastic mixing matrix strictly contracts every disagreement direction; its powers then converge to arithmetic averaging.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, fixed, undirected, and connected.
\(W\geq0\) is graph-compatible, symmetric, and doubly stochastic.
Every nonunit eigenvalue of \(W\) has modulus strictly below one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert W-J\rVert_2<1\) and \(\lim_{k\to\infty}W^k=J\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto the scalar consensus subspace.
Spectral contraction factor on disagreement vectors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weakly connected, connected, and strongly-connected weighted networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-specific connectivity terminology for a fixed, weighted, possibly directed communication network; its use of “strongly-connected” includes an additional positive-self-loop condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weighted network is weakly connected if, for every pair of distinct vertices, a path with nonzero scaling weights exists in at least one of the two directions. It is connected if such paths exist in both directions, with possibly different forward and backward paths. It is strongly-connected in this terminology if it is connected and \(a_{kk}>0\) for at least one vertex \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted network is weakly connected when every pair of distinct vertices is linked by a nonzero-weight path in at least one direction. It is connected when such paths exist in both directions, possibly along different routes. In the source's terminology, it is strongly-connected when it is connected and at least one vertex has a positive-weight self-loop.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a fixed, weighted, possibly directed network}
\text{Connectivity paths use edges having nonzero scaling weights}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}\text{weakly connected}&\iff \forall k\ne\ell,\ (k\leadsto\ell)\lor(\ell\leadsto k),\\\text{connected}&\iff \forall k\ne\ell,\ (k\leadsto\ell)\land(\ell\leadsto k),\\\text{strongly-connected (source convention)}&\iff \text{connected and }\exists k\;a_{kk}>0.\end{aligned}

children.title: Time-Varying Network Interface
children.top_down_role: Changing communication structures, with detailed graph theory owned elsewhere.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Varying Network Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform mixing assumptions exposing changing communication graphs to a splitting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((W_k)_{k\geq0}\) be doubly stochastic mixing matrices on \(m\) agents, with positive diagonal entries and every positive entry at least \(\eta>0\). Let \(G_k\) contain the directed communication edges represented by \(W_k\). The time-varying interface condition requires an integer \(B\geq1\) such that, for every \(t\), the union \(\bigcup_{k=t}^{t+B-1}G_k\) is strongly connected. Under these uniform positivity and joint-connectivity conditions, there exist \(C<\infty\) and \(q\in(0,1)\) such that \(\lVert W_{k:t}-J\rVert\leq Cq^{k-t+1}\), where \(W_{k:t}=W_k\cdots W_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly positive, doubly stochastic mixing over repeatedly connected graph windows yields geometric contraction toward average consensus despite changing communication links.
assumptions_latex: Each \(W_k\) is doubly stochastic with positive diagonal and positive entries bounded below by \(\eta>0\).
Every window of \(B\) consecutive communication graphs has a strongly connected union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert W_{k:t}-m^{-1}\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top\rVert\leq Cq^{k-t+1}\) for some \(C<\infty\) and \(q\in(0,1)\).

notation.meaning: Ordered product of mixing matrices from time t through k.

children.title: Directed Network Topologies
children.top_down_role: Distributed splitting over asymmetric communication graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Network Topologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability condition for consensus communication on a fixed directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), information sent from node \(j\) to node \(i\) is represented by \((j,i)\in E\). The topology is strongly connected when, for every ordered pair \((i,j)\), a directed path leads from \(i\) to \(j\). If a nonnegative mixing matrix \(W\) has this sparsity pattern, a positive diagonal, and is irreducible, then \(W\) is primitive. Consequently, normalized row-stochastic or column-stochastic iterations have a unique positive Perron direction; whether this direction represents the arithmetic average depends on the chosen stochasticity convention and balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly connected directed topology gives a unique positive Perron direction, but connectivity alone does not guarantee arithmetic-average preservation.
assumptions_latex: \(W\geq0\) is graph-compatible, irreducible, and has positive diagonal.
\(W\) is normalized as either row-stochastic or column-stochastic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\) is primitive and has a unique positive Perron direction, up to normalization.

children.title: Unbalanced Mixing
children.top_down_role: Mixing processes whose weights do not preserve the desired network average.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbalanced Mixing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted-consensus bias produced by one-sided stochastic mixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be primitive and row-stochastic, and let \(\pi\) be its unique stationary probability vector satisfying \(\pi^\top W=\pi^\top\). Then \(W^k\to\mathbf 1\pi^\top\), so the iteration \(x^{k+1}=Wx^k\) converges to \(\mathbf 1\pi^\top x^0\). This limit is the arithmetic average \(\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top x^0/m\) for every initialization only when \(\pi=\mathbf 1/m\), equivalently when the primitive row-stochastic matrix is also column-stochastic. Thus strong connectivity without balance generally yields biased weighted consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primitive row-stochastic mixing reaches consensus, but generally at a stationary-distribution-weighted value rather than the arithmetic average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{k\to\infty}W^kx^0=\mathbf 1\pi^\top x^0\), which equals arithmetic-average consensus for all \(x^0\) if and only if \(\pi=\mathbf 1/m\).

notation.meaning: Stationary probability vector of the row-stochastic mixing matrix.
Stacked scalar agent state at iteration k.

children.title: Network Bias Correction
children.top_down_role: Interfaces compensating for asymmetry or imbalance in distributed information flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Bias Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Push-sum normalization for arithmetic averaging under column-stochastic directed mixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a primitive column-stochastic matrix \(A\), local vectors \(z_i^0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and weights \(s_i^0=1\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), update \(z^{k+1}=(A\otimes I_d)z^k\) and \(s^{k+1}=As^k\), then form the corrected local estimate \(x_i^{k+1}=z_i^{k+1}/s_i^{k+1}\). Because primitivity makes every denominator eventually positive and \(A^k\) has a common positive right Perron factor, that factor cancels in the ratio. In exact arithmetic, every node estimate converges to \(m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m z_j^0\). The output after any stopping time is the collection of ratios \((x_i^k)_{i=1}^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Push-sum propagates values and normalization weights through the same column-stochastic matrix; their ratios remove Perron bias and recover the arithmetic average.
assumptions_latex: Updates are performed in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{k\to\infty}x_i^k=m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m z_j^0\) for every node \(i\).

notation.meaning: Unnormalized value maintained by node i.
Positive normalization weight maintained by node i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The push-sum algorithm and convergence claim are plausible and precisely stated, but the record has no citation. An authoritative push-sum source with an exact theorem, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Directional Reachability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Connectivity limitations that prevent adequate propagation through directed networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Reachability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of global agreement when directed information flow has multiple closed classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the agents into two nonempty sets \(V_1,V_2\), and let \(W=\operatorname{diag}(W_1,W_2)\), where each \(W_r\) is primitive and row-stochastic. The associated directed graph has two closed strongly connected classes and is not strongly connected. Initialize \(x_i^0=a\) on \(V_1\) and \(x_i^0=b\neq a\) on \(V_2\). Then \(Wx^0=x^0\), so every mixing iterate preserves the two distinct values and global consensus is impossible. More generally, communication-only methods cannot force all nodes to depend on information that is directionally unreachable from them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a directed network contains separate closed communication classes, distinct class values remain distinct; no mixing-only scheme can produce global consensus.
assumptions_latex: \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) are nonempty and have no directed edges between their closed classes.
Each diagonal block \(W_r\) is primitive and row-stochastic.
The two classes start from distinct constant values \(a\neq b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W^kx^0=x^0\) for all \(k\), hence \(x^k\notin\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}\).

notation.meaning: A closed strongly connected node class.

children.title: Communication Inexactness Interface
children.top_down_role: Noise, compression, and quantization represented as splitting errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Inexactness Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error model connecting noisy, compressed, or quantized communication to operator splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be an averaged operator with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Model one inexact communication-and-splitting step by \(z^{k+1}=Tz^k+e^k\), where \(e^k\) aggregates transmission noise, compression error, quantization error, and inexact local aggregation. If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert e^k\rVert<\infty\), then the perturbations have finite total magnitude: the iterates are quasi-Fejér with respect to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\), the residuals satisfy \(\lVert z^k-Tz^k\rVert\to0\), and \((z^k)\) converges weakly to a fixed point of \(T\). In finite dimensions the convergence is strong.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication distortions can be aggregated as additive splitting errors; absolute summability preserves fixed-point convergence for averaged operators.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T\) is averaged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^k\rightharpoonup z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(\lVert z^k-Tz^k\rVert\to0\); in finite dimensions, \(z^k\to z^\star\).

notation.meaning: Aggregate additive communication and computation error.
Fixed-point set of the exact splitting operator.

children.title: Network Disconnection
children.top_down_role: Agreement failure caused by persistent separation of communicating agent groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Disconnection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of global consensus under a fixed disconnected communication graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(q\ge 2\) connected components, and let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be a nonnegative row-stochastic mixing matrix satisfying \(W_{ij}=0\) whenever agents \(i\) and \(j\) are in different components. After a simultaneous permutation of rows and columns, \(W=\operatorname{diag}(W_1,\ldots,W_q)\), so the eigenvalue \(1\) has multiplicity at least \(q\). If every \(W_r\) is primitive with stationary distribution \(\pi_r\), then \[W^k\longrightarrow \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{1}\pi_1^{\mathsf T},\ldots,\mathbf{1}\pi_q^{\mathsf T}).\] Thus mixing reaches only componentwise consensus and cannot recover global consensus unless all component consensus values coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disconnected network mixes independently within each component, so it generally reaches several componentwise consensus values rather than one global value.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a fixed disconnected graph with \(q\ge 2\) components.
\(W\) is nonnegative, row-stochastic, and respects the component structure.
Each diagonal block \(W_r\) is primitive for the stated limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W^k\) converges to a blockwise consensus projector, not generally to a rank-one global consensus projector.

notation.meaning: stationary distribution of component block r

knowledge_statements.title: Mixing Periodicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of pointwise consensus for irreducible periodic stochastic mixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be an irreducible row-stochastic matrix with stationary distribution \(\pi\) and period \(d>1\). Its peripheral spectrum contains the \(d\)-th roots of unity, so modes other than the stationary mode have modulus one. Consequently, the powers \(W^k\) do not converge to the consensus projector \(\mathbf{1}\pi^{\mathsf T}\); for some initial states \(x^0\), the sequence \(x^{k+1}=Wx^k\) oscillates among cyclic classes. Although suitable Cesàro averages may converge to \(\mathbf{1}\pi^{\mathsf T}x^0\), the unaveraged mixing iteration does not attain pointwise consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An irreducible but periodic mixing matrix can perpetually cycle, preventing its ordinary iterates from converging to consensus even though time averages may converge.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is a finite-dimensional irreducible row-stochastic matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W^k\not\to\mathbf{1}\pi^{\mathsf T}\), and some trajectories \(x^{k+1}=Wx^k\) fail to converge.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias caused by nonuniform stationary weights in directed or unbalanced mixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be primitive and row-stochastic, with unique stationary probability vector \(\pi\), so \(W^k\to\mathbf{1}\pi^{\mathsf T}\). For the mixing iteration \(x^{k+1}=Wx^k\), every agent therefore converges to \(\pi^{\mathsf T}x^0\). The desired arithmetic-average consensus is \(n^{-1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}x^0\). These values agree for every initial state if and only if \(\pi=n^{-1}\mathbf{1}\), equivalently, under row stochasticity, \(W\) is also column-stochastic. Otherwise the limiting consensus is systematically weighted and hence biased relative to uniform aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primitive row-stochastic mixing reaches consensus, but nonuniform stationary weights make the consensus value a weighted rather than arithmetic average.
assumptions_latex: The intended aggregate is the uniform arithmetic average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The consensus is unbiased for every \(x^0\) if and only if \(\pi=n^{-1}\mathbf{1}\).

notation.meaning: unique stationary probability vector of W

knowledge_statements.title: Agreement–Optimality Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete demonstration that zero consensus error does not imply global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider two agents on \(\mathbb{R}\) with convex differentiable objectives \(f_1(x)=	frac12(x-1)^2\) and \(f_2(x)=	frac12(x+1)^2\). The consensus-constrained problem minimizes \(f_1(x_1)+f_2(x_2)\) subject to \(x_1=x_2\), and its unique solution is \(x_1=x_2=0\). The point \((x_1,x_2)=(2,2)\) has zero disagreement because \(x_1-x_2=0\), but \(

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents may agree exactly at a nonoptimal point; consensus residuals must therefore be paired with an optimality or stationarity residual.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are the displayed convex differentiable functions on \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \((x_1,x_2)=(2,2)\), agreement holds but the aggregate first-order condition fails.
